name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Head Start providers weigh Trump administration changes
description: Missouri’s Head Start programs reach only about 13% of the infants and toddlers eligible for them. The Trump administration says part of the problem is the program’s rulebook in Missouri and nationwide. Federal officials want to eliminate more than 1,400 requirements governing Head Start, arguing that less money spent complying with Washington’s rules could[...]
text:
The federal government says deregulating Head Start could save billions of dollars and open classrooms to more children. Missouri providers say other issues contribute to the strain (Vaughn Wheat/The Beacon).Missouri’s Head Start programs reach only about 13% of the infants and toddlers eligible for them.
The Trump administration says part of the problem is the program’s rulebook in Missouri and nationwide.
Federal officials want to eliminate more than 1,400 requirements governing Head Start, arguing that less money spent complying with Washington’s rules could help programs save money and serve more children.
Missouri Head Start leaders agree — somewhat. There are too many children they can’t serve, they say, and there are some federal rules they could live without.
Still, they’re uncertain about all of the things Washington wants to eliminate, and aren’t sure the proposed changes will actually help them get more kids through the door.
Head Start was established nationwide in 1965 as a part of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s War on Poverty. Head Start and Early Head Start were designed to serve as a child development program to help children from low-income families with their child’s educational, social, health, nutritional and even psychological needs. More than 40 million children have gone through the program since.
Nationwide, about 800,000 children are enrolled on an annual basis, and nearly 15,000 of those are from Missouri.
Across the state, 5,000 of those kids were enrolled in Early Head Start, including infants and children up to 3 years old, while the other 10,000 were enrolled in Head Start preschool programs.
Yet the programs reach only 13% of eligible Missouri infants and toddlers and 27% of eligible preschoolers.
The Trump administration’s proposals, which it says will help free up funds to expand enrollment, mark the most significant rewrite of Head Start’s rules in decades. The Office of Head Start has opened a 60-day comment period for the public to share their thoughts.
The proposal would eliminate many detailed federal requirements and give states and local providers greater control over how Head Start operates. It doesn’t expressly cut funding, though it would cap administrative spending at 5%, down from the current 15%.
For those running Head Start in Missouri, though, it’s unclear whether the federal rules are what’s actually keeping children out of the program. And if the universal standards are removed, they’re concerned about what children may lose as a result.
“I’m not opposed to reducing regulation,” said Kimberly Shinn-Brown, who has worked in Head Start for more than three decades and now directs Ozark Area Community Action Corp.’s Head Start offerings at more than 20 centers across southwest Missouri.
“Let us take away some of the regulations that don’t move us forward in terms of quality, in terms of outcomes for children, outcomes for families, outcomes for communities. Yeah, let’s strip those away,” Shinn-Brown said.
 Do fewer rules mean more kids in Missouri Head Start classrooms? 

Ashley Phillips, the executive director of the Community Action Partnership of Greater St. Joseph, said some of the federal regulations can be redundant with state rules.
“The current rules we have are very prescriptive,” Phillips said.
Things like CPR or first aid training for staff overlap with Missouri’s requirements. Federal rules also lay out timeline requirements for things like home visits or health screenings, which can be difficult to meet in rural areas with fewer providers, Phillips said.
Head Start programs currently must complete sensory, hearing and vision screenings within 45 days of a child starting a program and verify things like health insurance enrollment within 30 days.
“There are sometimes … requirements that are very difficult to meet because it is hard to find providers in our community,” Phillips said. “So we find ourselves in a situation where we are out of compliance, not because we don’t know that it’s important, but because finding providers is difficult for Medicaid.”
Phillips sees potential for the changes to free programs up from duplicative or limiting rules.
But Kasey Lawson, the director of Head Start programs for the Mid-America Regional Council, said federal regulations aren’t necessarily what keeps its programs in Jackson, Platte and Clay counties from growing.
“I would definitely say it’s available space for us,” Lawson said.
Many of their facilities are at capacity, and finding qualified staff who are dedicated to early childhood development can be difficult.
“It’s not just about having a person in the classroom,” Lawson said. “It’s really having a qualified person to work in early childhood.”
The numbers support what Lawson sees.
Missouri public schools reported nearly 500 vacant early childhood education positions in the 2025-2026 school year, one of the state’s three largest certification-area shortages.
The federal government estimates the proposed changes could save more than $2 billion. But W. Steven Barnett, an economist and the director of the National Institute for Early Education Research at Rutgers University, questions how the government can project so much in savings while also predicting more children will enroll in the program.
“You can have one of those two, but you can’t have both,” Barnett said.
 How is Head Start different from childcare? 

The proposed changes don’t just eliminate paperwork. In some cases, they would allow Head Start programs to rely on Missouri’s childcare standards in place of stricter federal requirements.
Barnett says that’s where deregulation risks changing the nature of Head Start.
“It’s a child development program,” Barnett said. “It’s not a childcare program.”
State standards establish minimum requirements for childcare, while Head Start is intended to prepare children from low-income households for school and provides comprehensive health screenings and employment support for families.
“What the states require is the baseline for minimum health and safety,” Shinn-Brown said. “It is not an indicator of quality by any measure.”
Classroom size is one example. The proposal would eliminate federal Head Start staff-to-child ratios and group size requirements, allowing programs to follow state licensing standards.
For 4-year-olds in Missouri, the standards are the same. But the difference is larger for younger children. Under current Early Head Start rules, the program limits classes for children under 3 years old to a maximum group size of eight or nine kids, with a staff ratio of one adult for every four toddlers.
“If we leave that requirement in the dust and we adopt the state licensing requirements,” Shinn-Brown said, “we would potentially be serving 16 2-year-olds in a group with two teachers.”
A randomized study Barnett co-authored found that preschoolers in classes of 15 had more one-on-one interactions with teachers and more literacy gains than kids in classes of 20, though they found no significant difference in vocabulary or math.
“With Head Start,” Barnett said, “if you want it to be effective, give teachers fewer kids, not more kids.”
Providers are also worried about what happens when detailed federal requirements around health and developmental services change or disappear.
The proposal doesn’t eliminate Head Start’s underlying obligation to support children’s health. Instead, it would wipe many of the federal rules telling programs how to meet those obligations.
Barnett sees that as a potential upside.
“The regulatory changes don’t mean that Head Start still doesn’t make sure that kids get those things,” he said. “It just means there’s not 100 pages telling us how to do that.”
He pointed to programs devoting time and staff to documenting screenings, referrals and other services for federal compliance.
“If that’s what you’re getting rid of, I say good riddance,” Barnett said.
Shinn-Brown, however, said her organization’s screenings are constantly identifying children with unmet health needs.
“That happens all the time, all the time,” Shinn-Brown said.
“We know that the healthcare system is fractured. There’s not another kind of one-stop shop that coordinates and connects families and young children with the care, support, resources and information that they need,” she said.
 If rules do change, what happens next for Head Start in Missouri? 

The proposed rules aren’t final, and programs could have the opportunity to shape new standards and requirements moving forward.
Phillips said her program could maintain standards beyond what Washington asks.
That could mean “internal policies that go above and beyond what the standard requires,” she said.
Missouri providers don’t dispute that Head Start could use reforms or that more families should have access.
What’s unclear is whether eliminating hundreds of federal requirements will truly address the constraints providers identify — such as space, staffing, healthcare provider shortages — or simply give them more control over the services they already provide.
“Fewer regulations can’t mean fewer results,” Shinn-Brown said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: The influencing power of political labels, whether they are accurate or not
description: In the weeks and months ahead, as we approach the midterm elections, we will hear a lot of political labels used to frame, define, categorize and box in candidates and their affiliated political groups — positively and negatively. What label defines you? Are you a Democrat, Republican, independent, Libertarian, Green, progressive, socialist, liberal, conserv[...]
text:
(wildpixel/iStock Images)In the weeks and months ahead, as we approach the midterm elections, we will hear a lot of political labels used to frame, define, categorize and box in candidates and their affiliated political groups — positively and negatively.
What label defines you?
Are you a Democrat, Republican, independent, Libertarian, Green, progressive, socialist, liberal, conservative, leftist, rightist, extreme leftist, extreme rightist, closet communist or some combination thereof?
Such labeling is no small affair. The effects can be powerful and defining.
I propose there is a better one we can aspire to as Americans.
But the latest combination label, and the one that seems to be taking on a life of its own, is democratic socialist. It has gained currency for two main reasons: as the Democratic Party tries to find its footing and a path forward this election season, and as candidates who openly identify as democratic socialists — or who have been defined that way by their opponents — win races or come close to winning them.
Most notable are the 2025 election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the Michigan U.S. Senate primary victory of Abdul El-Sayed and the near win of Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary.
Being a democratic socialist has become all the rage — both positively and negatively, depending on which side of the political contest you are on.
All the more reason for us, as decision-makers, to have a clear understanding of what these labels mean and what we can expect if we elect someone who identifies with or embraces one or the other.
Major initiatives that have defined, put at risk or killed policies and programs affecting the quality of life in America have come from someone we elected who represented and epitomized one of those labels.
What labels identified the leaders who created Medicare, Social Security, Medicaid, managed health care (HMOs, PPOs), voting rights and equal rights?
So, what labels define the candidates seeking your vote, and do you understand the differences?
For example, there are real differences among a democratic socialist, a socialist and a communist, whatever an opponent might lead you to believe.
What does it mean to be a democratic socialist? For the democratic socialist, democracy is non-negotiable. Democratic socialists support free and fair elections, separation of powers, freedom of the press and the right to protest. They do not seek to abolish capitalism but to regulate and correct its excesses so that it serves the broader public rather than a privileged few.
What does it mean to be a socialist? A socialist, on the other hand, holds that sharing ownership of the means of production across society would raise people’s quality of life. Socialists favor free access to basic necessities such as food, housing and health care, and some regard guaranteed employment as a human right. They differ among themselves over how to prevent the harms they attribute to unchecked capitalism, including poor treatment of workers and inequality.
What does it mean to be a communist? A communist believes wealth should be shared so that no one is too poor, no one is too rich and everyone has enough to survive and live well. Under communism, people work together to produce and distribute what they need, such as food, clothing and entertainment. Communists support some form of collective ownership, on the theory that if everyone is a part owner of the factories and farms, everyone holds equal rights to what those enterprises produce — and equal political rights in governing.
In this current political climate, it is important that we clearly understand what each of these labels means and not be confused by them. Depending on who is using them and how, the meaning can be negative, positive or altogether misrepresented and misused.
Most important, we need to understand which label accurately defines the candidates seeking our support and our vote in the upcoming midterm elections.
There is another overarching label that we as Missourians and Americans should be very concerned about: the autocrat.
What does the autocrat believe? An autocrat gains and maintains power through political repression of any opposition and co-optation of other influential or powerful members of society. The general public is controlled through indoctrination and propaganda, and an autocracy may attempt to legitimize itself in the eyes of the public through appeals to political ideology, religion, birthright or foreign hostility. Some autocracies establish legislatures, unfair elections or show trials to further exercise control while presenting the appearance of democracy.
Do such actions and behavior sound familiar when you think about how ballot measures have been presented for passage in our state? What about the executive orders and other measures to restrict citizen participation, and to change and defy laws, institutions and traditions, that are playing out on the national stage?
Aside from the labels that will be deployed in elections across the country in the coming weeks and months, one demands that we understand it and develop a defense against it, because it is the most destructive and lasting of all. It is the autocrat that poses the greatest threat to an America whose democratic governing structure, laws, values and principles have been the envy of societies across the world.
Given the negative direction and baggage associated with some of the prevailing labels commanding our attention today, why not give serious consideration to a new one that could be more fitting and inclusive, and that would bode well for a future America: the democratic independent.
What does the democratic independent believe? As I see it, a democratic independent is neither a Democrat nor a Republican — and does not adhere to any of their derivatives or bastardizations — but believes fervently in democracy and supports and votes for people and policies consistent with the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, which formed and sustain this nation and all of its citizens.
To be labeled or not to be labeled?
Which label accurately describes where we are headed, and who is trying to take us there?
These are the paramount questions.
Our answers — and the actions that follow — will be defining.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ, feds sue commission to protect drinking water from contamination
description: The Passaic Valley Water Commission has failed to cover three reservoirs to protect treated drinking water from contamination, a new lawsuit says.
text:
Federal and state authorities sued the Passaic Valley Water Commission on Aug. 12, 2026, accusing the public water system of longstanding noncompliance for failing to cover three reservoirs that provide drinking water to about 800,000 people. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)The state and the feds have teamed up to compel a North Jersey water system to cover three reservoirs that provide drinking water to nearly a million people.
The U.S. Department of Justice and the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office accuse the Passaic Valley Water Commission in a new federal lawsuit of violating the Safe Drinking Water Act by failing to properly protect and treat water from the Great Notch Reservoir, Levine Reservoir, and New Street Reservoir to ensure it’s free of pathogens and safe to consume.
The public water system serves about 800,000 people in Paterson, Clifton, Passaic, Prospect Park, Lodi, North Arlington, and Woodland Park, and 22 wholesale customers (municipalities and independent water companies) in Passaic, Bergen, Essex, Hudson, and Morris counties.
It treats water at the Little Falls Water Treatment Plant and distributes “finished” water that’s considered ready for human consumption to the three reservoirs downstream, according to the lawsuit. But because those reservoirs aren’t covered, stormwater runoff, animal waste, and other contaminants can taint them, the lawsuit charges.
The commission has failed to fully address the problem since at least early 2009, when it entered into a consent order with the state Department of Environmental Protection that established a phased schedule for compliance, the lawsuit says. But the reservoirs remain uncovered despite that and subsequent enforcement orders, it says.
That failure has led to periodic stormwater contamination and elevated lead levels, including a six-week water advisory stemming from Hurricane Ida flooding in 2021, the lawsuit says. It also leaves people who drink the water vulnerable to viruses and parasites including cryptosporidium and Giardia lamblia, which can cause diarrhea and other gut illnesses, the lawsuit says.
The feds and the state are seeking a judge’s order requiring the commission to cover the reservoirs or treat the water to ensure it complies with the Safe Drinking Water Act. They also want a judge to order the commission to notify the public of the problem, implement unspecified public health protections, and pay penalties for every day of noncompliance.
The commission did not respond to the New Jersey Monitor’s requests for comment.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Following Pillen’s budget memo, Nebraska leaders detail plans to cut staff, increase fees
authors: Jackie Ourada, Nebraska Public Media News, Noelle Annonen, Nebraska Public Media News
description: Records obtained Friday by Nebraska Public Media News show state agencies are using a number of strategies – ranging from cutting positions to potentially having employees sleep in cars rather than in hotel rooms – in response to Gov. Jim Pillen’s memo that said his State Budget Division would be withholding at least 5% of […]
text:
The top of the Nebraska Capitol Mar. 19, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)Records obtained Friday by Nebraska Public Media News show state agencies are using a number of strategies – ranging from cutting positions to potentially having employees sleep in cars rather than in hotel rooms – in response to Gov. Jim Pillen’s memo that said his State Budget Division would be withholding at least 5% of state agencies’ monthly allotments. The governor also implemented a hiring freeze on most state positions.
The governor’s order to state leaders in July followed a string of lower-than-expected tax receipts, which have continued to balloon the state’s financial hole. Nebraska is in a $208 million budget deficit and faces the next biennium with an already $840 million deficit on top of that. That’s despite lawmakers spending the past legislative session working to close budget deficits. A lack of funds prompted Pillen to release his memo in July.
In the submitted proposals, some departments offered up staffing reductions and fee increases to meet the conditions of the memo. Pillen’s office said all agency proposals are “hypothetical fiscal restraint considerations” and still require “substantial analysis” before being considered by the governor.
But not all agencies complied with the order. Many shared ideas for budget cuts but emphasized that staff have already been working to cut where they can for some time.
A few of the state’s largest agencies, such as the Department of Health and Human Services, the Nebraska State Patrol, the Department of Administrative Services and the Department of Motor Vehicles, did not submit budget plans, according to documents provided to Nebraska Public Media News by the Department of Administrative Services on Friday.
Departments detail their proposed changes
Significant changes could come to homestead exemptions, based on the preliminary budget cut proposals submitted by the Department of Revenue. Nebraska property owners eligible for a homestead exemption would pay at least 10% of their property taxes before credits are applied. That’s according to the department’s response that proposes narrowing homestead eligibility requirements. Previously, credits for the seniors and disabled people eligible for homestead exemptions were based on income, with the lowest earners receiving a 100% exemption.
The Department of Revenue also proposed closing its offices in North Platte and Norfolk.
In the report submitted about the Governor’s Emergency Fund, Military Department leaders wrote that the pot of money used to respond to natural disasters can’t withstand more reductions. The emergency fund continues to diminish as the state works on paying back money owed on former and current disasters, such as the 2019 floods. The report shows that only $1 million will be in the emergency fund for fiscal year 2027-28, assuming no new disasters take place.
The Department of Correctional Services said it will cut $10 million in general fund spending “while not impacting services and programs within the facility,” but will offset that spending by using $4 million from cash funds, such as the reentry fund and the correctional facilities fund. Corrections staff also reported that they will review all positions to see if the assigned duties can be absorbed by other staff members.
Agencies proposing staffing, operational cuts
The State Fire Marshal plans to cut positions, including a full-time deputy position and an accountant, while limiting training opportunities for staff.
The Nebraska Board of Barber Examiners would cut back on travel costs by doing fewer inspections, but when employees do travel, the agency proposed they sleep in their cars instead of getting hotel rooms. The State Electrical Division will reissue uniforms so long as they are clean and in good condition.
The Nebraska Commission for the Blind and Visually Impaired plans to discontinue a pilot Support Services Provider program for the DeafBlind community and focus instead on existing programs. Funding cuts will also affect paid public service announcements and community engagement efforts.
The Nebraska Public Employee Retirement Services is implementing software that will pre-answer any calls to reduce necessary call center resources. It will also reduce in-person seminars for members, even though educational outreach is required under statute.
The Tourism Commission will eliminate positions and reduce passport costs by lessening printing and increasing passport pickup events to lower postage costs.

Nebraska’s brand committee noted that it has the lowest number of employees in the committee’s history and is trying to keep both staff and travel costs low.
“Due to the many changes during the last Legislative session, we will be securitizing our field positions,” Brand committee staff wrote.
The Nebraska State College System plans to freeze 14 full-time positions, which would save more than $1 million, and leave 12 other positions vacant.
The Nebraska State Historical Society plans to cut around $240,000 by cutting positions. It also proposes increasing membership dues and History Nebraska Magazine Subscription rates, from $35 to $70, both of which have not been adjusted since 2018. The society will be raising fees, including Nebraska History Museum admission fees from $5 to $7 for adults and from $3 to $4 for kids. More fees will be raised at the Ford Conservation Center.
Agencies proposing fee increases
The Department of Insurance is raising licensing fees, anticipating collecting $2.2 million a year.
The Department of Labor plans to raise contractor registration fees to $40, up from $25. The department said the increase will raise an estimated $500,000. But the department will also ask the Legislature to increase that fee to $100 for a year, which could bring in as much as $2 million. Staff wrote that this is consistent with what surrounding states charge.
The Department of Water, Energy, and Environment said it will be able to raise $325,000 in increased fees to replace general funds from the state, although it did not clarify what fees it would increase.
The Department of Banking and Finance proposed raising fees on broker-dealers, investment advisors and others, expecting to bring in more than $3 million over the next few years.
The Department of Agriculture plans to rely on cash funds, which generally are funded by money raised from fees, to cover around $280,000 in staff salaries or state veterinarian costs.
State auditor takes aim at Pillen’s strategy
Mike Foley, auditor of public accounts, contributed the longest refusal in the cache of documents containing responses to Pillen’s memo. Over the course of five pages, Foley listed ways in which his office uncovered millions of dollars in government spending misuse. He pointed to his reports on discovering state employees using state vehicles for personal use, ineligible former state employees claiming benefits, and misuse of funds by non-profits.
Foley said some state agency responses to his office’s findings show they haven’t taken advantage of fixing systemic financial costs.
“Most disconcerting of all, perhaps, was the reaction of DHHS’ middle management to the WIC audit letter,” Foley wrote. “Rather than responding directly to the issues presented, DHHS managers enlisted Federal bureaucrats in an unsuccessful attempt to dissuade this office from publicizing some of the more startling details contained in the document.”
Foley made a case that his department works to save taxpayer dollars, and that a 5% budget cut would cost his office at least three auditors.
“Such a ‘penny-wise and pound-foolish’ approach to budgeting would unquestionably jeopardize countless taxpayer dollars by dramatically increasing their risk of undetected (much less unprevented) loss or misappropriation,” Foley wrote in his letter. He added that Pillen’s call for fiscal restraint is prudent and timely.
Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s office also declined to propose any reductions, arguing that the department already looks for opportunities to reduce spending and has carefully evaluated expenses.
This story was originally published by Nebraska Public Media News, a network of local reporters working with a National Public Radio station based in Lincoln.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Investigation ordered by Oklahoma governor will demonize Muslim people, expert says
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Gov. Kevin Stitt’s latest effort targeting Muslim groups is “political theater” meant to tap into a broader undercurrent of Islamophobia and create unwarranted fears during an election year, experts said. They said Stitt’s demand that state resources be used to investigate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR, is similar to prev[...]
text:
Gov. Kevin Stitt delivers his final State of the State Address on Feb. 2, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Gov. Kevin Stitt’s latest effort targeting Muslim groups is “political theater” meant to tap into a broader undercurrent of Islamophobia and create unwarranted fears during an election year, experts said.
They said Stitt’s demand that state resources be used to investigate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR, is similar to previous efforts nationally and in other Republican states. It comes amid a hotly contested election cycle where a Muslim American recently won a high-profile primary in Michigan and the GOP is looking to justify why the U.S. is at war with Iran. 
Stitt’s executive order earlier this month requires that the state’s Department of Public Safety and the Homeland Security office conduct an investigation to determine if CAIR or the Muslim Brotherhood present any terrorism-related threats to Oklahoma. It also seeks to ensure taxpayer-funded state resources do not support or enable terrorism and also requires the state agencies to “take lawful preventive and investigative action supported by the resulting intelligence.” 
Pauline Jones, a political science professor at University of Michigan and the former chair of the school’s Islamic Studies program, said CAIR is likely being targeted because of its success in advocating for the civil rights of Muslim Americans, the group’s sole focus. 
“There’s a paper trail of trying to undermine CAIR, and again, I think maybe it’s because it’s such a prominent, successful civil rights and activist organization,” Jones said.
Investigations and terrorist designations undercut the ability of CAIR to fundraise and function, she said. 
Some branches of the Muslim Brotherhood, the second group mentioned in Stitt’s order, have already been designated a terrorist organization by the federal government. The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in Egypt in the 1920s, is an Islamic political movement.
There is no evidence of CAIR being tied to the Brotherhood or terrorist groups, Jones said. CAIR has repeatedly condemned acts of terror and any violence against civilians. 
She said anti-Muslim efforts such as this create “fear that’s nonsensical, that doesn’t need to exist” and demonize the organization.
But Jones said Oklahoma’s executive order comes amid a tense midterm election year with Democrats seeking to regain the majority in Congress. She pointed to Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim American, who recently won Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate primary and would be the first Muslim senator if elected in November. 
Republicans are also “scrambling” to justify the war with Iran, Jones said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I think the Iranian war, that context is really important for this because it’s once again why we should fear Muslims and why we should demonize them,” she said. “Or that they shouldn’t have political power and representation in the United States. And there’s a sense, I think, among many Republicans that that narrative will be successful in the context of this war with Iran.”
Governor orders Oklahoma investigation 
Tevis Hillis, a spokesperson with Stitt’s office, did not answer questions about what Oklahoma-specific evidence or events suggest that CAIR presents a threat to the state. Hillis referred comment to state Sen. Christi Gillespie, R-Broken Arrow, despite executive orders being Stitt’s responsibility. 
Gillespie was not consulted about the executive order, has not reviewed it and therefore is not able to comment on it, a Senate spokesperson said. 
Earlier this year, the Republican governors in Texas and Florida have issued executive orders designating CAIR as a terrorist organization in their state. Those designations have been met with lawsuits. There was also a congressional bill in 2025 asking for CAIR to be designated as a terrorist organization that “didn’t go anywhere,” Jones said.
Oklahoma also has a history of Islamophobic rhetoric from public officials. 
In 2007, over a dozen state lawmakers returned gifted copies of the Quran to the advisory council that had given them to legislators. Muslim advocacy days at the state Capitol have been met with protesters and a need for increased security. 
This year, a Republican lawmaker proposed a bill to ban Sharia law in Oklahoma but it ultimately failed to move forward. Voters in 2010 had passed a state question banning Oklahoma courts from considering Sharia law in its decisions, but a federal court struck it down in 2012 because it discriminated against a specific religion. 
Construction of a proposed mosque in Broken Arrow was denied by the local city council over zoning requirements. The denial has since been met with a lawsuit from CAIR and an investigation from the Department of Justice. 
Targeting CAIR
Stitt’s executive order references a November order from President Donald Trump that designates certain chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist organizations. The Oklahoma order calls the Palestinian group Hamas a product of the Muslim Brotherhood and states that it has committed acts of terror. It also states that CAIR has been designated as a terror group by the United Arab Emirates, an action that at the time was rejected by the U.S. government. 
“Oklahoma will not turn a blind eye to organizations or networks that may support terrorism,” Stitt said in a news release. 
CAIR’s Oklahoma chapter said the civil rights organization has a history of protecting free speech, religious freedom and equality and has pursued it through successful lawsuits. 
“Our successful civil rights work in Oklahoma is exactly why Gov. Stitt is targeting our organization with debunked conspiracy theories,” CAIR said in a statement. “We look forward to continuing our civil rights work in Oklahoma and proving once again that the Constitution is stronger than any politician’s bigotry.”
Stephen Nemeth, a professor at Oklahoma State University with a focus on international relations and terrorism, said while ordering an investigation “sounds menacing,” it’s more of a “convenient bogeyman.”
“It’s probably just a way to kind of gin up maybe some activism or voter interest,” he said. “… It may be a way to drive up support for one segment of the Republican Party as opposed to another. So if you can tie someone as being sympathetic to the side that they’re going after, then you can gin up support for the more conservative side.”
Just the suggestion of an investigation is enough for most Americans to think there is something wrong or a reason to be suspicious, Nemeth said. 
“So people are going to become suspicious, and then they’re going to maybe think about ‘Who’s a politician that is anti these things that I find scary,’ and it might help to drive support for that particular person,” he said. 
While Nemeth said he doesn’t expect anything of importance to be found in an investigation, even a low-level individual with any ties or relation to someone with ties to terrorism will be enough reason for some people to “justify” the order.

title: Wyoming’s primary election live: The consequences of today’s election
description:
Follow along as WyoFile brings you the latest news from Wyoming's 2026 primary election. 
The post Wyoming’s primary election live: The consequences of today’s election appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
4:30 a.m. — The consequences of today’s election
Wondering how much is at stake in today’s election? By the end of the night, Wyomingites may have a pretty good idea who their next governor, secretary of state, schools superintendent, U.S. Senator and U.S. representative will be. Republicans so dominate Wyoming politics that whoever wins today will be the overwhelming favorite in November. (In 2018, for example, the AP called the governor’s race for then-candidate Mark Gordon minutes after the polls closed.)
Tonight could also decide who will control the statehouse for the next two years. Right now, the hard-line Wyoming Freedom Caucus controls the House, but a more traditional (or more moderate, depending on how you look at it) faction of the GOP controls the Senate. During this year’s legislative session, the Senate defeated many of the House’s more aggressive budget cuts to the University of Wyoming and the Wyoming Business Council. So today’s primary could have a huge influence on how those institutions and others fare financially over the next few years.
— Joshua Wolfson

4:25 a.m. — Need some last-minute voting info? Check out WyoFile’s election guide.
Primary day is finally here, and if you’re still trying to decide who to vote for, we can help. WyoFile’s election guide features biographical information and answers from dozens of candidates, from the governor’s office to statehouse races. Polls will be open until 7 p.m. Not sure where to vote? The Wyoming Secretary of State’s poll locator can help.

title: Colorado River crisis threatens crops, not Wyoming’s dam plans, experts say
description:
Feds’ new plan doesn’t resolve crop-threatening water shortage and likely will end up in court, two professors reckon.
The post Colorado River crisis threatens crops, not Wyoming’s dam plans, experts say appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A federal drought plan for the Colorado River and its tributaries in Wyoming shouldn’t stop Wyoming from building a new dam and reservoir in Carbon County, two Western water experts say.
The Bureau of Reclamation plan for the sweeping basin focuses on maintaining enough water in Lake Powell and Lake Mead to generate electricity and prevent degradation of critical infrastructure, professors from Utah and Arizona said last week.
The 10-year framework to manage water storage and releases in the complex seven-state, two-nation system seeks to balance predictability and flexibility in two-year increments. It also acknowledges that the government has little to no authority over water use in headwater states Wyoming, Utah, Colorado and New Mexico, said Sarah Porter, the director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University’s Morrison Institute.
“One way of reading the final environmental impact statement,” Porter said, “is the Bureau’s determination that it doesn’t really have any authority to limit water use in the headwaters.”
A controversial dam proposed on the West Fork of Battle Creek, which flows into the Little Snake River, above, and the Colorado River could still be built despite a drought that prevents Lake Powell and Lake Mead from filling. (EcoFlight)
Drought will likely cause agricultural stress in Arizona, Nevada and California, threatening the supply of winter vegetables and possibly other crops, she said.
“We probably won’t be eating as many salads,” she said, because Arizona is where winter lettuce is harvested. “It’s all grown in Yuma.”
More important for Wyoming might be that the Bureau of Reclamation’s final environmental impact statement recognizes the independence of headwater, or upper-division, states to essentially use water as they see fit. Efforts to conserve water in the Upper Basin “are not within the scope of this EIS,” the federal document states.
So while farmers downstream may see their traditional supplies cut, Wyoming forges ahead with plans for the 10,000-acre-foot West Fork dam and reservoir in Carbon County where 6,000 acre-feet a year would be poured onto fields for late-season irrigation on ranches.
Energy equation
The Bureau is imposing the plan after the seven states failed to agree on how to share Colorado River flows as drought crimps traditional allotments that were based on too-rosy estimates.
“We have the lowest reservoir storage we’ve ever seen,” said David Rosenberg, a Utah State University professor and water researcher. “We have very low inflows.”
He and Porter spoke in a Zoom webinar hosted by SciLine, a nonprofit that connects reporters with scientists.
The two called the Bureau of Reclamation plan a decision-making framework for distributing water in the three Lower Basin states — initially for two years.
“It doesn’t place the basin on a path to stabilizing the system at all,” Porter said. “It doesn’t resolve conflict at all. It doesn’t achieve the [long-term] things that the basin really needs at this point.”





Click to enlarge: The Colorado River Basin, shown as upper and lower basins. (Bureau of Reclamation)

But the plan is “a very clear statement,” Rosenberg said, “of how they’re going to protect infrastructure.”
That infrastructure includes the two major dams, associated power plants and canals that would become useless, even degraded, if the water levels in Powell and Mead drop below critical levels. With the plan, Rosenberg said, the Bureau states: “We’re still going to be generating hydropower.”
Powell’s Glen Canyon and Mead’s Hoover dams can generate some $443 million of market-price electricity a year when operating fully, according to calculations from the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Energy Information Administration. To keep those two reservoirs flush, the Bureau will release water from Wyoming’s Flaming Gorge Reservoir and from Colorado’s Blue Mesa Reservoir and New Mexico’s and Colorado’s Navajo Reservoir.
Beyond that, the Bureau’s plan targets the three Lower Basin states for reductions, depending on water in the river system and reservoirs.
Headwater states largely rely on stream and river flows determined by spring runoff. The at-risk region in Wyoming includes the Green River and its tributaries and the Little Snake River in Carbon County.
In contrast, the Lower Basin “gets all of its water, Colorado River water, from the reservoirs,” Porter said. It’s a lot more complicated to curtail Upper Basin use “than simply to not deliver water out of a reservoir,” she said. “And that’s a sore point with the Lower Basin.”
The two professors predicted a fight. “We expect they’ll be challenging this administrative process,” Porter said of the lower division states’ reaction to the Bureau’s EIS.
Compact call coming
There’s more on the horizon too.
“I also expect that within the next year and a half, or maybe two years, there will be what we call a compact call,” Porter said, “a demand from the Lower Basin for water that the Lower Basin contends the Upper Basin is obligated to deliver.
“That challenge will occur in the United States Supreme Court and that could take 10, 20, 30 years.”
Under the 1922 Colorado River Compact and associated agreements, the upper division states can’t diminish the flow from Lake Powell below 7.5 million acre-feet annually, calculated on a 10-year rolling average. That’s half what engineers originally calculated the watershed would produce; half belonging to the headwater states, half to the Lower Basin. That estimate is now considered to have been exuberantly optimistic.
“…[W]ithin the next year and a half, or maybe two years, there will be what we call a compact call, a demand from the Lower Basin for water that the Lower Basin contends the Upper Basin is obligated to deliver.”Sarah Porter
“We really need to figure out a way collectively to be reducing demand in the Colorado River by at least 3 million acre-feet out of the 15 million,” Porter said, “and that probably can’t all fall on the Lower Basin.
“The Lower Basin,” she said, “didn’t agree to be junior to the Upper Basin.”
If Upper Basin states don’t deliver the 7.5 million acre-feet past the Lee Ferry gauging station just below Lake Powell, headwaters curtailment will begin, starting with the most recent, or junior, water-right holders.
Until then, conservation in Wyoming will be voluntary, generally meaning that if an irrigator or other user forgoes their water right, they will need to be paid. In previous trial conservation programs, that has cost $500 an acre foot.
But a compact call by Lower Basin states would lead to curtailment — a mandatory cutting off of Upper Basin water use starting with the most recent, or junior, rights’ holders. Long-established ranches and irrigators hold senior rights while Wyoming municipalities and industries in the Green River Basin are likely among the first to be curtailed.
An aerial view of the site of the proposed West Fork Dam at the head of the Little Snake River Valley in Carbon County. The proposed dam would be 264 feet high, 700 feet long and made out of concrete. (Major King for WyoFile)
Under the “Law of the River,” Wyoming has rights — on paper — to 14% of the Upper Basin’s 7.5 million acre-feet annually. That’s about 1 million acre-feet. But the state engineer estimated in 2010 that Wyoming’s rights amount to 847,000 acre-feet a year, according to the state’s 2010 plan for the basin. Wyoming uses 680,076 acre-feet and has rights to another 166,924, the latest plan states.
That makes the 100,000 or so Wyomingites who rely on or use Green River water relatively water rich compared to the 40 million down-streamers who rely on the river for some or all of their agricultural and municipal needs. In essence, 100,000 Wyomingites have rights to almost 1 million acre-feet while 39.9 million down-streamers divvy up 7.5 million acre-feet.
The implications go beyond the scarcity of your garden-variety salad.
“If there are big reductions in water supplies to those [Lower Basin] areas, there really will be impacts on our food supply nationally, not to mention other impacts,” Porter said.
Recycling water
While the prospect of southwestern metropolises crashing headlong into ugly sewerage problems caused by the crisis would seem to loom, don’t put all your money into wag-bags and porta potties yet. The municipalities are figuring out how to cope.
“Those cities are making massive investments in advanced water purification to treat reclaimed water to potable to reduce reliance on annual deliveries of Colorado River water,” Porter said. “That access to other water supplies or other water management strategies isn’t really available to agricultural water users or, to a great extent, the tribes who are significant rights holders to Colorado River water.
“We may see impacts to cities really smoothed out and not be very disruptive,” she said. “If we do have disruptive impacts, they will probably fall on rural areas and tribal communities in the Lower Basin.”
The Bureau stepped in after the upper and lower division states couldn’t agree on how to collectively trim water use.
“I don’t think the development [and] the release of the final EIS has moved the seven states closer to consensus,” Porter said. “I think, if anything, it has moved them farther away. I don’t see the state saying we will waive what we think are our rights under the Colorado Compact and come up with a new agreement.
“We are in for a lot of legal conflict, and meanwhile, we don’t have good reason to hope that hydrology is going to bail us out,” she said. “So we could have a lot of fighting over less and less water.”

title: Private equity is already reshaping rural healthcare in Wyoming
description:
As investors eye more hospitals and medical services for short-term returns, Wyoming needs to establish safeguards to protect patients, writes guest columnist Niel Ritchie.
The post Private equity is already reshaping rural healthcare in Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Rural America has always been worth fighting for, and today one of its most essential lifelines — the local hospital — is under growing threat. As private equity firms expand across the healthcare system, rural communities need protections against investment and ownership models that can extract resources, weaken care, and leave entire regions with fewer options in an emergency. Investment is welcome in communities where capital can be scarce. But healthcare is different: When a hospital closes, lives are at risk. 

Opinion

For Wyoming, this is not a distant or imaginary concern. Three of the state’s eight privately owned hospitals are now owned by private-equity firms — one of the highest proportions in the country. In a state where distance can turn a service reduction into a medical emergency, decisions made in corporate boardrooms can have immediate consequences for families hundreds of miles away.
For too long, private equity in healthcare has been treated like a story about Wall Street dealmaking. A new Campaign for Accountability report found that private equity-owned hospitals collected an average of $669 more per patient than hospitals operating under other ownership models, without a meaningful increase in the cost of delivering care. Much of the difference came from higher prices, particularly for privately insured patients. 
Since 2005, 197 rural hospitals have closed or converted to other uses. Roughly half are operating at a loss, and 418 are considered vulnerable to closure. In communities with so little margin for error, unstable ownership and rising costs can determine whether care remains available at all.
Every Wyoming resident should be concerned! 
In many small towns, the hospital is both a medical lifeline and one of its largest employers. When it’s weakened, patients face higher prices, reduced services, longer travel times and fewer options for emergency, maternity and behavioral healthcare, among others. 
And concerns about quality are not merely anecdotal. A 2023 study published in JAMA examining more than 660,000 hospitalizations found that hospital-acquired conditions — including patient falls and bloodstream infections — increased by 25% after private equity acquisition, even as those same harms were declining nationally. The consequences are measurable. 
As of 2023, private equity firms  owned at least 130 rural hospitals in at least eight states and had invested heavily in emergency department staffing, medical transport, behavioral health and hospital management companies. Yet a 2026 study in Annals of Surgery found that rural hospitals acquired by private equity experienced increases in postoperative mortality and complications compared with similar hospitals that were not acquired.
The risks extend well beyond hospital walls. Private equity backed firms now staff nearly a quarter of all U.S. emergency department visits. In emergency transportation, private equity companies control 64 percent of the Medicare helicopter air-ambulance market, and charge substantially higher rates than competing operators. In behavioral health — a critical service in areas with limited alternatives – private equity accounted for roughly 60 percent of all facility acquisitions between 2010 and 2021. For many rural communities, these services are not interchangeable. They are essential components of an already fragile healthcare network.
Access problems continue to worsen as well. Since the end of 2020, 139 rural labor-and-delivery units have closed, leaving fewer than half of rural hospitals still delivering babies. In that environment, any ownership model that prioritizes short-term returns over long-term stability should raise serious concerns.
Wyoming residents have come together and refuse to accept that decline. In 2018, Riverton community members created the nonprofit Riverton Medical District and began pursuing a locally governed hospital. Their new facility, now named RiverPeak Health, is scheduled for completion later this year. Plans include 13 inpatient beds, two labor-and-delivery rooms, emergency care and surgery available around the clock. 
None of this means that rural hospitals do not need investment. They do. Rural communities understand better than anyone the financial challenges these institutions face. But there is a profound difference between investors committed to strengthening hospitals in the long term and investors seeking to maximize short-term returns. 
Wyoming should establish its own safeguards before the next hospital or medical practice changes hands. Public officials should require full disclosure of hospital and acquisition-related debt, scrutinize real estate and management-fee arrangements and track whether maternity care, emergency services, behavioral health, surgery or local employment could be affected.
Rural hospitals are not financial assets to be traded. They are community lifelines that must remain intact. Wyomingites deserve a healthcare system built around care, stability, and accountability — not profit extraction.

title: US District 1 candidates: Idahoans face high healthcare costs. Here’s how they want to fix it.
description: Idaho U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher will face three election challengers for his seat this November. The candidates in the race acknowledged that the increasing cost of living is a major challenge Idahoans are facing, but largely disagree on how to solve it. Democrat Kaylee Peterson, independent Sarah Zabel, and Constitution Party candidate Brendan Gomez are […]
text:
From left, Democrat Kaylee Peterson, independent Sarah Zabel, and incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher. (Photos courtesy of the candidates)Idaho U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher will face three election challengers for his seat this November. The candidates in the race acknowledged that the increasing cost of living is a major challenge Idahoans are facing, but largely disagree on how to solve it.
Risch v. Achilles may be Idaho’s most active US Senate race in years. Here’s where they stand.

Democrat Kaylee Peterson, independent Sarah Zabel, and Constitution Party candidate Brendan Gomez are running against the Republican incumbent to represent Idaho’s 1st Congressional District, which covers the Idaho panhandle and western side of the state.
The Idaho Capital Sun sat down with Fulcher, Peterson and Zabel to talk about where they stand on healthcare, immigration and public lands.
Gomez did not respond to a request for an interview.
The general election will take place Nov. 3.



Who are the candidates?
Fulcher, 64, was first elected to represent Idaho in Congress in 2018. The Meridian native previously served as an Idaho state senator for 10 years and worked for 24 years in the tech industry at Micron Technology and Preco Electronics. 
He said he wanted to run again because, “we’re making some progress, and when I say progress, I’m talking about major issues to Idaho, and I’m positioned pretty well to continue that effort.” 
Peterson, 36, is running for the position for the third time since 2022. The Eagle resident worked in political advocacy before stepping back to raise her kids, she said. She’s pursuing associate degrees in criminal justice and political science at the College of Western Idaho. 
“I knew right away that it was going to take years to build the kind of infrastructure, the team, the contacts, the messaging, the strategies that would be necessary to get new representation in the district, so that’s why I committed to running multiple cycles,” Peterson said. “And why I’ve stuck with the federal race, because I know the district like the back of my hand … So the hope is we can use the platform to support all the other working class candidates that are stepping up into this new movement.” 
Zabel, 61, lives in Bayview in North Idaho. She served in the Air Force for 31 years, including teaching at the Air Force Academy and at the Pentagon working on policy and the budget. She retired as a major general. Zabel later cared for her father and worked for the policy think tank, RAND Corporation. 
“The two parties have gone so far into their own corners, they have placed themselves in a position where they cannot solve our problems anymore,” Zabel said. “That’s how I got activated to do something, and it was specifically at the federal level because that’s where my experience is.” 



 Candidates agree healthcare is too expensive, present different solutions

Nearly all the candidates said high healthcare costs are one of the top challenges Idahoans face. 
Zabel said healthcare costs need to be addressed in four different areas: hospital services, physician services, prescription drugs, and the insurance marketplace. 
She proposed breaking up hospital systems that buy up and eliminate competition, allowing healthcare workers such as nurse practitioners and physician assistants to provide higher levels of care when appropriate, and requiring transparency of costs of different medical services and pharmaceutical options. 
She would also support providing something similar to enhanced premium tax credits, which were meant to make health insurance purchased through state marketplaces more affordable, but expired at the end of 2025. 
“We’ve seen where the biggest holes were,” she said. “So look at where are the people most affected, and let’s see if we can patch those parts at least where the people are most affected, and where it’s driving the worst part of the insurance spiral, so hopefully it’s not the whole thing, but it is a big chunk.” 
Peterson would support a single-payer health insurance program, often called Medicare for all,  for base-line coverage with private insurance options. 
“For me, the government needs to step in, and we have to reimagine a system in which we’re not also paying the taxes for healthcare and paying thousands of dollars a month,” Peterson said. “I think single-payer options right now would seem like the most affordable. While allowing the private market to do its thing, we bring some competition back into our healthcare market.” 
She said it would provide more oversight and transparency to the healthcare market. 
Fulcher said that rising costs since the Affordable Care Act was enacted in 2010 have shown that it has a number of problems. However, he said it’s a “landmine” issue and can’t be eliminated at the moment because there’s no replacement with enough support. 
He said he’s supportive of a proposal to create a “voluntary parallel path” for private market-place insurance. Fulcher said he’s working with the sponsor, Alabama Republican U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer on the proposed legislation. 
“If you chose, you could sign up for a market-based deal,” Fulcher said. “And the brief summary is, you get the benefit paid directly to you, and then you go figure out what channels you want to invest that healthcare in …you pick the provider, you pick the healthcare service, and you manage it yourself.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Candidates say immigration reforms needed to support workforce

Peterson said she supported the Farm Workforce Modernization Act, which would’ve created a temporary legal status for undocumented farm workers, streamlined the migrant agricultural worker visa H-2A program and updated some of its processes, and created a green card option for long-term farm workers.
It also would’ve required employers to all use the federal work authorization verification system E-Verify to determine if workers were legally allowed to work in the U.S. Versions of the bill have been proposed since 2019, and it passed the House in 2021 but failed to move forward in the Senate. 
Fulcher voted against it, and fellow Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson voted in favor. 
Peterson said she’d support funding more immigration judges and streamlining processes for legal immigration “for a fraction of the cost that we are paying masked federal agents to invade  our communities.” 
Fulcher said he opposed immigration reform proposals that didn’t include amnesty, which would allow undocumented people already in the country a pathway to legal authorization. 
Unauthorized immigrants are key players in Idaho’s economy, agricultural sector, study shows

“I’m open to negotiating that, trying to put some intelligence into right-sizing the number of slots available and the window of time it’s valid,” Fulcher said. “But I really don’t subscribe to scrapping it, or opening up to just amnesty either. So I think the probably the best solution there is to work with our industries. And it doesn’t have to be a national thing.” 
He said he supported making changes to the program that differ state by state and industry by industry depending on needs. Currently, the program is only for temporary, seasonal work and cannot be used for year-round farm labor, including dairies. 
Zabel said she supported an effort proposed this year, the Securing Agriculture’s Workforce Act, which would expand the H-2A program and allow for year-round work.  
She would also support similar visa programs for industries like construction and hospitality, which often rely on undocumented labor.
“We have needs all year round, and they’re not being met,” she said. “… it’s not something that you need a think tank to figure it out. The solution is right there.”
 Idaho’s public lands are a top priority for candidates. Fulcher says he doesn’t want to sell lands.

Fulcher named management of public lands as one of his top priorities. 
“The popular perception out there is, ‘Fulcher wants to sell lands.’ I do not. That’s not it,” he said. “But what I do want to do is I want to figure out a way to manage it better.” 
Part of that perception stems from a late-night committee vote in May 2025 on a proposed provision to the passive tax-and-spend budget reconciliation, which became the “big beautiful” law. Fulcher voted in favor of an addition that would have sold off thousands of acres of federal lands in Nevada and Utah, the Idaho Press reported. The amendment passed the committee but ultimately was not included in the final budget package. 
Fulcher said the amendment was backed by Nevada Republican U.S. Rep. Mark Amodei. 
Idaho U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher seeks input on federal land management in survey

“It was a Nevada issue, and I support them,” Fulcher said about his vote. “The landscape in Idaho is a lot different than Nevada.”
He said he doesn’t want the federal government adding acreage to public lands because of the strain of managing existing land. He also said the state and private entities need to be more involved with the federal government to manage Idaho’s more than 30 million acres of federal public land. 
Zabel said she strongly opposed the idea of transferring management to the states. 
“The state doesn’t have the resources, the wherewithal to manage the (federal) public lands,” she said. 
She said she supported allocating more federal resources to management because the lands “are a public trust.” She said she’s also concerned about recent federal decisions, such as the U.S. Bureau of Land Management decision to swap an approved solar power generation and battery storage facility for a data center instead on Nevada federal land. 
“I am afraid that bad choices and bad solutions will be shoved down on us,” Zabel said. “We need our congressional delegation and our senators to be firm that public lands are a public trust, that these federal lands are federal lands because they belong to everybody.” 
Peterson criticized cuts to federal agencies that oversee these lands, like the BLM or U.S. Forest Service. 
“We’ve watched Idaho’s congressional delegation chip away at the federal agencies and staffing responsible for managing that land, and then complain about the maintenance backlog,” she said.
She said she supports using timber harvesting to reduce wildfire risk, but that the market for it needs to be expanded to support it. 
“With responsible leadership … willing to take an interest, we can expand these markets while protecting public use, public land management, (and) making sure it’s being done sustainably,” Peterson said. “So we have long-term lucrative job opportunities.” 
 Fulcher leads candidates in fundraising 

Fulcher’s campaign has raised a total of more than $660,000 between Jan. 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026, according to the latest available data from the Federal Election Commission. Just over $300,000 of that comes from contributions from political action committees, or PACs, such as the Georgia-based Freedom Fund, the Idaho-based J.R. Simplot Company PAC, and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee PAC, known as AIPAC. 
His campaign has spent nearly $600,000 as of June 30. 
Peterson’s campaign had garnered just over $181,000 as of June 30, which included a $3,000 loan from herself, and $11,000 from three other PACS, according to FEC filings. The PACs represented a machinists association and union plumbers and pipefitters. 
Her campaign spent almost $171,800. 
Zabel’s campaign collected nearly $81,500, which included a $30,000 loan from herself, and $500 from the North Idaho Working Families PAC, according to FEC data. Her campaign has spent around $57,000.

title: After falling out, East Idaho hospital reaches deal to re-join network for health insurer
description: After a public contract dispute that led an East Idaho hospital to become out of network with a major health insurer, the two businesses agreed to a contract. The deal brings Portneuf Medical Center in-network for Regence BlueShield of Idaho, according to a joint announcement made Saturday by the hospital and insurer. For two months, […]
text:
Portneuf Medical Center in Pocatello, Idaho, is an acute care facility that has provided health care to eastern Idaho since 1907. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)After a public contract dispute that led an East Idaho hospital to become out of network with a major health insurer, the two businesses agreed to a contract.
The deal brings Portneuf Medical Center in-network for Regence BlueShield of Idaho, according to a joint announcement made Saturday by the hospital and insurer. For two months, the hospital had been out of network for Regence, the insurer for state government employees and other private plans.
The fallout also spurred the attention of state lawmakers, who assembled a new working group to study the practices of health insurance companies that spent much of its first meeting last week focused on the insurer. 
The in-network agreement is retroactive until June 15, when the two split, the hospital and insurer say. 
The deal “includes reimbursement updates that support the long-term sustainability of care delivery,” the two businesses said in a news release. The contract also lasts until 2029, Regence spokesperson Lou Riepl said in an emailed statement. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Regence BlueShield of Idaho President Mark Ruszczyk thanked the hospital for its “willingness to work with us on” the agreement.
“We are also grateful to the Pocatello community for its patience as we advocated for affordability on behalf of our members and customers,” he said. “Members who received care while Portneuf Health was out of network can be assured those claims will be covered at in-network rates.”
Portneuf Health CEO Nate Carter said hospital officials believe terms in the deal that improve operations “will help create a better experience for patients and caregivers moving forward.”
“This agreement is an important step forward for patients who rely on our teams for care,” he said in a written statement. “It restores in-network access, provides greater certainty for patients and families, and establishes a foundation that supports the long-term delivery of high-quality care in our region.”



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



But the insurer and the hospital didn’t release much more specific information about the new deal — including whether it could affect premiums for state employees. 
“While we don’t disclose the specific financial terms of our provider contracts, what we can say is that both sides were able to reach compromises in key areas that were important to each, such as access to affordable health care for Regence members and reduction in administrative burden for Portneuf Medical Center,” said Riepl, who is with Regence.
But Portneuf Health spokesperson Katie Damron said the agreement “addresses our concerns of high denial rates and outstanding unpaid claims, as well as provides reimbursements on par with the market.”
When news about their contract dispute became public in May, Regence argued the for-profit owner of the hospital was asking for an unreasonable pay increase. But the hospital said Regence denied the vast majority of its claims. 
Last week, Faith Knowlton, who leads the state office that oversees the contract between the health insurer and the state, told state lawmakers serving on the new panel that if Regence had accepted the hospital owners’ terms for a reimbursement rate increase, monthly premiums for all state employees and their family members on the plan would’ve jumped.
The hospital could not be reached for comment on terms of the deal.

title: Alabama commission studying students’ screen time holds first meeting
description: A state commission charged with studying the risks and benefits of screens in classroom instruction held its first meeting Monday. The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, created by Gov. Kay Ivey through an executive order last month, discussed goals and heard research-based presentations from two fellow commissioners. Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville, th[...]
text:
A child with a finger on a tablet. An Alabama commission charged with studying the risks and benefits of screen time instruction held its first meeting on Monday. (Oscar Lopez Rogado via Getty Images)A state commission charged with studying the risks and benefits of screens in classroom instruction held its first meeting Monday.
The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, created by Gov. Kay Ivey through an executive order last month, discussed goals and heard research-based presentations from two fellow commissioners.
Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville, the chair of the commission and a former state director of Early Childhood Education, said in an interview Monday that she wants to survey parents and teachers.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We want to know what’s happening in Alabama, and we can address the issue when we know exactly what’s going on with our parents and teachers and administrators in the schools, according to what type of screen time and amount of screen time,” Ross said. “Because we’ve learned, particularly today, it’s been emphasized that all screen time is not equal. We want to focus more on what is quality and what does enhance instruction, not replace it.”
During the 2026 regular session, Ross sponsored HB 78, signed by Ivey in March, which set screen time limits for children up to five years old in licensed child-care facilities. Ross also filed HB 584, which would have expanded the screen time limits for all public school students. The bill failed to pass before the Legislature adjourned in April.
Members of the Commission on Screen-Based Instruction as seen on Aug. 17, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)
Ross said Monday she hopes to refile the legislation “based on what (the commission’s) recommendations are.”
Nashedra Barry, a child psychologist with Children’s Hospital of Alabama in Birmingham and a member of the commission, said during a presentation that the commission should consider the quality of the content being put in front of students rather than focus on strict time limits for screens.
“We have found that the quality of the screen use that you are consuming, as well as individual factors like child temperament, parental factors and all of those things, have a mitigating impact on the effects of screens on kids,” she said. “Child-centered designs are generally seen as better quality, so things that support language, cognition and social-emotional development for kids. Whereas things that we call engagement-based designs are seen to have a greater negative impact.”
Cailin Kerch, a clinical associate professor of early childhood education, curriculum and development at The University of Alabama and member of the commission, said during her presentation that while the usage of technology is prominent in classrooms, there isn’t evidence showing it’s the best way to educate students.
“One-to-one devices are almost universal in Alabama and in states across the U.S. However, we don’t have evidence yet to provide that that is the best way to educate young children,” Kerch said. “States are starting to focus on the quality of screen use versus the quantity, so not the number of minutes on the screen, but the number of minutes that’s really enhancing education, which is really central to our commission.”
Sen. Linda Coleman-Madison, D-Birmingham, said in an interview Monday that the commission isn’t looking to eliminate technology in schools.
“We don’t want to get rid of technology, that’s not what we’re saying,” she said. “We’re just saying that we need to back up and take a look at it to make sure, because the things that we do right now have long-term impacts. We want to make sure that we are intentional about teaching our students, that we’re intentional about what they learn, that we are concerned about the outcomes.”
The commission will report its findings to Ivey on Dec. 1.

title: Metro Nashville joins lawsuit claiming feds withheld millions
description: Metro Nashville filed suit Monday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security in federal court, claiming the Trump administration withheld tens of millions of dollars for anti-terrorism efforts unless states and local governments adopted certain election-system policies to check citizenship. Metro joined Harris County and El Paso County, both in Texas,[...]
text:
Metro Nashville is one of several jurisdictions that have sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security over claims the agency withheld anti-terrorism funds. Pictured: the Davidson County Courthouse. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) Metro Nashville filed suit Monday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security in federal court, claiming the Trump administration withheld tens of millions of dollars for anti-terrorism efforts unless states and local governments adopted certain election-system policies to check citizenship.
Metro joined Harris County and El Paso County, both in Texas, and the city of Columbus, Ohio in saying they lost 20% of their federal DHS allotment for not using a national citizenship verification system they consider “notoriously error-filled” to check the status of pollworkers and register voters. They claim in the filing that the conditions violate the U.S. Constitution and put public safety and election security in jeopardy.
In a release, the local governments, which are represented by Protect Democracy, the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU, Public Rights Project and the Jacobsen Lawyers Group, said the Department of Homeland Security is “holding public safety funding hostage” to “coerce” states and local governments to adopt policies the administration has failed to impose in court.
The group of local governments notes that the Federal Emergency Management Agency put new eligibility requirements on states in order to receive money from the Homeland Security Grant Program set up by Congress 25 years ago to help local governments deal with terrorism acts. Under those conditions, states must use DHS’s “notoriously error-filled” Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system to “verify” citizenship for all pollworkers and registered voters, putting higher and “impractical” costs on electronic voting systems and charging a 5% manual paper-ballot audit, the local groups say.
The local governments’ complaint contends the new conditions are “arbitrary and illegal” and violate the Administrative Procedure Act and the Constitution’s separation of powers, which give federal spending authority to Congress, not the executive branch. It also points out the Constitution gives states and Congress authority to set federal election rules.



Quotation







Courts have consistently rejected the administration’s efforts to meddle in elections. We are proud to join other cities and counties across the country to ensure that our access to federal funds designated for first responders is protected.


– Tyler Yarbro, Metro Nashville Law Director


The plaintiffs also said the Trump administration’s demand came as it “engages in a coordinated campaign to undermine the mid-term elections.”
“This lawsuit seeks to secure necessary funding that would provide equipment and training to Nashville’s first responders in handling emergency or terrorist events in our city,” said Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County’s Director of Law Tyler Yarbro. “The Trump administration wants to withhold those funds unless we implement wholly unnecessary and costly changes to our election procedures. Courts have consistently rejected the administration’s efforts to meddle in elections. We are proud to join other cities and counties across the country to ensure that our access to federal funds designated for first responders is protected.”
