name: West Virginia Watch
title: Huntington organizers to hold citywide signature drive for ‘Get The Flock Out’ ballot initiative
description: Residents in Huntington angered over their city council’s approval of a $2.1 million contract with Flock Safety to install license plate readers, cameras and more throughout the city are organizing a weekend-long canvassing campaign later this month to collect the signatures for their ballot initiative petition. The residents, led by Huntington Community Act[...]
text:
Protestors gather outside of Huntington City Hall as they respond in opposition to Flock Safety items listed on the Huntington City Council agenda on Monday, July 13, 2026, in downtown Huntington. (Photo by Ryan Fischer/The Herald-Dispatch)Residents in Huntington angered over their city council’s approval of a $2.1 million contract with Flock Safety to install license plate readers, cameras and more throughout the city are organizing a weekend-long canvassing campaign later this month to collect the signatures for their ballot initiative petition.
The residents, led by Huntington Community Action Group, a local chapter of the West Virginia Citizen Action Group, will spread across all nine of Huntington’s city council districts this Saturday and Sunday as part of their “Rolling Rally.” Organizers will be present at several of the city’s “busiest weekend gathering places,” including 9th Street Live, the Ritter Park Small Business Market and Central United Methodist Church to collect signatures from residents who want to vote on whether mass-surveillance tools should be utilized.
“We’ve had such an overwhelmingly supportive response to our petition that we’ve decided to take copies to every district across city in these two days,” said Katie Norman, a volunteer with Huntington CAG, in a news release. “People are realizing that their city government isn’t going to fix this mess and are excited to be part of the solution.”
According to the Huntington city charter, a petition for a ballot initiative must be signed by at least 10% of the number of voters who were registered during the last municipal election. That would mean about 2,000 valid signatures must be collected in Huntington for the petition to be considered. Per a news release from the West Virginia arm of the American Civil Liberties Union, organizers in Huntington are planning to collect twice as many signatures as needed. If enough signatures are verified, the city will hold an election for residents to vote on the initiative.
Huntington CAG launched its “Get the Flock Out” ballot initiative at a rally earlier this month. The group wants to pass an ordinance prohibiting mass surveillance systems in the city. One provision of the ordinance would require the city to void the contracts it approved with Flock Safety last month. 
In the early morning of July 14 — after hours of comments from more than 50 residents, nearly all of whom disapproved the move to partner with Flock — Huntington City Council voted 6-4 to enter into a five-year contract with Flock Safety for surveillance tools. The tools, including automated license plate readers, voice recorders, drones and cameras, are meant to be used by law enforcement to stymie crime. Huntington Mayor Patrick Ferrell and Huntington Police Chief Phil Watkins urged approval of the contract.
Flock Safety devices have raised privacy concerns in other jurisdictions they’ve been used in. In December, 60 Flock cameras in California were compromised, leaving public livestreams available for anyone to access and download from a 30 day period. In Houston, at least six Flock cameras were cut last month after residents complained about the devices. The Los Angeles Police Department announced in July that it would not renew its contact with Flock, citing concerns over privacy.
In recent months, investigations have revealed that numerous police across the country have misused the technology to stalk people unrelated to criminal investigations.
A few days after the Huntington City Council meeting, ACLU-WV filed suit against the City of Huntington on behalf of a resident over allegations that the city neglected key procedural matters before awarding the contract. Per the suit, the city’s own laws stop private companies, like Flock, from using or benefitting from the use of city-owned property. There is a proper process that, if followed, would allow the city to grant use of its property, but that process was not followed, the lawsuit contends.
Representatives for ACLU-WV have indicated that further legal action could come related to the contract signed by Huntington City Council.

title: Higher ethanol blends would benefit consumers, corn industry, panel says
description: Consumers would have more opportunity to save money on gasoline with higher levels of ethanol if Congress can remove a long-standing restriction, members of an ethanol industry roundtable said Monday.  The U.S. House has passed a bill to allow year-round sales of gasoline with 15% ethanol, known as E15. Current rules do not allow E15 […]
text:
A truck delivers corn to the Tharaldson Ethanol plant near Casselton, North Dakota, on May 15, 2024. (Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) Consumers would have more opportunity to save money on gasoline with higher levels of ethanol if Congress can remove a long-standing restriction, members of an ethanol industry roundtable said Monday. 
The U.S. House has passed a bill to allow year-round sales of gasoline with 15% ethanol, known as E15. Current rules do not allow E15 sales during the summer, though the federal Environmental Protection Agency granted a waiver this year. 
Year-round ethanol blend bill passed by US House faces uncertain Senate path

The roundtable, hosted by Rep. Julie Fedorchak, R-N.D., mostly consisted of members connected to agriculture, which would benefit from easier access to corn-based ethanol. 
Dave Olson, bulk petroleum manager of West Fargo-based fuel retailer Petro Serve said E15 is about selling at a 15 cent discount to regular unleaded in the Fargo area. 
“They’re looking for a bargain,” Olson said of consumers. 
While his company is committed to offering E15, he said others are not interested in selling a fuel they can only offer for part of the year. 
Dave Ripplinger, a bio energy economist and associate professor with North Dakota State University, said he understands that hesitation with thin profit margins in the retail world. 

“They can’t afford to make mistakes,” Ripplinger said. Knowing E15 could be sold year-round, “changes the economics” for those businesses, he said. 
In the 20 years since ethanol production has taken off, North Dakota has gone from less than a half-million acres of corn to 4.5 million acres of corn. 
North Dakota’s five ethanol plants process 80% of the corn, with livestock feed one of the main byproducts of fuel production. 
Ripplinger said the possibility of carbon capture at ethanol plants has the potential to boost North Dakota oil production, further advancing the importance of ethanol production. 
“That provides this whole additional list of benefits that will support state economic activity,” Ripplinger said. 
Corn-based sustainable aviation fuel, ethanol use in maritime shipping and tractors that could burn ethanol instead of diesel are other potential areas where the ethanol market could expand, roundtable members said. 
The Gevo ethanol plant near Richardton is expanding with sustainable aviation fuel in mind. 
The U.S. House was able to pass a year-round E15 bill in May, something Fedorchak called a “small miracle,” in part because some key House leaders voted against it. 
The bill still needs to clear the Senate. Fedorchak said she expects the Senate to make some changes to the bill, meaning if it passes the Senate, the House would have to take it up again.
The restriction on higher ethanol use exists because of past studies showing possible detrimental effects of burning E15 in the summer months. 
Dave Olson, a manager with Petro Serve, and Brenda Elmer, executive director with the North Dakota Corn Growers Association, take part in an ethanol industry discussion in Fargo on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Fedorchak called that “old science” that has been refuted. 
Panel members pointed out that some other countries allow much higher ethanol blends. 
Brenda Elmer, executive director of the North Dakota Corn Growers Association, noted that Brazil, a key U.S. competitor in the corn and ethanol industries, as of Aug. 1 is mandating at least 32% ethanol in gasoline. 
“We’re just asking for the option to sell E15,” Elmer said.
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Trump-inspired political cynicism continues to transform NC conservatives
description: It may or may not be apocryphal, but there is an infamous World War II era quote attributed to Russian dictator Josef Stalin in which he responded to the suggestion that the leader of the Catholic church might be able to use his moral influence to help resolve a portion of the conflict. “The Pope?” […]
text:
House Speaker Destin Hall, State Auditor Dave Boliek, and Senate President Phil Berger. (File photos)It may or may not be apocryphal, but there is an infamous World War II era quote attributed to Russian dictator Josef Stalin in which he responded to the suggestion that the leader of the Catholic church might be able to use his moral influence to help resolve a portion of the conflict.
“The Pope?” Stalin interrupted. “How many divisions does he have?”
Over the last several decades, Stalin’s crude remark has regularly been cited as the very definition of cynical, amoral, ends-justify-the-means statecraft. And for most of that time, and in most places, American leaders across the political spectrum did not understand that to be a compliment.
In 2026, things have changed.
Today, longstanding American political traditions in elections and lawmaking like respect for one’s adversary, self-discipline and sacrifice, abiding by established rules and roles, and commitments to open debate, widespread voter participation and honorable, nonpartisan public service are fast becoming passé. Instead, accumulating and maintaining power at all costs now trumps all other priorities.
And in few places is this disturbing trend more readily evident than in North Carolina. Especially over the last decade as Donald Trump’s transformation of conservatism has come to full flower, it’s not an exaggeration to say that the state’s Republican leaders have made Stalin’s brand of raw power politics their North Star.
The examples are sadly and tragically numerous, but for a most recent, egregious and high-profile example, consider the appalling transformation of the office of the state auditor – the state’s accountant.
While there’s no doubt that past Democratic and Republican auditors brought different temperaments and agendas to the position, at no time was the auditor’s office designed or understood to serve as a powerful administrator of broad executive authority – much less a repository of powers illegitimately snatched from other constitutional officers and transformed into hyperpartisan weapons.
Unfortunately, thanks to the results of the 2024 election in which Democrats swept the state’s higher-profile Council of State offices, Republican legislators decided that remaking the auditor’s office in such a way was just the ticket for blunting the will of voters and expanding their power.
And so it is that current Republican Auditor Dave Boliek – a willing and happy accomplice in this sudden, unprecedented, and undemocratic scheme – is now not only overseeing the state’s elections but doing so in a blatantly and embarrassingly partisan fashion. One need look no further than the scandal surrounding Boliek’s hiring of veteran right-wing political operative __ Dallas Woodhouse as a key election administrator to understand the deep and overt nature of the corrupt cynicism.
Indeed, as NC Newsline’s Lynn Bonner reported recently, email exchanges obtained under a public records request reveal numerous incidents during Woodhouse’s brief tenure as Boliek’s special “elections liaison” to local county election boards in which – surprise!! – he sought to convince and advise local boards to craft rules in hopes of aiding GOP candidates.
But, of course, as sobering as such actions are, none comes as any kind of shock. North Carolina Republican legislative leaders have long been employing (and continue to employ) the very same brand of amoral, win-at-all-costs tactics in countless other arenas.
From the overtly partisan and racial gerrymandering (i.e., election rigging) repeatedly injected into the state’s electoral maps, to the never-ending efforts in the Legislative Building to consolidate power and avoid and silence debate, to the constant efforts to defund the offices of Democratic officeholders, to the embarrassing politicization of the state’s judiciary, the priority of obtaining, maximizing and holding onto power at all costs has come to guide virtually all significant policymaking decisions for the state’s GOP leadership.
Just two weeks ago, Republican lawmakers passed the latest of several bills approved in recent years that have been designed to elevate right-wing state Chief Justice Paul Newby into a virtual judicial autocrat. House Republican Speaker Destin Hall even voiced support for Newby using the powers included in the bill to suspend judges without pay who issue opinions with which the political right disagrees.
What’s next – the distinctly Stalinist idea of suspending legislators who vote the wrong way?
And lest anyone dismiss as naïve the citation of the above actions as a failure to grasp the reality of “business-as-usual, hardball politics,” rest assured, it’s the defenders and apologists for the GOP’s transformation who are the naïve ones. Yes, North Carolina has always been a home to hardball politics, but the repeated cynical and amoral power grabs of the present era make the actions of late 20th-century Democratic power brokers like Jim Hunt and Marc Basnight look like child’s play.
As David Denby noted in a recent profile of famed political philosopher Hannah Arendt in The New Yorker magazine, it was the conservative Arendt who explained in the “The Origins of Totalitarianism” how democratic institutions can gradually morph into “bureaucratic despotism” through the working of many of the practices now embraced by the modern GOP. And it’s one of the great tragedies of our time that so many people who once claimed to despise the tactics and ethics of autocracy now so readily and energetically embrace them.

title: Tennessee reports $1.2 billion surplus during past fiscal year
description: Tennessee’s next governor will enter office with a $1.2 billion surplus, after the state finalized the books on its most recent fiscal year.  State Finance and Administration Commissioner Jim Bryson said in a news release that the surplus was partly driven by inflation and higher-than-expected corporate tax collections.  “It’s important to remain cautious,”[...]
text:
Tennessee officials reported a $1.2 billion surplus in fiscal year 2025-26. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s next governor will enter office with a $1.2 billion surplus, after the state finalized the books on its most recent fiscal year. 
State Finance and Administration Commissioner Jim Bryson said in a news release that the surplus was partly driven by inflation and higher-than-expected corporate tax collections. 
“It’s important to remain cautious,” Bryson said. “These corporate estimated payments may require some adjustments.”
Tennessee had a budget of nearly $60 billion in 2025-26, about half of which is covered by state tax revenue. The state is currently in the 2026-27 budget year and the surplus revenue from last year’s budget will factor into the 2027-28 budget.
The budget process for that starts in November and is finalized at the end of the legislative session in the spring of 2027. 
In November, Tennessee will elect a new governor to replace term-limited Gov. Bill Lee. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn is the Republican nominee, Memphis city councilwoman Jerri Green is the Democratic nominee, and two prominent independent candidates, David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston, are running. The state’s surplus is not an indication of the state’s economy, according to Mandy Spears, the executive Vice President at The Sycamore Institute, a nonpartisan think tank that tracks Tennessee’s budget.
“A surplus is almost always driven by estimations, which most years is done conservatively to create this scenario,” Spears said.
During Lee’s eight years in office, he’s largely overseen a growing state budget with yearly surpluses sometimes in the billions.
Lee has used past surpluses to create a new education funding formula, expand private school vouchers, cut business taxes and provide additional funding for road construction.

text:
Participants race during the 2025 Special Olympics Delaware Cycling Classic. Photo Courtesy of Special Olympics Delaware.
The Special Olympics Delaware Annual Cycling Classic will be held on August 22, at DelDOT’s Danner Campus in Dover.
 
Special Olympics Delaware announced that the 2026 Special Olympics Delaware Cycling Classic will be held at the Danner Campus located in Dover, Delaware, on Saturday, August 22, via a press release on August 13. 
The event will bring over 90 athletes and 30 coaches from Delaware and surrounding states to the campus to compete in multiple different cycling events. The other states represented in the event are Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia, according to the release.
“Cycling showcases so much more than athletic achievement. Behind every athlete is a network of coaches, family members, volunteers, and supporters who help make success possible,” said Director of Sports & Area Engagement for Special Olympics Delaware, Kylie Lavelle, via the press release. “The encouragement athletes receive throughout training and competition builds confidence, creates meaningful connections, and reinforces the sense of belonging that is at the heart of Special Olympics. It’s inspiring to see our community come together to celebrate each athlete’s accomplishments both on and off the course.” 
The event will start at 8:00 a.m. with registration and warm-ups for participants. The opening ceremonies will begin at 9:30 a.m. and the racing will start at 10:00 a.m. The event will end around 3:00 p.m.
Awards for racers will be given out throughout the day. 
To learn more about the event and Special Olympics Delaware check out their website here.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Ed Blackmon redrew Mississippi’s political map. Now he’s watching the Supreme Court unwind it
description: Former state Rep. Ed Blackmon talks about the historical context of voting rights and redistricting at his Blackmon & Blackmon law office, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Canton.
text:
Ed Blackmon Jr. was 16 years old, locked in a Canton jail cell with the roar of a poultry truck engine still fresh on his mind, when he decided to become a lawyer. 
The police had just jailed him and dozens of others on trumped-up charges of participating in a parade without a permit after orchestrating a mass protest in the middle of the Civil Rights era in support of voting rights for Black Mississippians. 

The demonstrators had only marched 30 yards from a local church when police put them in handcuffs, hauled them off in a poultry delivery truck that still had chicken dung in it, and threw them into the Madison County Jail to face the bogus charges.
While lying on the hot jail floor during the summer, the young protester encountered someone who would change his trajectory in life, arguably the course of Mississippi. Blackmon met Carsie Hall, a sharp-dressed NAACP attorney who defended protesters during Freedom Summer. 
Former state Rep. Ed Blackmon describes an editorial cartoon depicting himself and a political rival in the mid-70s debating Canton redistricting, at his law office on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Canton. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“Carsie walked up to the cell, and he told us, ‘Don’t worry about it. On Monday, I’m getting y’all out of here.’ At that moment I said, ‘I want to be a lawyer.’” 
Hall followed through on his promise, and law enforcement released the protesters from jail. Blackmon graduated from law school in Washington, D.C., a few years later. 
Now 78, Blackmon has spent his life using the law to build Black political power in Mississippi: suing to dismantle at-large electoral districts, redrawing legislative maps to more than double Black representation in the Legislature and even engineering the state’s first majority-Black judicial subdistricts. 
But the U.S. Supreme Court has largely unwound the Voting Rights Act, which made much of Blackmon’s work possible, in its recent Callais decision. The landmark decision has cleared the way for Southern states such as Mississippi to dismantle majority-Black political districts. 
Both House Speaker Jason White and Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann have created committees to explore redistricting over the summer and fall. Gov. Tate Reeves has indicated he will likely call a special legislative session before January for lawmakers to redraw the state’s legislative districts. 
The Canton attorney and former legislator of 40 years says he’s watched this movie play out before, and Blackmon knows how it ends: not well, but it’s not forever. 
“Mississippi is a good example for the rest of the country,” Blackmon told Mississippi Today in an interview at his law office. “The country right now is where Mississippi is, where Mississippi’s been for a long time.” 
An editorial cartoon at the law office of former state Rep. Ed Blackmon depicting Blackmon and a political rival in the mid-70s debating Canton redistricting, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Canton. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
When Blackmon first returned to his hometown after law school, very few Black officials were elected to local or state offices, including in Canton. A reason Black candidates faced steep odds of winning office is that local candidates had to run in at-large districts, a voting system in which officials represent an entire city or county rather than a specific slice of it, such as a ward or district. White politicians used this system to effectively prevent Black candidates from winning office. 
Blackmon filed a federal lawsuit under the Voting Rights Act to force the city of Canton to create proportional, single-member districts, which divide a city or county into distinct pieces, each electing its own candidate. This way, a concentrated minority population in one area of a city had a real chance to elect someone of their choice.
The litigation was successful, and he successfully replicated these lawsuits in cities across the state. But these lawsuits took precious time, money and effort to tackle bit by bit. 
By 1984, Blackmon was elected to the House himself, one of only a handful of Black legislators at the time. To his surprise, the speaker appointed him to the Apportionment and Elections Committee, which had jurisdiction over redistricting. 
During the 1992 redistricting cycle, Blackmon realized he had a golden opportunity to attempt to redraw the entire state at once by working from within the political system rather than using the courts to challenge the maps district by district. 
He fought to substantially redraw the 122 House districts and overhaul the map by creating more majority-Black districts.
But his plan got a cold reception, even with other Black legislators, because, like their white colleagues, they also wanted to protect their districts and not have to campaign in a new area.
“At the end of the day, we’re  selfish politicians just like everybody else,” Blackmon said. You want to protect your district. That’s the first thing that comes to mind. You want to protect your district, and that’s it.”
Blackmon pressed ahead and took his own legislative map and traveled with Carrol Rhodes, his friend and fellow attorney, to the U.S. Department of Justice, which at the time still had to approve, or “preclear,” any changes to Mississippi’s election maps. 
The Justice Department was able to compare it to the Legislature’s map, which it rejected. This sent the fight back to a three-judge federal panel, which told lawmakers to either draw new maps themselves or have the courts do it for them. 
The panel’s threat coincided with an ongoing battle for House speaker, arguably the most powerful position in state government. With the House divided over who should be speaker, Blackmon suddenly found he could wield new power when Speaker Tim Ford needed to secure more votes to continue serving.   
He struck a deal with Ford: Blackmon could secure him nine votes for speaker, in exchange for control over redistricting, a Black speaker pro tempore, Black committee chairs and secretaries. 
Ford won the speakership. Blackmon got his maps. The next election, Black representation in the Legislature more than doubled, from 21 members to 47.
Looking back, Blackmon said one regret of his was not building enough flexibility into those maps to keep evolving them as Mississippi’s political landscape changed. 
LISTEN: Veteran lawmaker: ‘The most depressing legislative session I’ve ever seen’
He planned to gradually reduce the concentration of Black voters in some districts over time, spreading them into more districts to make them competitive rather than packing them into a smaller number of safe seats.
But when he attempted to “unpack” the majority-Black districts into more competitive ones, his own Black colleagues, who were by then protected incumbents, didn’t want their districts touched.
Now, the Legislature could be on the verge of reducing the number of majority-Black seats in the Capitol, erasing a lot of Blackmon’s work, though the longtime legislator said he thinks it would take a lot to fully eradicate the system he helped build.  
Blackmon said he isn’t counting the fight as over,  just paused. He points to his sons, state Sen. Bradford Blackmon and state Rep. Lawrence Blackmon, as evidence that the work continues, even if progress now comes in smaller increments than the sweeping changes of the 1990s.
The elder Blackmon said the next generation will have to continue this fight and learn from his successes. He believes when the pendulum swings back toward opportunity for Black candidates to make gains, they have to seize it. 
 “It may not even be in my lifetime, but I guarantee you it will swing,” Blackmon said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Remembering Memphis Rep. Joseph Hanover and his role in Tennessee’s women’s suffrage
description: This week is a great week for celebrating Tennessee’s pivotal role in the 19th Amendment’s ratification.  On August 18, 1920, the Tennessee House of Representatives voted in a special session to ratify the 19th Amendment, which enshrined the right to vote for American women in the U.S. Constitution.  The House concurred with the Senate which […]
text:
The National Votes for Women Trail Committee placed a plaque honoring the late Tennessee Rep. Joseph Hanover for his role in ratifying the 19th Amendment on his family home in Memphis. (Photo: Paula Casey)This week is a great week for celebrating Tennessee’s pivotal role in the 19th Amendment’s ratification. 
On August 18, 1920, the Tennessee House of Representatives voted in a special session to ratify the 19th Amendment, which enshrined the right to vote for American women in the U.S. Constitution. 
The House concurred with the Senate which had voted 25-4 on August 13 to ratify. 
The 72-year-long struggle culminated with victory in Tennessee — the movement to enact women’s suffrage needed 36 of the 48 states to ratify, and other states had opted not to vote — thanks to the unceasing efforts of suffragists across the state, a united Shelby County legislative delegation and the leadership of Rep. Joseph Hanover, a Memphis independent. 
Gov. A.H. Roberts signed the ratification papers on August 24 despite enormous opposition and sent them to the U.S. Secretary of State , who signed the final ratification papers on August 26, now known as Women’s Equality Day. 
Prior to 1998, there was nothing inside the Tennessee Capitol that depicted Tennessee’s pivotal role. U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen, then a state senator, sought to rectify that. He understood the importance of public art and worked with the Tennessee Arts Commission to hold a competition, which artist Alan LeQuire of Nashville won.  LeQuire’s bas relief sculpture was subsequently installed between the House and Senate chambers. 
It is the only recognition in the Capitol that celebrates our state’s greatest gift to this country and democracy: the enfranchisement of nearly 27 million American women.
 On the morning of August 18, Hanover knew he was two votes short of ratification and he didn’t know whose votes he would get to fill the gap. 
Hanover was the real hero because he kept the pro-suffrage votes together despite the fierce opposition of such powerful forces as House Speaker Seth Walker,the L&N Railroad and even Jack Daniel’s Distillery.
In 2019, Memphis attorney Bill Haltom published a book detailing the role of Rep. Joseph Hanover in ensuring women gained the right to vote. (Photo: Paula Casey)
Hanover told his personal story, that of a 5-year-old boy escaping tyranny in Poland and finding a new home in America. He told his fellow legislators, “We all crossed the seas to get here … Let’s make Democracy real by securing the vote for every American.”
Walker tried to kill it with a motion to table. But Hanover, along with a surprise vote from Rep. Banks Turner, a Yorkville Democrat,  defeated the motion not once, but twice. Rep. Harry Burn, a Niota Republican voted twice to table.
Hanover’s finesse in keeping the pro-suffrage votes together, followed by the surprise votes in favor by Turner and Burn made votes for women a reality. 
Memphis attorney and author Bill Haltom has written a superb book about Hanover’s life and his importance to the suffrage cause titled “Why Can’t Mother Vote? Joseph Hanover and the Unfinished Business of Democracy.” 
After the bas relief sculpture unveiling in 1998,  the Knoxville Suffrage Commission commissioned LeQuire to create the Tennessee Woman Suffrage Memorial in Knoxville which was unveiled in 2006. 
That was followed by a six-year effort for the Tennessee Woman Suffrage Monument in Nashville’s Centennial Park which was unveiled in August 2016, followed by work on the Memphis Suffrage Monument “Equality Trailblazers.” LeQuire designed and created the Memphis monument which was dedicated in March 2022, at the Cecil D. Humphreys School of Law at the University of Memphis, facing the Mississippi River.
I was determined that Hanover, who was not recognized anywhere in Memphis, would be on that suffrage monument. As chair of the National Votes for Women Trail Committee, NVWT, I worked hard to get a marker for Hanover at 2519 Broad Avenue, the former family home and dry goods store. It is the only NVWT marker in Memphis. 
You can learn more about Tennessee’s role on the podcast, “Her March to Democracy … Stories Along the National Votes for Women Trail – Tennessee episode.”
Michelle Duster, Ida B. Wells’ great-granddaughter, said when she speaks around the country about her great-grandmother, she mentions what Tennesseans have created with our suffrage monuments and markers. 
When we’re all gone, those monuments and markers will continue to tell the story of these extraordinary people who believed in democracy and the rule of law.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Katie Britt and Tommy Tuberville’s rhetoric about Abdul El-Sayed is dangerous
description: I was troubled to recently read comments by Alabama U.S. Sens. Katie Britt and Tommy Tuberville about Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, and his supporters. Britt called him a “terrorist sympathizer” and a “jihadist sympathizer” on television. Sen. Tuberville went a step further and posted online that Dr. […]
text:
I was troubled to recently read comments by Alabama U.S. Sens. Katie Britt and Tommy Tuberville about Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, and his supporters. Britt called him a “terrorist sympathizer” and a “jihadist sympathizer” on television. Sen. Tuberville went a step further and posted online that Dr. El-Sayed is a “terrorist” and a “radical Islamist.” These are inflammatory accusations leveled at a physician and public servant who has spent his career trying to make the lives of Americans better.
I have been a fan of Dr. El-Sayed for years, reading his books (“Healing Politics” and “Medicare for All”) and listening to his podcast (“America Dissected.”) He is a family man who went into public health after seeing how broken our health care system is. El-Sayed became an avid advocate for better and more affordable access to health care for Americans. His campaign for the U.S. Senate is centered on “Medicare for All” and reducing corporate influence in government, ideas reflecting what many Alabamians want, too.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Disagreeing with his positions on health care or foreign policy is fair in a democracy. For example, I don’t expect that our U.S. senators will wake up tomorrow supporting universal health care or agreeing with serious criticisms of Israel. But calling him a “jihadist” is not a policy criticism. It uses language that has real, potentially fatal consequences.
That difference matters, especially here in Alabama. We have a small but vibrant Islamic community made up of people who are as American as anyone else and who already navigate suspicion they did nothing to earn. When U.S. senators use words like “jihadist” and “terrorist” to describe a Muslim candidate, it doesn’t stay confined to one race in Michigan. It reinforces the idea that all Muslim Americans are inherently suspect. It puts ordinary Muslim Alabamians at greater risk of harassment or worse. 
We have seen how demonizing language aimed at a public figure, or a type of people more broadly, can translate into real hostility, even violence, towards a whole group of private citizens. For example, anti-Muslim hate crimes went up significantly in the lead-up to the 2016 election when Islamophobia was so prevalent at the national level. What’s to say there couldn’t be similar consequences here in Alabama in 2026 due to our senators’ words and attitudes? 
Additionally, I’d ask the senators to consider how their language mischaracterizes El-Sayed supporters like myself who simply see the country differently than they do. Sen. Britt said that El-Sayed’s supporters “hate America.” Sen. Tuberville’s rhetoric had a similar tone, only more extreme. As James Baldwin put it, loving this country more than any other in the world is exactly why he insisted on the right to criticize it perpetually. When elected officials frame the deeply American act of dissent as evidence that someone “hates America,” it suggests either a troubling misunderstanding of civics and American history or a desire to exploit that misunderstanding in others. 
I don’t expect Sens. Britt and Tuberville to agree with El-Sayed’s politics, and I don’t expect every Alabamian to either. But I do expect the senators representing our state to debate ideas rather than brand their opponents as terrorists. That shouldn’t be controversial. It should be the bare minimum.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky says these children need families. So why is the state preventing it?
description: For 10 years, I was a certified foster parent in Kentucky. I recently closed my home, but one lesson still defies common sense: Kentucky has somehow made adopting one of its own waiting children harder than adopting a waiting child from another state.  The Kentucky Adoption Profile Exchange, or KAPE, is supposed to find permanent […]
text:
Adoption is not a temporary arrangement. It is a permanent legal commitment that must carry enforceable  obligations. (Getty Images)For 10 years, I was a certified foster parent in Kentucky. I recently closed my home, but one lesson still defies common sense: Kentucky has somehow made adopting one of its own waiting children harder than adopting a waiting child from another state. 
The Kentucky Adoption Profile Exchange, or KAPE, is supposed to find permanent families for children who are legally free for adoption and lack an identified adoptive home. As of August 2026, Kentucky’s public waiting-child page contained more than 350 listings. Many are older children and teenagers. 
Before someone can formally inquire about a child, that person generally must complete Kentucky’s foster/adoptive certification process: training, background checks, interviews and a home study. Kentucky tells families certification commonly takes six to nine months. Only then can the family formally inquire about the child who inspired them — assuming that child is still available. For a 17-year-old, that timeline is astonishing. 
Even approved families face barriers. To pursue a KAPE child, I need my home study. DCBS created it, approved it and stores it in TWIST. Yet I have been required to file an open-records request to obtain the Cabinet’s own document for its own adoption process. 
That home study may also be badly outdated. Foster homes are recertified every three years, but the original narrative is not rewritten. When I obtained mine after almost a decade, it still reflected my family as it existed years earlier. Yet that is the document the adoption review committee relies on when evaluating a match. 
Kentucky also limits families to one KAPE inquiry at a time, except for sibling groups. I cannot explore several potentially appropriate situations and determine where the strongest fit might exist. I must choose one child from a public profile containing very limited information about the child’s history, trauma and realistic needs. 
Then an adoption review committee gets up to 15 working days — three weeks — to decide whether it thinks the child is a good match for my family. 
The committee has never met me. It may be reviewing an outdated home study. I have limited information about the child, and we have not met. Yet if Kentucky decides we are an appropriate match, I am asked whether I want to move forward before receiving the fuller presentation information needed to understand the child’s history and needs.
The committee can have an outdated picture of the family while the family has an incomplete picture of the child. How is that meaningful matching? 
Kentucky already has approved foster and adoptive homes, yet it does not routinely appear to search that pool for every waiting child. Why are children sitting on an adoption website while approved families sit in open homes without a system bringing the two together? 
Perhaps most baffling is Kentucky’s decision to end the specialized Wendy’s Wonderful Kids recruitment model. Its recruiters knew the children and actively searched for permanent families. Kentucky’s own 2025–2029 Diligent Recruitment Plan calls the model evidence-based and says KAPE children receive child-focused recruiters. Yet Kentucky is now folding those workers into its existing adoption infrastructure. 
Keeping the employees is not the same as keeping Wendy’s Wonderful Kids. Kentucky should be expanding this model, not dismantling it. 
Wednesday’s Child brought public reach and privately raised funds for recruitment and matching. Yet it has stepped away from individual child features. I tried to connect its director with DCBS leadership. Her emails went unanswered. 
A couple of years ago, I explained these problems directly to the DCBS commissioner. She appeared surprised by how the process worked. Nothing substantial changed. I also contacted the governor’s office multiple times and received no response at all. 
Kentucky owes the public the numbers. How many KAPE children find families through KAPE? How many adoptions finalize? How long do children wait? How many families walk away? How many approved homes are proactively considered for each child? How many children age out? 
If those statistics exist, publish them. If they do not, how can anyone credibly claim this system is working? 
After a decade inside Kentucky foster care, I wish I could say this was shocking. It isn’t. Once again, common sense seems to have escaped Kentucky’s child-welfare system. 
Kentucky owes taxpayers the numbers, willing families a process that makes sense, and waiting children leadership that facilitates connections with families already willing to adopt them — rather than discouraging those families at every turn.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Does Beshear’s data center executive order have ‘teeth’ without state law to back it up?
description: During a press conference earlier this month, Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear stood firm behind the power of his executive order he issued seeking to limit the impacts of data centers eyeing Kentucky.  “The executive order is fully enforceable, and if you don’t believe it, watch me,” Beshear told reporters. “Watch what happens as we […]
text:
Gov. Andy Beshear issued an executive order on Aug. 6 directing the Kentucky Public Service Commission and the Energy and Environment Cabinet to take specific actions to limit data center impacts. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)During a press conference earlier this month, Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear stood firm behind the power of his executive order he issued seeking to limit the impacts of data centers eyeing Kentucky. 
“The executive order is fully enforceable, and if you don’t believe it, watch me,” Beshear told reporters. “Watch what happens as we move forward. Watch how these companies present their plans as they have to. Watch the actions of the various agencies.”
Those agencies he’s referring to include Kentucky Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator, and the Energy and Environment Cabinet, which regulates water and air pollution. Among other things, he directed the agencies to deny utility rate increases and prevent negative environmental impacts from data centers.
But some people who watch energy policy in the state wonder how the executive order will be implemented and if a governor can compel an agency like the Public Service Commission, which has to follow a mandate defined in state law, to deny requests from utilities. The governor’s executive order doesn’t have the backing of any specific state law regulating data center impacts, potential legislation that the GOP-controlled state legislature has failed to take up so far.
Lane Boldman, the executive director of the environmental advocacy group Kentucky Conservation Committee, described Beshear’s executive order as a “document of intent” that makes clear to state regulators what the governor wants to see happen. But she said the regulators still have to show evidence for their decision-making with data centers.
“I think anything that starts bringing more attention to the very real impacts of these facilities and has any teeth at all is welcome. And this has a little bit of teeth, but it certainly could be enhanced more with strong legislation,” Boldman said. 
Another environmental legal group agrees with Boldman. In a recent statement, the Kentucky Resources Council wrote it supports the governor’s goals but that executive branch agencies are “creatures of statute and their authority and discretion are bound and limited by law.” The organization also called on the state legislature to adopt new laws for data centers.
Boldman said she wishes state lawmakers had addressed the impacts of data centers sooner. After a bill to limit data center impacts on electricity ratepayers died during this year’s legislative session, a key GOP lawmaker told the Lantern he’s working on new legislation.
“You invite a high impact economic development industry into your state, and you are surprised now at the impact because they’re coming on so fast. That should have been anticipated,” Boldman said. 
Regulator independence
Specifically, Beshear’s executive order directed the Kentucky Public Service Commission, or PSC, to deny any request from utilities to raise rates that would have other ratepayers pay for data center construction and operations. 
Yet a former chair of the commission told the Lantern the executive order doesn’t have an enforcement mechanism to ensure the commission complies. 
“I don’t think it has any legal weight. I don’t think it needs to necessarily have legal weight for the PSC to take it seriously,” said Kent Chandler, a non-resident senior fellow in energy and environmental policy at the think tank R Street Institute. “Either they’re going to take the governor’s public demands at face value, or they’re not.” 
In quasi-judicial cases, the commission weighs whether to grant utilities a rate increase to recover cost from utility investments including power plants. The governor appoints and reappoints the five commissioners on the board, who are then confirmed by the Kentucky Senate. The PSC is guided by state law — including that utility rates be “fair, just and reasonable” —  on whether to approve or deny a request. 
Chandler said parties can appeal a decision if they believe the commission didn’t follow state law or regulations. He also doesn’t believe the executive order bucks how the commission was already operating with utility cost allocation. 
“I just don’t think there’s anybody out there beating the door down at the PSC saying, ‘Yes, please, let’s allow utilities to raise rates on other customers for costs they didn’t incur for the benefit of data centers,’ right?” Chandler said.
Chandler said he also doesn’t recall a time when a governor has issued an executive order dictating to the commission how to rule on utility requests. 
Chandler pointed to the U.S. Supreme Court overturning a precedent giving President Donald Trump control over federal agencies that Congress intended to be independent. He also pointed to a new state law giving the Public Service Commission more independence in its operations from the rest of the state executive branch.
“I think it just goes to show how important regulator independence is,” Chandler said. 
He said that new state law indicated the commission is “independent from the rest of the executive branch and that they should have the ability to do their jobs without fear or favor.” 
In an emailed statement, current Public Service Commission chair Angie Hatton told the Lantern the executive order is consistent with “what the PSC has already tried to do” under its statutory mandate of setting “fair, just and reasonable” rates. 
PSC chair Angie Hatton
“When it comes to data centers and other very large load customers, fair cost allocation means striving to ensure those large loads pay for the costs they cause,” Hatton said. She said the regulator would conduct a “prudency review” to determine the cost allocation.  
The commission recently held a conference with data center developer TeraWulf to discuss the executive order as the regulator weighs whether to approve a special contract between the developer and utility Big Rivers Electric Corporation. 
Permits and energy plans 
The governor also has stood firm on his oversight of environmental permitting. 
When asked in a recent MS NOW interview about a massive hyperscale data center and natural gas-fired turbines being built on or near a federal site in McCracken County — a project he said he wasn’t briefed on ahead of time — he referenced the Energy and Environment Cabinet’s permitting power.
“You can’t operate without an air or water permit,” Beshear said. “If you’re going to invest $100 billion to build something, you probably ought to go talk to the person in charge of the state.” 
The cabinet oversees a variety of permitting for industrial sites including for water withdrawal, floodplain construction, storm water runoff and air quality, and those permits set limits on the amount of pollution allowed by an operation. Beshear’s order directed the cabinet to deny any permit request from a data center that would “negatively impact” water, air, and natural resources. 
Additionally, Beshear’s executive order requires data center developers to submit an “energy plan” to the cabinet explaining how the developer plans to protect residential ratepayers and meet its energy needs. In a PSC filing, TeraWulf said it provided on Aug. 14 an 88-page energy plan to the cabinet.  Earlier this month, Energy and Environment Cabinet Secretary John Lyons said the state has received only a few water-related permits from data center developers.
Robin Hartman, a spokesperson for the cabinet, in a statement said the cabinet is drafting “guidelines” for the energy plans. 
“All related projects – past, present and future – must provide an energy plan to Team Kentucky’s Energy and Environment Cabinet, as well as meet all other requirements outlined in the executive order,” Hartman said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Louisville woman in ICE custody after attending scheduled immigration interview
description: A 21-year-old Louisville woman was detained by federal immigration officials when she attended an interview last week for her marriage-based immigration application to get a green card.
text:
Photo of Armelle Bondonga. (Provided by Ryan Davis)A 21-year-old Louisville woman was detained by federal immigration officials when she attended an interview last week for her marriage-based immigration application to get a green card. 
Armelle Bondonga came to the U.S. on a visitor visa when she was about eight years old, said her attorney Arianit Osmani. She and her husband, a U.S. citizen, have an 19-month-old child. 
Bondonga and her husband “were attempting to follow the legal process available to them and resolve her immigration status lawfully,” Osmani said in an email to the Lantern. She was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). 
“One of the most concerning aspects of this situation is that Armelle was not hiding from immigration authorities or attempting to evade the immigration system,” Osmani added. “Quite the opposite: she voluntarily appeared before the government for an immigration interview as part of the process she and her husband were pursuing.”
Bondonga’s husband, Terrance Bradshaw, said in a statement that the interview “was seemingly going smoothly” before they “quickly took a turn for the worse — becoming a living nightmare for our family.” ICE agents put the couple in separate rooms and he was told about Bondonga’s detainment.
“I felt completely powerless kissing my wife goodbye, not knowing when I would see her next,” Bradshaw said. “Wheeling our son out of that building in his stroller without his mom is a feeling no human should ever have to endure. We left feeling trapped, betrayed, lost, and uncertain of what lies ahead for our family.”
Bondonga came to the U.S. with her family from the Democratic Republic of Congo. Since moving to Louisville in 2020, she has been active in her community with organizations like Future Ancestors and Empower Youth. 
“Her immigration history is complicated because, as a child, she was included as a derivative family member in asylum proceedings initiated by her father,” Osmani said. “There are ongoing legal proceedings concerning that matter, which are being handled by separate immigration counsel.”
A spokesperson for ICE said in a statement Bondonga entered the country in 2013 on a visa that was set to expire the following year.
“She overstayed her welcome in violation of our nation’s immigration laws, and under the Obama administration began accruing more than a decade’s worth of unlawful presence in the United States,” the spokesperson said. “On November 6, 2025, she was given a final order of removal by an immigration judge. She received due process.”
The ICE spokesperson also said being “in detention is a choice” and added that the U.S. is “offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now.”
“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream,” the spokesperson said. “If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”
Bondonga is being held in the Clark County Jail in Indiana, according to online records. Osmani said the immediate legal priority is “to prevent Armelle from being removed from the United States before the significant legal issues in her case can be meaningfully addressed.” 
“We are pursuing the legal remedies available to her, including seeking an administrative stay of removal through ICE. A stay asks ICE not to execute her removal while the pending legal matters are being addressed. We are also communicating with ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations regarding her custody and removal situation and evaluating the other legal remedies available to her,” Osmani said. He added that Bondonga’s husband has also filed a petition to ask the federal government to recognize their marriage for immigration purposes. 
Ryan Davis, a former teacher of Bondonga, said Monday evening that he had spoken to her since she has been detained by ICE. Since graduating from a Louisville high school, Bondonga has continued to help students with community groups and they’ve since kept in touch, Davis said.
“The idea of being separated from your family, especially separated from such a young child — I don’t even know the words to put in the amount of pain that someone must feel, or the amount of difficulty that must be to go through that separation,” Davis said. “And at the same time, Armelle is one of the most unbelievably strong people I have ever met.”
Earlier this month, another Louisville woman, Sarafinah Bukirwa, was released from ICE custody after being detained at the airport on her way to a conference on sickle cell anemia, a disease which she also has. Her family and Democratic U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey said she was not receiving adequate medical care for sickle cell anemia.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Alongside Kiggans, US House Speaker says Va.’s 2nd District ‘will determine the fate of the country’
description: As part of an 18-state tour through more than 30 congressional districts, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, said Monday that “Virginia’s 2nd District will determine the fate of the country because this will be a close election.”  As Johnson stumped for U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, at the Cavalier Hotel on Monday, he […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, speaks at a campaign event in Virginia Beach featuring U.S. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)As part of an 18-state tour through more than 30 congressional districts, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, said Monday that “Virginia’s 2nd District will determine the fate of the country because this will be a close election.” 
As Johnson stumped for U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, at the Cavalier Hotel on Monday, he and the incumbent congresswoman framed partisan control of the nation’s legislature during this year’s congressional midterm elections as a battle between “common sense” and “chaos.” 
“This is not a new fight now we’re in,” Kiggans, who is seeking another term in Congress, said. “It’s a fight right now between craziness and common sense and real civility and communism, socialism, and the direction that the Democratic party has gone in to the left.”
Amid a wave of non-establishment Democrats winning primary elections earlier this month in other states and internal struggles within the party’s centrist and progressive factions, Johnson said “they don’t know where they stand, what they stand for, and who stands with them — they’re kind of a rudderless ship.”
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana speaks at a campaign event for U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans in Virginia Beach on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
Leftist democrats gained traction elsewhere in the primaries, but Virginia’s establishment democrats prevailed in the state’s Aug. 4 contests. 
At the Democratic National Committee meeting over the weekend, former Virginia Gov. Terry McAuliffe urged his party to end any  “hand-wringing” over internal differences. Virginia was also confirmed as an early primary state for the 2028 election cycle at the meeting.
Democrats across the spectrum, however, have spent much of this year attacking Kiggans and other Republicans over healthcare policy and the rising costs of living. 
As Kiggans and Johnson spoke at the Virginia Beach fundraiser, her opponent, Democrat Elaine Luria, highlighted Kiggans’ record, including her vote in favor of the reconciliation bill Congress approved last summer that put thousands of Virginians at risk of losing their Medicaid health insurance. 
Luria also noted that Kiggans voted to allow Affordable Care Act subsidies to expire, which has led to thousands of people in the state losing that form of insurance.
Health care fight intensifies as Congress weighs GOP-backed insurance changes

When asked about the ongoing war in Iran that Republican President Donald Trump initiated without congressional approval earlier this year, Johnson said he believed the conflict will be resolved soon. 
“I talk to the president multiple times every day on average. He is laser focused on this,” Johnson said. 
Luria — a former member of Congress whom Kiggans ousted from the seat in 2022 — said Kiggans and Johnson “refuse to stand up to Donant Trump, and Hampton Roads is paying the price.”
“As corrupt Jen Kiggans and Mike Johnson meet with wealthy donors today, working Virginians are seeing their gas and grocery bills skyrocket, their friends and family members in uniform sent to fight in another foreign war, and their healthcare taken away to pay for tax cuts for billionaires,” Luria wrote. 
Kiggans and Johnson took jabs at Luria over her wealth, as bipartisanship efforts to ban congressional stock trading have ramped up over the past year. Kiggans is a co-sponsor of a recent attempt to reign in the practice.
Luria, who previously spoke against congressional stock trading while in congress, has evolved in her support for it as the issue has gained traction nationally. 
With early voting set to kick off Sep. 18 and Election Day on Nov. 3, Kiggans and Luria are escalating their campaigns in one of the country’s most competitive swing districts this cycle. 
Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District has been represented by both parties over the years but leans Republican. Still, its nearly 600,000 residents backed Democratic Gov. Spanberger last year by 53%. Luria first flipped it to Democratic control in 2018 before Kiggans flipped it back to Republican in 2022. 
While Kiggans did not take questions from the media at the event, Johnson made his pitch for Republicans on ballots nationwide this year.
“If you believe in America, you believe in individual freedom, limited government, the rule of law, peace through strength, and fiscal responsibility, and free markets, human dignity —  we have a place for you,” he said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia secures $17 million to upgrade rail service and improve transportation infrastructure
description: Virginia has received $17 million in federal funding to improve transportation in Staunton and Chesterfield County, and to invest in new Amtrak trains serving routes across the commonwealth. U.S. Sens. Tim Kaine and Mark Warner said the funding comes from the Department of Transportation’s Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail Grant Program,[...]
text:
A railroad crossing in Waverly, Virginia. (Photo by Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury) Virginia has received $17 million in federal funding to improve transportation in Staunton and Chesterfield County, and to invest in new Amtrak trains serving routes across the commonwealth.
U.S. Sens. Tim Kaine and Mark Warner said the funding comes from the Department of Transportation’s Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail Grant Program, created by the Infrastructure Investments and Jobs Act. The law has supported several transportation and environmental projects in Virginia, including the Long Bridge Project’s expansion, since 2021.
“Reliable passenger rail plays a critical role in connecting Virginians to their jobs, families, and communities, while also giving travelers more options to get where they need to go,” the senators said in a joint statement. 
“This funding will help modernize the Amtrak services that folks rely on, improve accessibility in Staunton, and lay the groundwork for safer rail crossings in Chesterfield County,” they added.
As part of the program’s efforts to improve passenger rail, the new trains will replace aging equipment and expand Amtrak’s fleet. This will allow additional state-supported service and aid numerous services operating in Virginia, including the Carolinian and routes connecting Washington D.C. with Newport News, Norfolk and Roanoke. 
The Virginia Passenger Rail Authority, which manages Amtrak Virginia’s passenger rail service, will receive $15 million to make the Staunton Station safer and more accessible. The upgrades will support the platform, canopy and accessibility upgrades, including handrails and curb ramps.
Chesterfield County was awarded a $2 million grant to improve two railroad crossings on Curtis Street and West Street. The goal is to separate the roads from the railroad tracks with an overpass or underpass so vehicles and trains do not have to cross paths.
The current authorization of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law is scheduled to expire on Sept. 30, barring subsequent congressional action. 
IIJA is the current law, but lawmakers are seeking to pass the BUILD America 250 Act, a five-year surface transportation reauthorization bill that would succeed IIJA by investing in America’s roads, bridges, transit, rail transportation, and highway and motor carrier safety programs.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Three weeks out, McKee is still 20 points behind Foulkes in governor’s race
description: Three weeks and a day out from the primary, Gov. Dan McKee has failed to narrow a 20-point gap with his Democratic gubernatorial challenger, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a survey published Tuesday by The Pell Center at Salve Regina University finds.  The poll of 857 likely primary voters echoes surveys by other organizations, which also showed […]
text:
Helena Buonanno Foulkes, left, continues to lead in polling over Gov. Dan McKee, but 22% of respondents in a recent poll remain undecided with three weeks to go before the Democratic primary. (Left photo by Michael Salerno, right photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Three weeks and a day out from the primary, Gov. Dan McKee has failed to narrow a 20-point gap with his Democratic gubernatorial challenger, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a survey published Tuesday by The Pell Center at Salve Regina University finds. 
The poll of 857 likely primary voters echoes surveys by other organizations, which also showed Foulkes with a 20-point or higher lead over McKee. 
“There’s no strong surprises there,” said Katie Sonder, Pell Center associate director and fellow. “Helena Foulkes has been leading McKee over the last few months.”
The new survey is the Pell Center’s first 2026 election-specific poll, conducted Aug. 3 to 11 by Embold Research. The margin of error is 3.6%, with a 4.2% error margin for Democratic primary-specific questions.
Survey results were shared with Rhode Island Current in advance. 
More than 1 in 5 voters were still undecided at the time of the survey, which ended one day before the first televised gubernatorial debates. 
“With those undecideds, we could see it swing in either candidate’s direction,” Sonder said.
And the governor is “running strong,” said Sophie Mestas, a spokesperson for McKee’s campaign.
“Public polling has been notoriously inconsistent this cycle, and in the final weeks of the race, Governor McKee is running strong – going 2-0 in debates against his opponent, earning the backing of Rhode Island’s labor unions, and delivering an Affordability for All agenda that lowers costs for working families while protecting the health care and food assistance Donald Trump is trying to take away,” Mestas said in an emailed response Monday.”
Foulkes’ campaign did not immediately return requests for comment.



Quotation







With those undecideds, we could see it swing in either candidate’s direction. 


– Katie Sonder, Pell Center associate director and fellow, on the governor’s race


McKee trails Foulkes in nearly every demographic group: age, gender, race, education level and county of residence, according to Pell’s survey. Foulkes, 62, of Providence, had the strongest margin among voters ages 18-34, white voters, and those who live in Bristol and Newport counties.
McKee, 75, of Cumberland, came closest to Foulkes among voters 65 and older and in Kent County, where he trailed by just 1 point. Sonder declined to speculate about the support for McKee in Kent County, which leans more conservative than the state as a whole. McKee had more support than Foulkes among people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, though Foulkes was still favored by registered Republicans, according to the survey results.
McKee’s campaign has repeatedly tried to link Foulkes to conservative causes and candidates, noting her past political donations to the political action committees for CVS, her former employer, and The Home Depot, where she served on the board. CVS gave $35,000 to the Trump Victory Fund in 2017, while The Home Depot has donated to GOP candidates, and its late cofounder was a vocal Trump supporter. 
Foulkes responded that she never made personal donations to Trump, and that her contributions to company PACs were spent without her personal input.
A new conservative political group, The League of RI Businesses, has publicly encouraged Republican voters to disaffiliate to participate in state Democratic primaries. Yet data from the Rhode Island Department of State shows few GOP voters have left the party in the last three months.
Turnout in the Sept. 9 primary will be the biggest factor in the outcome, and margin, of the gubernatorial race, Sonder said. Nearly 17% of voters cast ballots in the 2022 state primaries, in which McKee defeated Foulkes by 3 points in four-way race. Just under 10% of voters participated in the 2024 primaries, which did not include state general offices.
‘Undecided’ voters loom large in down ballot races
This year’s primaries also feature close contests for lieutenant governor and attorney general. Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos maintained a 2-point edge over her top challenger, Newport City Councilor Xay Khamsyvoravong, according to the Pell Center survey. But nearly half of Democratic voters surveyed were undecided in the five-way primary, which also includes Providence City Councilor Sue AnderBois, former state Sen. Cynthia Coyne, and science teacher Ross McCurdy.
“Down ballot races tend to have a much higher number of people who are unsure,” Sonder said, noting that despite Matos’ incumbency, her challengers include several other sitting or former officeholders with name recognition.
The open race to succeed Attorney General Peter Neronha, who is term-limited, is also undecided, with 46% of Democratic voters unsure. But while prior surveys suggested all four Democratic contenders on the same level, former Cannabis Control Commission Chair Kim Ahern now has a 10-point edge, with support from nearly one in four voters, the survey shows.
Josh Block, a spokesperson for Ahern’s campaign, called the poll results “encouraging.”
“With three weeks left until the primary, we’re not taking anything for granted, and Kim will continue working hard in every community to show why her unparalleled experience uniquely prepares her to take on the big fights and protect Rhode Islanders’ fundamental rights as our next Attorney General,” Block said in an emailed response.
Keith Hoffmann, Neronha’s former policy chief, had the next most support at 13%, followed by Rep. Joe Solomon Jr. at 10% and Rep. Jason Knight at 5%.
Across the political aisle, Republican gubernatorial candidate Elaine Pelino maintained a commanding 20-point lead over Aaron Guckian, with more than 4 in 10 voters undecided. Pelino, a retired comedian first-time candidate and self-proclaimed MAGA Republican, also outperformed Guckian in prior public polls despite having less name recognition, less money and having lost the state GOP endorsement to Guckian. Guckian previously worked as an aide to Gov. Don Carcieri and ran unsuccessfully for lieutenant governor in 2022.
The survey also took the temperature in the rare Republican Congressional primary for the 2nd Congressional District seat, held by U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner. Party-endorsed challenger Stephen Skoly, a Cranston oral surgeon, led Marine Corps veteran Vic Mellor by 7 points, just outside the 5.6% margin of error for questions specific to Republican voters.
On the U.S. Senate side, Rhode Island’s senior Democratic senator, Jack Reed, had the backing of more than 6 in 10 voters, compared with 12% support for primary challenger Connor Burbridge. One in 5 Democratic voters were undecided.
The survey was more heavily weighted toward registered Democrats and Republicans than independents to better gauge the feelings of those most likely to participate in party primaries, said Erin Barry, a Pell Center spokesperson. Of the 857 respondents to the survey, 46% were registered Democrats, while 26% were Republican voters, with 27% unaffiliated. State voter registration data shows more than half of the 691,000 registered voters are independent, with another one-third registered as Democrats, and the remainder Republicans. 
Participants represented both genders and a range of ages and education levels. More than 8 in 10 survey respondents identified as white.
Early voting begins Thursday ahead of a Sept. 9 primary.

title: After pushback, DNC votes against changing rules around ranked choice voting
description: The national Democratic Party voted this weekend against a proposal that could have restricted the use of ranked choice voting in presidential primaries. In a voice vote at the Democratic National Committee’s full meeting in Austin, Texas, members voted against adding language to the rules governing the delegate selection process that would have only conside[...]
text:
Maine's ranked-choice 2024 presidential ballot. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)The national Democratic Party voted this weekend against a proposal that could have restricted the use of ranked choice voting in presidential primaries.
In a voice vote at the Democratic National Committee’s full meeting in Austin, Texas, members voted against adding language to the rules governing the delegate selection process that would have only considered first round votes.
Maine allows voters to rank their preference in primaries for the state legislature, governor, Congress and president, but only in general elections for federal offices. After the presidential primary, each state sends delegates to the national nominating convention in accordance with the rules set by the party.
Jim Roosevelt Jr, co-chair of the Rules and Bylaws Committee, said that the committee had only intended to “clarify existing rules,” but that the suggested changes “caused a bit of a stir.”
Ranked choice voting advocates in Maine and elsewhere had raised concern that the changes would confuse voters and amounted to the national party trying to steamroll state election processes.
Under the proposed changes, the rules would have stated: “No ballot used for purposes of allocation of delegates among presidential preference shall permit voters to express more than one presidential preference. Where state law provides for multiple presidential preferences in a primary, only the first round will be considered for delegate allocation purposes.”
Previously, the committee had worked with states that use ranked choice voting on their delegate selection plans, said committee member Frank Leone of Washington, D.C., who moved to strike the new language. 
Speaking in favor of the plan, Artie Blanco of Nevada encouraged other members to “respect the work of the committee.”
But Jessica Cook of Alaska, which also employs ranked choice voting, argued the proposal “would render a voter’s choice meaningless.” 
“We know what works best for our voters and what we need to do to compete,” Cook said. “That’s why we are fired up about this.”
