name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Bills for kratom regulation, synthetic ban advance to North Dakota special session
description: North Dakota lawmakers on Monday advanced two complementary proposals to regulate kratom and ban synthetic substances.  The bill drafts, the result of a Kratom Working Group, will be considered in September during a special session called by Gov. Kelly Armstrong to address the substance’s lack of regulation in North Dakota.  A bill draft proposed by […]
text:
Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, speaks during a meeting of Legislative Management on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers on Monday advanced two complementary proposals to regulate kratom and ban synthetic substances. 
The bill drafts, the result of a Kratom Working Group, will be considered in September during a special session called by Gov. Kelly Armstrong to address the substance’s lack of regulation in North Dakota. 
A bill draft proposed by Rep. Pat Heinert, R-Bismarck, would adopt regulations for natural kratom products that mimic existing laws for tobacco products like cigarettes. 
The bill would prohibit the sale of kratom products to anyone under 21 years old, create labeling requirements for kratom products that include a warning it may be addictive, and empower the attorney general to regulate the sale of such products in North Dakota. 
It also bans packaging that imitates candy products or otherwise is marketed in a manner that appeals to children.
“That has become a big thing in the kratom industry. Bright colors, flashy stuff,” Heinert said. “Those things are all marketed towards the underage people.”
Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, said she considers Heinert’s proposed legislation to be a good starting point. 
Rep. Pat Heinert, R-Bismarck, speaks during a meeting of Legislative Management on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Sen. Janne Myrdal, R-Edinburg, said she doesn’t see the benefit of leaving kratom legal at all. 
“I would prefer a total ban because I don’t see how good this is for anyone,” Myrdal said. 
The second half of the working group’s legislation, proposed by Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, proposes a ban on synthetic derivatives of kratom such as 7-OH and any other derivatives that hit the market in the future. The bill also includes criminal penalties for use and possession of synthetic derivatives of kratom. 
“It matches the penalty structure of marijuana,” Axtman said. 
Use of synthetic derivatives of mitragynine, a chemical in kratom, would be an infraction for a person’s first offense and a misdemeanor for all future offenses. 
Possession of synthetic kratom derivatives would be considered an infraction for the first offense, misdemeanor on the second occasion, and a felony for all future incidents.
Axtman said the bill was written to add kratom synthetic derivatives as a Schedule I drug to match the expected action from the Drug Enforcement Administration. 
“That is their plan,” Axtman said. “This will match that.”
Both bills, if passed by the Legislature, would take effect as soon as they are filed with the secretary of state. 
Armstrong announced his plans to call for a special session during a press conference earlier this month, and on the same day he issued an executive order banning the sale of kratom products in the state for 30 days due to a public health emergency. 
The governor said his decision was prompted by the DEA’s move to temporarily classify 7-OH and three related compounds as controlled substances.

title: WA state Senate primary separated by 4 votes, set for recount
description: Two Democratic Washington state Senate hopefuls are headed for a recount as just four votes separate them for second place in the primary and a spot on the November ballot.  After examining challenged ballots Monday, Michael Shepard led Eamonn Collins with 13,125 votes to 13,121 in the 42nd Legislative District. Nearly 50,000 votes have been […]
text:
Left, Eamonn Collins and, right, Michael Shepard. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)Two Democratic Washington state Senate hopefuls are headed for a recount as just four votes separate them for second place in the primary and a spot on the November ballot. 
After examining challenged ballots Monday, Michael Shepard led Eamonn Collins with 13,125 votes to 13,121 in the 42nd Legislative District. Nearly 50,000 votes have been counted in total.
The results will be confirmed by a hand recount next week. Recounts don’t often shift electoral outcomes, but the counts are rarely this close. 
“For me, this is uncharted territory,” Shepard said Monday evening. He noted his campaign had been reaching out to voters with challenged ballots to resolve the concerns to ensure their votes could be counted.
Collins didn’t immediately return a request for comment.
The two Democrats are running for an open seat with Sen. Sharon Shewmake, D-Bellingham, forgoing reelection. Shepard or Collins will face Republican Erika Creydt, a psychologist and Blaine school board member, in November.
On Monday, the county canvassing board reviewed challenged ballots, of which there have been a few hundred. Those ballots either were unsigned or the signatures didn’t match those on file. Voters had until 4:30 p.m. Monday to cure ballots challenged for signature issues. An additional 125 votes were tallied Monday.
Going into Monday’s latest tally Shepard had climbed up to 20 votes ahead of Collins. At one point, Collins was just two votes behind Shepard. 
The district covers north Bellingham and rural Whatcom County, including Ferndale, Lynden and Blaine. In recent years, it has become more reliably blue. As recently as 2022, it was represented by a Republican state senator.
Shepard is a Bellingham port commissioner and anthropology instructor at Western Washington University endorsed by Shewmake. Collins, a science teacher at the Lummi Nation School, considers himself a grassroots progressive running to the left of Shepard’s more establishment lane. He’s also a former U.S. Senate policy adviser.
County results are set to be certified Tuesday. The secretary of state’s office will certify them by Friday.
The recount is expected to take about three days and additional time for the canvassing board to certify the final results, said Whatcom County Auditor Stacy Henthorn. The county election’s office will post further details about the recount online Tuesday afternoon, Henthorn said.
The bar for a manual recount like this is that candidates have to be separated by fewer than 150 votes and 0.25% of the total votes. A machine recount is triggered when the difference between two candidates is under 0.5% of the total ballots cast and fewer than 2,000 votes.
The top two candidates in Washington primaries advance to the general election regardless of party.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Creydt picked up 44.6% of the primary vote while the two Democratic candidates combined total was nearly 53%. That bodes well for the party’s chances of retaining the seat. Senate terms last four years.
Creydt, the only Republican in the race, leads the fundraising battle, bringing in $199,000. She’s spent almost all of it. Shepard has raised $105,000 and Collins $75,000.
The two Democrats recently filmed a video together for social media to discuss the close race and to commit to support whoever advances.
“If anyone ever tells you your vote doesn’t matter,” Shepard said, “think differently because we know it does.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Ashley Hinson speaks in support of $1.5 trillion defense funding package
description: U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson said Monday she supports providing the U.S. Department of Defense funding that allows the nation to have a strong military presence during their war with Iran. Earlier Monday, Hinson, who running for U.S. Senate in 2026, appeared alongside U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for a campaign event supporting U.S. Rep. Zach […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat, gave a speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 17, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson said Monday she supports providing the U.S. Department of Defense funding that allows the nation to have a strong military presence during their war with Iran.
Earlier Monday, Hinson, who running for U.S. Senate in 2026, appeared alongside U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for a campaign event supporting U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn at JR’s Southpork Ranch. Hegseth called for Iowans to support Nunn’s reelection campaign in the 3rd District because President Donald Trump “needs the type of leaders who understand why a $1.5 trillion dollar budget, a one-time generational investment, is what is necessary” for the Defense Department.

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Monday was the third day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic gubernatorial candidate: Rob Sand
Republican secretary of agriculture candidate: Mike Naig
Democratic secretary of state candidate: Ryan Peterman
Republican secretary of state candidate: Paul Pate
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Republican 3rd Congressional District candidate: Zach Nunn
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Republican 4th Congressional District candidate:  Chris McGowan


Hegseth, who leads the department, made the $1.5 trillion request — the largest request in U.S. history — earlier in 2026, as the U.S. continues its conflict with Iran. But the defense secretary has faced trouble getting this budget across the finish line, with Politico reporting that some Republicans have expressed skepticism about the Trump administration’s large defense budget proposal, especially ahead of a contentious midterm election.
When asked about the funding proposal after speaking at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, Hinson spoke about a bipartisan meeting with one of the vice chairmen of the Joint Chiefs of Staff to “talk about what the Department of War is going to need going forward across all the branches.”
“Let me say, I support our war fighters in this mission,” Hinson said. I want to make sure that our Iowans who are fighting, anyone who’s fighting, is resourced properly and has what they need. The most important thing is deterrence, not just with the situation with Iran, but other conflicts potentially around the world. So I think a strong military, as the secretary talked about, focusing on readiness, not DEI in the military, is going to continue to be my priority.
There are also concerns about the high price tag of the DOD budget request for people concerned about federal spending or an increased national debt. “I would say both parties are blaming for where we are right now in terms of government spending,” Hinson said, adding that she voted against a $6 trillion budget proposal from former President Joe Biden.
Hinson currently represents Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, but joined the Senate race after U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst, who currently holds the seat, announced she would not seek reelection. Hinson is running against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in the upcoming midterm election.
Political forecasters rate the seat as “leans Republican” — a designation that means while Republicans are predicted to maintain control of the seat, it will be a more competitive race than seen in previous recent election cycles.
Hinson was met with a passionate crowd of  supporters — and some opponents — as she spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday. While a majority of people held up signs supporting her campaign before she spoke, some in the crowd held signs saying “Decent Iowans Support Josh Turek,” and others posing questions to the congresswoman.
During her Soapbox speech, Hinson said Turek was an “absentee legislator,” and criticized him for attending a Democratic fundraising event instead of being present at the Iowa State Fair Monday. Turek has been at the fair previous days, and gave his own soapbox speech Friday.
Hinson said Turek “skipped” the Iowa State Fair Veterans’ Parade earlier Monday, “and he also skipped the vote to fund the Department of Veterans Affairs here in Iowa.”
Supporters of U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson’s campaign for U.S. Senate, as well as some opponents who are supporting Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, held up signs before her speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 17, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
On Saturday, Turek was asked by reporters about criticisms that he had missed votes at the Iowa State Capitol this year. The Democrat responded that he was spending time “meeting Iowans all over the state” as he ran for U.S. Senate — then competing in a primary against Iowa Sen. Zach Wahls — and said his record showed he was an effective state legislator.
“Something that I’m very very proud of is my my time in the Iowa Legislature — one of the most effective, one of the most bipartisan,” Turek said. “Ashley Hinson has already also missed 193 votes in her six years up in Congress. … Look, when I joined the Iowa Legislature, I was told, ‘you’ll never get a subcommittee, you’ll never get a committee, you’ll certainly never get anything signed by the governor.’ And I went out there and I worked really, really hard behind the scenes –the kind of work that nobody you will see or hear from — to find strange bedfellows, build relationships across the aisle, and I was able to get a lot of policy to the finish line. That’s what’s missing in D.C., that’s exactly the kind of senator that I will be.”

title: Naig says Secretary of Agriculture race presents ‘distinct’ choice
description: Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig, speaking at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, said he and his opponent have “fundamentally different” views of the office.  Naig is running against water quality researcher and advocate Chris Jones, who has the Democratic nomination for the seat. Jones has been critical of the large-scale farm model […[...]
text:
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig speaks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig, speaking at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, said he and his opponent have “fundamentally different” views of the office. 
Naig is running against water quality researcher and advocate Chris Jones, who has the Democratic nomination for the seat. Jones has been critical of the large-scale farm model that is dependent on corn, soybeans and ethanol. 
“He just has a very fundamentally different opinion about how to work on the issues that we need to work on,” Naig said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jones has suggested policies to improve water quality by taxing or restricting things like fertilizers and animal sales and banning things like new tile drainage lines, fall tillage and chemical applications to ditches. 
Naig said this approach would lead to a “smaller” and “diminished” agriculture. 
“That kind of taxing and regulating drives farmers out of business, which will put our land and our farms in the hands of fewer and fewer farmers, and that is the opposite of what we need to be seeing,” Naig said. “So there is a distinct difference between him and me when it comes to this race.” 
Meet Iowa’s secretary of agriculture candidates

Jones called the attacks “desperate” and said Naig has been “responsible for Iowa’s declining water quality for the past decade.” 
“Under Naig’s policies, the average Iowa farmer is sentenced to an endless and desperate cycle of trying to acquire more and more land, which has led to consolidation and driven the population downward in 70 of our 99 counties while hollowing out many of our small towns,” Jones said in a statement. “I think we need a new approach.”
Naig, who has held the position since 2018, said all Iowans “benefit from a strong agriculture.” 
“A strong agriculture leads to strong families and strong communities, and a stronger Iowa because of it,” Naig said. 
Naig said to continue supporting Iowa agriculture, the state needs to continue expanding international, national and local markets to make sure farmers can get paid for the things they grow and to secure more funding for conservation practices that improve water quality. 
Iowa has continued to adopt conservation practices like cover crops, but Naig said it’s “not good enough.” 
“We need to do more,” Naig said.
Cancer
Iowa’s high cancer incidence rates, which have also been tied to the state’s water quality concerns, has become a top issue in many of Iowa’s political races this year. 
While speaking to reporters about the subject, Naig said, “we’re not in a good place as a state.” 
“I think what we know is that this is more complex than what some want to make it, and I think you’ve got some who have decided that it’s a political issue, and I think that can be very dangerous,” Naig said. 
Farmers he has spoken with, he said, told him they are frustrated at being blamed for Iowa’s cancer crisis as many reports and groups point to nitrate concentrations in the water and pesticide exposure as cancer drivers. 
“It’s okay to to wonder, to ask questions, to want to know the causes, that’s where we need to go,” Naig said. “But let’s actually understand what’s going on, and then let’s address that.” 
Jones is slated to speak at the Soapbox Saturday, the full Soapbox schedule can be found here.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Ex-NU Regent Elizabeth O’Connor given 1-year sentence for felony DUI
description: OMAHA — A former University of Nebraska regent will spend at least the next six months in jail for driving under the influence and causing serious bodily injury during a May 2025 crash. Douglas County District Judge Jeffrey Lux on Monday sentenced Elizabeth O’Connor of Omaha to one year behind bars. Under Nebraska’s “good time” law, […]
text:
Then-University of Nebraska Regent Elizabeth O'Connor of Omaha, center, talks with NU Regent Tim Clare. Dec. 5, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — A former University of Nebraska regent will spend at least the next six months in jail for driving under the influence and causing serious bodily injury during a May 2025 crash.
Douglas County District Judge Jeffrey Lux on Monday sentenced Elizabeth O’Connor of Omaha to one year behind bars. Under Nebraska’s “good time” law, Lux said, O’Connor could be released for good behavior after serving half her sentence. Lux also sentenced O’Connor to 18 months of post-release supervision, which is similar to probation. She was credited with one day of time served from the night she was arrested in July 2025.
O’Connor and her attorney had asked for probation and no jail time. 
A police-drawn diagram of a car crash that occurred the evening of May 21, 2025, involving University of Nebraska Regent Elizabeth O’Connor, whose vehicle is illustrated in green. (Courtesy of Omaha Police Department)
She will lose her driver’s license for five years and likely face disciplinary action related to her law license.
Prosecutors charged O’Connor with a Class IIIA felony in late July 2025. After first pleading not guilty, she changed her plea to guilty in mid-May. She could have faced up to three years in prison.
“It’s five people that went through this crash,” Lux said, referring to the five passengers in the car O’Connor hit. “I won’t call it an accident, because it wasn’t. It was a crash. You caused it.”
Three of the passengers were young children who were returning home from Bible study with their grandparents. The grandmother, Latonda Johnson, sustained a broken back and pelvis. 
After the crash, the children’s father, Johnson’s son-in-law, publicly urged O’Connor to resign.
Court records
The crash occurred about 8:30 p.m. May 21, 2025, in the Benson area of Omaha in O’Connor’s former NU Regents District 4 in eastern Douglas County. Prosecutors said tests showed she had a blood alcohol content of 0.321% after the crash. That’s four times the legal limit.
Douglas County District Judge Jeffrey Lux. (Photo courtesy of Nebraska Judicial Branch)
In court records, an investigator said police had found a half-empty bottle of Fireball Whisky in O’Connor’s vehicle, and she was showing symptoms of intoxication after the crash. A field sobriety test confirmed her condition, as did the blood analysis.
Lux said he works with veterans and assists with veterans treatment courts. Of those he’s seen at a blood alcohol level that high, Lux said, it’s “such a scary level” that could be potentially life-threatening, such as the person becoming unconscious or having alcohol poisoning.
“I don’t think this was a one-time kind of drinking experience,” Lux said.
Since the incident, Omaha City Prosecutor Kevin Slimp said, Johnson has made limited progress in physical therapy and needs help with daily activities. He said the crash cut short Johnson’s 25-year career with Omaha Public Schools, where she helped at-risk youth.
‘I was not coping’
For the first time publicly Monday, O’Connor detailed how she had been struggling in ways she had “not fully recognized or addressed” around the time of the crash. Her father, whom she described as her best friend, died in summer 2024 from pancreatic cancer. Shortly after his death, O’Connor gave birth to her daughter, who is now 2 years old.
Her attorney, Marcus Sladek, said O’Connor faced a diagnosis of severe postpartum depression and significant depressive episodes.
“I was not healthy, and I was not coping with these challenges in a healthy way,” O’Connor told Lux.
The University of Nebraska Board of Regents. Dec. 5, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Voters reelected her to a second six-year term in November 2024. She resigned as a deputy county attorney in the Douglas County Attorney’s Office civil division days after prosecutors brought charges last summer. Because she had worked in that office, the case was handed off to Slimp’s office.
O’Connor said that once she saw how her actions hurt others, she knew she needed to begin “rebuilding” her life and that “things had gotten out of control.”
“Throughout my life, I have tried to be the kind of person who makes others feel welcome, comfortable and safe,” O’Connor told Lux. “And knowing that I did the exact opposite that day, and that I took away from someone else’s sense of safety, is something that I’m going to carry with me for the rest of my life.”
If she hadn’t resigned in early January as a regent, O’Connor could have faced impeachment this spring, the first such action in two decades.
The Nebraska Constitution bars felons from holding public office unless the Nebraska Board of Pardons restores the person’s civil rights. O’Connor would have been forced to leave office had she still been on the board. She also can’t vote until the completion of her full sentence.
There is a special election for the final four years of O’Connor’s elected term on Nov. 3.
‘Uncharacteristic outlier’
O’Connor and Sladek said she is about 15 months sober, attends weekly Alcoholics Anonymous meetings and meets with her sponsor. This is her first criminal offense, and she has continued to seek mental health and substance use counseling, according to Sladek and O’Connor.
Sladek said O’Connor’s risk of reoffending is low and probation would be well suited to help with rehabilitation and treatment. He described the incident as an “uncharacteristic outlier.”
“If there is a perfect or appropriate way to respond to such an offense in such a situation, I think Elizabeth has done that,” Sladek said.
Sladek also pointed to about 19 letters in support of O’Connor’s “true character.” He responded to a victim impact statement from Johnson, who attended the sentencing.
From left, then-UNL Student Regent Paul Pechous and then-Regent Elizabeth O’Connor and Regent Rob Schafer. Oct. 5, 2023. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The attorney said that insurance will cover Johnson’s pain and that O’Connor — no matter the sentence — would not get a “slap on the hand.” Sladek said that was the phrase Johnson used in describing her frustrations to the court and weighing in on what she did not want to see occur.
Sladek also said O’Connor’s husband and daughter would experience “excessive hardship” if O’Connor faced jail time. Because O’Connor has been unemployed, Sladek said, her husband has been the primary breadwinner.
“I’m in no way suggesting that Elizabeth is a victim here. She’s not, and all of these consequences that I just cited are, frankly, foreseeable consequences that she understands she brought on herself,” Sladek said. “But she has waded through the treacherous waters that have followed this with silence and with grace, with remorse and with a single-minded focus on self-improvement.”
Sladek similarly sought to appeal to Lux that lawyers, including O’Connor, are in the business of helping others and solving their problems. However, Sladek said, it’s “far too easy” for attorneys to neglect their own problems and “far too difficult to ask for help for ourselves.” Sladek said O’Connor has learned that it’s OK to ask for help and speak up about what’s wrong.
“I know that it’s devastating to her that it took this to realize that, and more devastating to her that somebody else was [hurt] in the wake of that,” Sladek said.
‘I’m truly sorry’
Lux, a former prosecutor for Douglas County and the state, said he would have made a similar argument regarding O’Connor’s daughter. But he said three of the 19 letters for O’Connor referenced another victim and that he had to recognize O’Connor hurt another mother.
“A grandmother here, who can’t interact with her grandkids the same way that she could before you came into her life, by force,” Lux said.
Omaha-area lines for the University of Nebraska Board of Regents in Douglas County. (Photo courtesy of Nebraska Legislative Research Office)
Slimp said he was not opposed to probation but suggested it be for multiple years if so. He did suggest that if jail time was imposed, it be served up front. Because of the nature of the DUI, O’Connor served one night in jail when she was arrested in late July 2025, rather than longer while waiting for DUI test results, Slimp said.
Lux said he believed incarceration plus post-release supervision would be the “fairest way to achieve justice in this case.” He told O’Connor the sentence “takes into account the good things that you’ve done up to this point,” including her public service and path to recovery.
At the end of the hearing, the Douglas County sheriff’s deputies handcuffed O’Connor and took her into custody.
“I’m truly sorry for the harm and the pain that I caused through my actions,” O’Connor said earlier in the hearing. “What I can do now is continue taking responsibility, continue the work of recovery, of facing what I did, and continue proving through my actions that I’m never going to let this happen again.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Greenbelt back as next home for FBI, after court rejects ‘unlawful’ plan to stay in DC
description: A federal district judge in Maryland Monday overturned Trump administration plans to build the next FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C., restoring Greenbelt as the likely next home for the agency.
text:
The current FBI headquarters at the aging J. Edgar Hoover Building in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)A federal district judge in Maryland Monday overturned Trump administration plans to build the next FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C., restoring Greenbelt as the likely next home for the agency.
The 47-page ruling and two-page order by U.S. District Judge Theodore Chuang said the abrupt decision last year by the FBI and the General Services Administration to say they would move the headquarters into the Ronald Reagan Building in downtown Washington exceeded their authority and was “unlawful.”
Chuang’s order vacated the decision by the two agencies, which tossed out years of debate and study that led to the selection of Greenbelt site in 2023, and ordered them to reverse their plan to reprogram $555 million of Greenbelt funding “to relocate to, renovate, build-out, and furnish” the Reagan Building as the next FBI headquarters.
The White House referred requests for comment to the FBI, which did not immediately respond to a request Monday evening. But Maryland officials were tripping over themselves to cheer the ruling.
Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown, who was first to report the decision late Monday afternoon, said that by blocking the Trump administration attempt to move the project and divert the funds, “the Court has cleared the path back to Greenbelt.”
“This victory is about more than a building. It is about ensuring that when Congress makes a decision, the Federal Government cannot simply ignore it because they do not like the outcome,” Brown said in a prepared statement.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Trump “tried to take from Maryland what Maryland had already won. He failed.”
“I am grateful to all of Team Maryland – especially Congressman Steny Hoyer – who have worked tirelessly for decades to make this a reality,” he said in a statement released by his office. “Now it is time to stop the games and get to work building the world-class FBI headquarters that our public servants deserve, where it belongs: in Prince George’s County, Maryland.”
Team Maryland is a reference to the coalition of state, local and federal officials who pushed back against the Reagan Building proposal, and filed the lawsuit last November that Chuang ruled on Monday.
All sides agree that a new headquarters building is needed to replace the current facility, the J. Edgar Hoover Building on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington. The brutalist, concrete building, which opened in 1974, long ago outlived its usefulness and has been literally falling apart for years, with pieces of concrete falling off the building at times.
The dilapidated building is too small for current agency functions, forcing the FBI to lease office space around Washington, which is not only costly but does not allow for efficient management of the sprawling FBI.
Repairing the Hoover Building has been determined to be neither technically nor economically feasible. Congress in 2011 directed the GSA to find a new site on federal land in the Washington area, within 2 miles of a Metro station and 2.5 miles of the Capital Beltway, for a new consolidated headquarters building. Proceeds from the sale of the Hoover Building were to be dedicated to the project.
The GSA quickly developed a short list of sites: Greenbelt and Landover in Maryland, and Springfield, in Northern Virginia. In 2017, Congress approved funding for the project.
But in July 2017, during Trump’s first term, the FBI and GSA hit the brakes on the project, saying Congress had not appropriated sufficient funding for the entire project. It stalled for the rest of Trump’s term.
In 2022, Congress restarted the process and in November 2023 — after serious wrangling between lawmakers in Maryland and Virginia — the director of a special GSA selection committee announced Greenbelt as its choice.
The Trump administration upended that on July 1, 2025, when the FBI and GSA jointly announced that they were abandoning Greenbelt and moving the headquarters to the Reagan Building, a few blocks away from its current location.
Maryland officials sued, claiming that the selection of Greenbelt had been authorized by Congress and could not simply be reversed by executive agencies.
Chuang agreed, saying the agencies exceeded their authority and their actions violated the law and the Administrative Protection Act. He also issued an injunction against the government taking any actions or spending any funds to facilitate the Reagan Building move.
The government argued in court that rejecting the Reagan Building would “likely result in the FBI Headquarters remaining in the Hoover Building indefinitely,” since it would not order construction to start on Greenbelt. But Chuang disagreed, saying rejecting the Reagan Building would have the effect of reinstating Greenbelt as the selected site for the project.
Team Maryland — eight of the nine members of the state’s congressional delegation — vowed to keep fighting to make the new headquarters in Greenbelt a reality.
“We will not stop fighting to fulfill our promise to the men and women of the Bureau to deliver a new, secure headquarters in Maryland so they can do their work without compromising their safety or our national security,” they said in a joint statement last night.
Prince Ge0rge’s County Executive Aisha Braveboy (D) welcomed the decision, saying the FBI project would be “the single largest economic development project in the history of Prince George’s County.”
“It is estimated to create over 7,500 jobs and add approximately $4 billion to the GDP of the County and State,” she said in a statement released by her office. “If you look at the history of economic development in the Metro DC region, landing a major federal agency like the FBI has been the catalyst for significant economic development.
“Prince George’s County simply wants the opportunity to reap the economic benefits that would flow from locating the FBI HQ in Greenbelt,” Braveboy said.
— Maryland Matters reporter William J. Ford contributed to this report.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Secretary of State Paul Pate says 2026 ‘potential noncitizen’ list unlikely
description: Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate said Monday his office is unlikely to issue guidance in the upcoming election for county auditors to challenge the ballots of people identified as as potential noncitizens, a situation that happened in 2024. Two weeks before the Nov. 5, 2024 election, Pate issued guidance to county auditors to challenge […]
text:
Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate speaks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate said Monday his office is unlikely to issue guidance in the upcoming election for county auditors to challenge the ballots of people identified as as potential noncitizens, a situation that happened in 2024.
Two weeks before the Nov. 5, 2024 election, Pate issued guidance to county auditors to challenge ballots of 2,176 registered voters identified as potential noncitizens, because they had reported to the Iowa Department of Transportation or another government entity they were not U.S. citizens in the past 12 years and went on to register to vote. Pate said at the time the action was necessary because his office was denied access to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database to confirm the current voting eligibility of these individuals.
After his speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, Pate answered a question from a reporter on whether similar guidance would be issued in 2026 — something Pate said would not happen as Iowa gained access to the SAVE database, resolved through a lawsuit in 2025.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Pate said, “I hope we never have to do anything like that again.”

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Monday was the third day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Republican 3rd Congressional District candidate: Zach Nunn
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Republican 4th Congressional District candidate:  Chris McGowan
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood
Democratic secretary of state candidate: Ryan Peterman

“It was unfortunate last time, when the Biden White House wouldn’t give us the list,” Pate said. “So we we had no choice but to do what we did. I hated it, and quite frankly, that’s why I wasn’t a fan of when (media) and others wanted the list. I’m going, ‘no, that’s like putting the scarlet letter on these people.’ I’m trying not to do that. We’re trying to make this as subtle as we can, to help them through the process without putting the scarlet letter on. But now since we do have the access to the list, we’ve already went through the list. And we’re doing that to make sure we’re comfortable with where we’re at. And so I don’t see that as a necessary thing to happen.”
In March 2025, Pate said 277 of the 2,176 individuals identified as potential noncitizens in the 2024 general election were confirmed to not have U.S. citizenship, and could not legally participate in U.S. elections.
Pate has served as secretary of state since 2015, and previously held the position from 1995 to 1999. He’s challenged in the 2026 election by Democrat Ryan Peterman, who has criticized Pate for sharing Iowa voter information with the U.S. Department of Justice.
In May, Pate announced Iowa had decided to comply with the DOJ’s request for voter registration data, which included personally identifiable information like driver’s license and Social Security numbers, after consulting with secretary of state’s legal team and the Iowa Attorney General’s Office. Pate had said these legal advisers determined the U.S. attorney general had the power to demand this information, and that his office was required to share the data.
However, Peterman has argued this conclusion was incorrect. He pointed to officials in other states refusing the DOJ demand. The DOJ brought legal challenges to 30 states’ decisions not to share information. So far, 20 of these cases have been dismissed, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.
Pate told reporters he understands why others are “sensitive” about his decision to share this information, saying, “I’m very sensitive to it as well.” He said it was not a decision he made lightly — but also said that critics are misrepresenting the situation as him fully giving over information to the DOJ. He said the DOJ also asked his office to sign a memorandum of understanding, which he refused to do, saying he instead laid out conditions for how the federal department would be able to use the shared voter information.
“This was all before all these court cases were popping up, so it was like, Monday morning quarterbacks come to me now and said, ‘Well, what do you think now? All these other states have done this.’ … Well, I understand, time goes on … They’re still not done with it. They’re still in court, so we’ll see how everything resolves in the end. But I had to keep a decision based on what I had for information at the time, so that’s where I’m at on it.”
Pate said he wanted to make sure the information was being used for the purposes the DOJ informed Iowa about “and not beyond that.” He also said the work with the federal government was part of his office’s efforts to ensure Iowa’s voter rolls were accurate.
“We’re always looking to make sure we have the cleanest, most accurate list of eligible voters,” Pate said. “That’s our primary focus, and so in working with the federal government on some of this, that was the goal, and it still is.”
Speaking at the Soapbox, Pate told Iowa fairgoers Monday that voting in Iowa matters — and said this was why his office is also focused on stopping noneligible people from participating in elections. He referenced U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meek’s 2020 win against Democrat Rita Hart by a margin of six votes as proof that in Iowa, voting matters.
“Every one of you need to be out there voting,” Pate said. “You need to inspire your friends and neighbors to vote because your voice is so important. And after the election, you can have people might complain about some of the results, but did they vote? Their voice really counts. We had a congressional race here in Iowa a few years ago that was won by six votes. So yes, your vote counts, and that is why we combat voter fraud the way we do.”
Pate told the crowd that the only acceptable amount of voter fraud was “zero,” which is why Iowa implemented voter ID requirements, and why his office is focused on sharing information about how to vote and register to vote ahead of the election.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Nunn: Conflict over Strait of Hormuz could lead to ‘mass famine’
description: Zach Nunn, the Republican representing Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, said conflict in the Middle East and Strait of Hormuz trade complications could cause mass famine if farmers around the world don’t get access to necessary fertilizers.  Nunn spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, which also happened to the the fair’s veteran’s day.[...]
text:
Rep. Zach Nunn spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox with members of his family joining him on stage Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Zach Nunn, the Republican representing Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, said conflict in the Middle East and Strait of Hormuz trade complications could cause mass famine if farmers around the world don’t get access to necessary fertilizers. 
Nunn spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, which also happened to the the fair’s veteran’s day. Nunn, who served in the U.S. Air Force, said working in Congress is “not about the bipartisan tagline.” 
“It’s about being able to do what we’ve always done in the military, what each of us do for our families: come up with a plan, work hard, deliver,” Nunn said. 
When asked by reporters after his soapbox speech about the nation’s current conflict with Iran, Nunn said he, “never want(s) to see Iran with a nuclear weapon.” Nunn said strategies like the White House’s maximum pressure campaign and his own Preventing the Escalation of Armed Conflict in Europe, or PEACE Act, are “logical solutions” to some of the “really hard problems” in the conflict.
“I never want to see the number one sponsor of terrorism being able to threaten the United States or take more U.S. lives, including our own soldiers,” Nunn said. “And I never want to see Iran trying to threaten the rest of the world by what they’re doing in the Strait of Hormuz.”
Nunn said “walking away” from the conflict, as he alleged Democrats have suggested, is “not a solution” to the conflict.
Nunn said he has spoken with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — who was recently in Iowa — about setting up a “humanitarian corridor” to bring fertilizer inputs through the Strait of Hormuz, which remains inaccessible due to ongoing conflicts with Iran. He noted there would be a “mass famine situation” if a solution isn’t reached to export the farm input. 
“Let’s put pressure where pressure needs to be put on the people who would starve half the planet,” Nunn said, pointing to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. 
He said the U.S. also needs to become more energy and fertilizer “independent” to tackle these issues.

Nunn’s soapbox speech focused largely on his efforts and accomplishments while in office; he is running for reelection against Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: How this Georgia factory is surviving America’s solar policy whiplash
description: This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Inside the vast QCells factory in Cartersville, Georgia, workers — and a bevy of robots — move ultra-thin slices of polysilicon through a lengthy series of machines and chemical baths to transform them into what are known as […]
text:
Workers at the QCells factory in Cartersville, Ga. conduct a final quality inspection on finished solar panels. (Matthew Pearson/WABE)This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Inside the vast QCells factory in Cartersville, Georgia, workers — and a bevy of robots — move ultra-thin slices of polysilicon through a lengthy series of machines and chemical baths to transform them into what are known as wafers.
In June, the plant, about an hour northwest of Atlanta, expanded beyond assembling the major components of solar panels. Now the whole production process is here under one roof. 
“The $2.5 billion, the 3.5 million gallons of water, the 90 megawatts of power, the 60 tons of chemicals on site, and all of the football fields worth of infrastructure you’ve seen is to arrive at this,” said Scott Bell, vice president of external affairs at QCells, holding up one of the paper-thin blue wafers.
It’s the basic building block of a solar panel.
QCells’ expansion here is a major milestone for the U.S. solar industry. China has dominated solar panel manufacturing since the 2010s, flooding the global market with far cheaper panels than anyone else could make. For varying reasons — national security, labor practices, job creation, boosting the clean energy industry in the face of climate change — both the Trump and the Biden administrations have tried to bring back domestic production. 
“Having the full supply chain is critical,” said solar manufacturing expert Ben Damiani, chief technology officer at Atlanta-based solar developer Cherry Street Energy. But moving that supply chain to the U.S., he said, hasn’t been a smooth road. “Probably the biggest hindrance has been the constant change of our own policies.”
In the latest move, the Trump administration plans to levy new tariffs and impose minimum import prices on polysilicon, the key ingredient for solar wafers. The new measures go into effect in December. 
The Biden administration had taken a carrot approach to attracting solar panel makers: the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included tax credit bonuses for solar projects that used U.S.-made panels. QCells, a South Korean firm that already had a gigantic solar panel factory in Dalton, Ga., has said those incentives were a major reason they built their Cartersville plant. 
The Trump administration, by contrast, is taking a stick approach. While last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act revoked most of the tax credits, it also made solar equipment from certain countries — including China — ineligible for the few tax credits that remain. That, along with the new tariffs, may help a U.S. manufacturer like QCells compete with Chinese imports, which are now more expensive.
The two policy approaches have the same ultimate goal, according to researcher Coco Zhang of the banking and investment firm ING. But it’s been whiplash for companies.
Following Trump’s latest executive actions, QCells is still likely able to find a way to be successful, Zhang said. But other manufacturers may have a tougher time. QCells had already made a multibillion-dollar investment in its brand new facility. And that plant took more than three years to come online. For companies with less capital and poorer timing, the supply-side incentives for domestic production may not be enough — especially when the policies could completely change again.
“For any business, including the clean energy industry, they like consistency, they like predictability,” Zhang said. 
A complex future for solar
In the long run, Zhang is optimistic that the U.S. solar panel industry can complete its shift to domestic production. But rules under the Trump administration cutting deeper into the supply chain, as well as the policy back-and-forth, could make things harder to navigate in the short-term, she said.
The short-term outlook is complicated for those buying solar panels, too. The phaseout of federal clean energy tax credits removed a major incentive to develop new solar projects, and the Trump administration has taken steps to cancel federal funding for clean energy projects and add new hurdles for solar and wind installations on federal land. The courts have blocked or reversed some of those actions, but the delays add costs and uncertainties even for projects that do ultimately move forward. 
In the first quarter of this year, clean energy advocacy group E2 tracked nearly $13 billion in abandoned investments in solar, wind, and battery projects. But some $18 billion in new projects were announced as companies scrambled to meet the deadline of the expiring tax credits. While the new tariffs and price controls on polysilicon could help U.S. manufacturers compete to supply the solar developments that remain, they could also drive up costs for developers, Zhang said, and “limited U.S. supply means many will still depend on imports and face higher costs.”
But industry experts maintain that solar isn’t going anywhere. It’s still one of the cheapest sources of electricity at a time when energy demand is growing fast. Solar panels are also readily available, while gas turbines are backordered for years. Solar and storage made up 90 percent of new power added to the U.S. grid in the first quarter of the year, according to the Solar Energy Industries Association.
“We absolutely should make solar, right? Like it is the fastest deployed, lowest cost,” said Damiani. “Solar will be, for the next hundred years, a good portion of our energy.”
The questions, experts agreed, aren’t whether solar development will continue, but how quickly it’ll happen, how much it will cost, who will make the solar panels — and where that manufacturing will happen.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Kindergarten vaccine rates still below 90% in Georgia, with exemptions on the rise
description: Kindergarten immunization rates are falling and vaccine exemptions are on the rise, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released this week. In a press release, the CDC said the data shows vaccine rates remain high and encourages parents to talk to their doctors about vaccine options. Nationally, vaccine rates for […]
text:
In Georgia, vaccine rates for diseases like diphtheria, measles and polio sit around 89% for kindergarteners entering the 2025-2026 school year. Photo by Jan Sonnenmair/Getty ImagesKindergarten immunization rates are falling and vaccine exemptions are on the rise, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released this week.
In a press release, the CDC said the data shows vaccine rates remain high and encourages parents to talk to their doctors about vaccine options.
Nationally, vaccine rates for diseases like diphtheria, measles and polio hover around 92% for kindergarteners entering the 2025-2026 school year. In Georgia, that number sits around 89%, slightly up from last year’s 87% vaccination rate.
Roughly 5.1% of kindergarteners claimed a vaccine exemption this year, meaning they opted out of school vaccine requirements for personal or medical reasons, up from 4.8% last year. Georgia is also one of 24 states whose vaccine exemption rate now surpasses 5%. 
Only 0.1% of kindergarteners in the state were granted an exemption for medical reasons. 
That puts Georgia below the 92% immunity rate needed to ensure herd immunity from diseases like measles, which has infected more than 2,500 Americans this year according to the CDC.
Trump urges shift in childhood vaccine recommendations, calls for splitting up MMR vaccine

The new data also comes on the heels of a sweeping executive order from President Donald Trump that sought to reshape federal guidance on childhood vaccines and threatened legal action against states that don’t allow personal or religious exemptions to school vaccine requirements. As he signed the order, Trump also echoed false claims linking vaccines to autism.
Dr. Cecil Bennett, a primary care physician with Newnan Family Medicine, emphasized that any link between autism and vaccines is coincidental, and does not mean that vaccines caused autism.
“There’s no doubt about the efficacy of vaccines and the importance of vaccines,” he said. “So parents need to know that vaccines are safe and vaccines are effective.”
He said the vaccine rates in Georgia and across the nation were a result of misinformation about vaccines and what he called a “lack of leadership from Washington D.C.” 
He also encouraged parents to talk to their child’s healthcare provider about their vaccine concerns rather than trying to navigate conflicting narratives about vaccines online.
“If you want to find information why your child should not be vaccinated, you can find that information [online],” he said. “I would rather parents who talk to their child’s pediatrician or their child’s family physician and get correct information.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Conservationists sue feds over plan to allow cattle grazing on 24 million western acres
description: A nonprofit conservation group is suing the federal government over plans to allow cattle grazing on more than 24 million previously restricted federal acres across the West. The Center for Biological Diversity and the group’s endangered species co-director, Noah Greenwald, filed the lawsuit to stop the plan from moving forward on Thursday in U.S. District [[...]
text:
Cattle graze along the Snake River. Snake River Basin steelhead are among species that conservationists are concerned could be harmed by expanded cattle grazing under a new federal plan. (Photo courtesy of the Bureau of Land Management)A nonprofit conservation group is suing the federal government over plans to allow cattle grazing on more than 24 million previously restricted federal acres across the West.
The Center for Biological Diversity and the group’s endangered species co-director, Noah Greenwald, filed the lawsuit to stop the plan from moving forward on Thursday in U.S. District Court in Portland. It names as defendants Doug Burgum, head of the U.S. Department of the Interior, and Brooke Rollins, head of the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Lawyers for the Center for Biological Diversity allege that Rollins, Burgum and officials at their departments violated federal laws including the Endangered Species Act by approving the grazing plan without consulting U.S. Fish and Wildlife and National Marine Fisheries officials about federally protected species and designated critical habitat.
The group in April provided the defendants a 60-day notice of intent that a lawsuit was coming unless their concerns were addressed but did not hear back, according to the filing. A USDA spokesperson said the agency “will not comment on pending litigation.” Spokespersons for the Interior and the U.S. Forest Service did not respond to Capital Chronicle requests for comment Monday.
Rollins first announced the proposed plan in October 2025 to “strengthen support for America’s ranchers,” according to a news release at the time.
“For too long, bureaucratic overreach and activist-driven lawfare have undermined the multiple-use mandate of our National Forests and Grasslands. Today, we are empowering line officers with clear direction and reaffirming grazing as an essential tool for healthy landscapes and vibrant rural communities,” she said in a statement included in the announcement.
The Forest Service and Land Management agencies also in a recent memorandum agreed to fast-track grazing permits under the banner of wildfire fuels reduction or temporarily relocating natural disaster-displaced livestock.
But within a recently published interactive map illustrating the proposed expansion, the group found dozens of new U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management allotments identified for potential grazing that are also home to federally protected species, according to the lawsuit.
They include areas around Oregon’s Blue Mountains and Mt. Hood National Forest, as well as areas near federally protected landscapes including the Pony Express Trail in Utah, Canyons of the Ancients National Monument in Colorado and Sonoran Desert National Monument in Arizona.
Among the threatened species that could be impacted by expanded grazing are grizzly bears and gray wolves, which are often killed when conflicts arise between the wild and domesticated animals, according to the suit, as well as Oregon spotted frogs, Snake River Basin steelhead, Colorado pikeminnow, Mexican spotted owls and western yellow-billed cuckoos.
“Grazing on our country’s public lands harms vulnerable animals. Letting cattle trample millions more acres of public land isn’t just wrong, it’s also illegal,” said Andrea Zaccardi, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity, in a statement.
Federal wildlife and land management officials have found large livestock including cattle erode water quality in rivers with their feces and urine, damage riparian areas and soil health and overgraze native species in some areas leading to a proliferation of invasive grasses and shrubs that exacerbate drought and wildfire. Many of the species listed in the lawsuit received federal protection in recent decades in part because their lives or habitat had been critically impaired by livestock grazing.
Matt McElligott, president of the Oregon Cattlemen’s Association, said it’s too early to comment on the lawsuit or the expanded grazing plan itself since the map showing possible new grazing areas was only recently published, and the lawsuit is likely to impede access for an undefined time.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Black legislators demand transparency from Mississippi law enforcement on fatal police shooting of 1-year- old in Senatobia
authors: Joseph Cranney, Verite News and Mukta Joshi
description: Marquell Bridges, president of Building Bridges Coalition, left, and Alaila Jefferies, stepmother of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, place a memorial in honor of her stepson outside Walmart in Senatobia on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. The state Department of Public Safety says a police officer responding to a shoplifting call on Sunday, June 14, 2026, shot at a car tha[...]
text:
Joseph Cranney is a reporter with the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center in collaboration with The New York Times. Learn more about the center’s work here. Mukta Joshi is an investigative reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow examining immigration and criminal justice issues. She can be reached at mukta.joshi@nytimes.com.
After two months of silence from law enforcement officials on the police killing in June of a 1-year-old boy in Senatobia, the Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus is demanding “direct, timely and ongoing updates” on the state-run investigation meant to determine if any officers involved will face criminal charges.Veronica Shanell, the grandmother of Kohen Wiley, the Black toddler shot and killed by Senatobia police in a Walmart parking lot, said nobody from the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation had contacted the family. That includes Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, who was holding him in her arms in the front seat of a car when he was shot.
“I am asking if anyone seen something please say something. If anyone know somebody that was there please have them to inbox me,” Shanell posted on Facebook Monday. “I just want answers that’s all!”In an open letter published Monday, Rep. Kabir Karriem, chairman of the caucus, called the “lack of meaningful” communication by the authorities “unacceptable.”“Kohen’s family should not have to fight the State of Mississippi for information about the investigation into their child’s death,” Karriem, a Columbus Democrat, wrote in the two-page letter. It was addressed to state Attorney General Lynn Fitch and Sean Tindell, commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, which oversees the MBI. Karriem’s letter demands that a liaison for information between the agency and the family “be established immediately.” Wiley, 20, has said that police fired three or four shots at the Ford Fusion driven by her friend, who was wounded in the shooting. The two of them were suspected of shoplifting a pack of diapers and baby clothes. Neither has been charged with any crime, Shanell said.
“Tell the family what can be shared, what cannot and what they should expect next,” Karriem wrote. ”But do not leave them in silence.”In records, the MBI said it had erroneously released, the name of a Senatobia officer, Sgt. Hunter Foster, was listed as the subject of its investigation. The Senatobia City Council placed Foster on leave two days after the June 14 shooting, but no one involved has said whether Foster fired his weapon.Foster, who is white, directed a racially offensive remark toward a co-worker two days before the shooting, according to an internal complaint Mississippi Today obtained last month.At a previous department, Foster was accused of exaggerating the risks that a car posed to officers during their response to a suspicious vehicle call, an incident that resulted in a federal civil rights lawsuit against that police department. 
Vellesiya Wiley pictured with Kohen Wiley, who was her only child.  Attorneys representing the 1-year-old’s family are calling for law enforcement in Senatobia to release body and dashboard camera footage and on Monday, June 22, 2026, announced plans for an independent autopsy. They said both can help provide the family with answers. Credit: Ben Crump Law
Foster claimed that the driver had almost run over another officer, though surveillance footage shows no evidence that the car nearly hit, or even drove toward, any of the officers.Martin Zummach, a Southaven lawyer who has represented police accused of excessive force, said Monday that he had been retained to represent Foster following the Walmart shooting, but declined to discuss details of his actions.“I am very convinced that Hunter will be cleared of any allegations of wrongdoing in this unfortunate event,” Zummach said.
 In a statement released the day of the shooting, the MBI said that officers had attempted to stop the car, but that “the driver drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one.”An MBI spokesperson declined to say anything else on Monday about the actions of the police or the status of their investigation. At least one key witness has yet to be interviewed by law enforcement agents.Desirae Smith, an eyewitness, posted a video from the Walmart parking lot that showed officers scrambling on foot moments after the gunfire. The video was widely shared on social media along with her name and published by news outlets, including CNN, in late June. Smith said neither state investigators nor local law enforcement had contacted her.
“I just think they’re not bothered by it because ain’t nobody really bringing up the baby’s name anymore,” Smith said. “They’re just letting it fade away.”The Senatobia Police Department and the MBI have declined multiple requests to release footage of the incident captured on police body-worn cameras, though Tindell told Senatobia aldermen that his agency had obtained that footage. Walmart declined to release its surveillance footage, saying that it had been turned over to the MBI.Karriem said the case reveals “broader concerns” around Mississippi’s rules for releasing body-camera footage, a subject he pledged the Black Caucus would address during the next legislative session.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth joins Rep. Zach Nunn at Iowa State Fair
description: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Iowa State Fairgoers Monday he honored the Iowa soldiers killed in Kuwait, while saying the U.S.-Iran conflict was necessary to keep Americans safe. The defense secretary also spoke on the anti-DEI (diversity, equity, and inclusion) policies and other changes made at the U.S. Department of Defense, renamed the “Depart[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posed for photos at a Nunn campaign event held at JR’s Southpork Ranch at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Iowa State Fairgoers Monday he honored the Iowa soldiers killed in Kuwait, while saying the U.S.-Iran conflict was necessary to keep Americans safe.
The defense secretary also spoke on the anti-DEI (diversity, equity, and inclusion) policies and other changes made at the U.S. Department of Defense, renamed the “Department of War” since President Donald Trump took office for a second term. He said “at the Department of War, we do training, not tr***ies,” using a slur to refer to transgender people.
“It is a day and night difference,” Hegseth said. “Training, lethality, accountability, discipline, readiness — the bedrock of what it means to be an American warrior — is the only focus of our department. Colorblind, gender-neutral, merit-based. That’s it.”
Hegseth joined Republican U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn at the JR’s Southpork Ranch at the Iowa State Fair for “Operation Top Nunn: Salute to the Troops,” an annual campaign fundraiser and event benefiting veterans support organizations. The event — with Hegseth as a special guest — was originally scheduled for March, but was postponed.
The March plans were canceled shortly after the deaths of two Iowa soldiers in an Iranian strike on a Kuwait facility on March 1. The Iowa soldiers were identified as Major Jeffrey O’Brien, a 45-year-old from Waukee, and Sgt. Declan J. Coady, a 20-year-old from West Des Moines. These two Iowa soldiers, alongside the four others who died in the strike, were all assigned to the 103rd Sustainment Command, based in Des Moines.
Hegseth said he and Trump had been at the Dover Air Force Base for either all or “near all” of the dignified transfers of U.S. soldiers killed in the U.S.-Iran conflict, which began Feb. 28, “because I want to see and understand firsthand the cost, the sacrifice when we send our men and women into harm’s way.” He spoke on the “cost” of military action, but also explained why the United States took this action, bringing up concerns about nuclear capabilities.
“There is a cost to doing very difficult things, to going out and defending your country, and ensuring radical Islamist crazies don’t get a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth said. “I’m not willing to look my kids in the eye and say, ‘We had a chance to do something about it, but we didn’t,’ when they were building a conventional arsenal of missiles and drones so large — they’re trying to use the North Korean approach effectively … Iran wanted to do the same thing.”
The deaths of O’Brien and Coady came just months after two Iowa National Guard members, Sgt. William Nathaniel Howard of Marshalltown and Sgt. Edgar Brian Torres-Tovar of Des Moines, were killed in Palmyra, Syria, during a Dec. 13, 2025 attack by a lone gunman associated with ISIS.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gave a speech supporting U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn’s 2026 reelection campaign at JR’s Southpork Ranch at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Nunn brought up the families of Howard and Torres-Tovar to speak at the event and he asked for Iowans to keep military members and families in their thoughts and prayers.
“That’s what the days like this are about: recognizing how we can help those who survive with us and honor those who’ve given the ultimate sacrifice,” Nunn said.
Hegseth called for Iowans to support reelecting Nunn to the U.S. House as he faces Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott in the 2026 election. He said Nunn was a needed ally for the administration and a trusted voice advocating for U.S. military needs as a veteran.
“President Trump needs the type of leaders who understand why a $1.5 trillion dollar budget, a one-time generational investment, is what is necessary to ensure that my kids and your kids, that your grandkids and my grandkids, live in a free country, defended by the most powerful military in the world,” Hegseth said.
Trone Garriott said in a statement: “It’s disgraceful that Zach Nunn and Pete Hegseth are partying together at a campaign stop in Iowa while our service members are under threat and facing poor conditions overseas. Our leaders should be focused on ending this war and keeping Americans deployed overseas safe, not fundraising for Zach Nunn’s campaign.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Southwest Idaho resident contracts meningitis from West Nile Virus infection, health officials say
description: A Canyon County resident over the age of 65 is Idaho’s first reported human case of West Nile virus meningitis this year, public health officials announced Monday. The infected person was hospitalized but is recovering at home, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare announced in a news release.  Infected mosquitoes spread West Nile virus […]
text:
West Nile virus is present each year across Southeast Idaho. (Courtesy of Pixabay)A Canyon County resident over the age of 65 is Idaho’s first reported human case of West Nile virus meningitis this year, public health officials announced Monday.
The infected person was hospitalized but is recovering at home, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare announced in a news release. 
Infected mosquitoes spread West Nile virus through bites.
Idaho health officials pointed to the case of the disease to encourage people to take steps to prevent mosquito bites while outdoors and on their properties.
“The report of the first severe West Nile virus disease of the season in an Idaho resident is a good reminder for all of us to take protective measures against mosquito bites,” Idaho State Epidemiologist Dr. Christine Hahn said in a written statement. “This includes wearing insect repellent and protective clothing in addition to reducing standing water around gardens and homes where mosquitoes can lay eggs.”
Most people infected with West Nile don’t feel sick. A fifth of people infected develop a fever and other symptoms like a headache, body aches, joint pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, swollen lymph glands or a rash. Risk of severe illness, and death, can be up to 40% higher in people that take immune system suppressants, such as treatments for cancer, autoimmune disease, and organ transplants, said Southwest District Health Epidemiologist Lekshmi Rita Venugopal.
“With West Nile virus detected in mosquitoes in Southwest Idaho again this summer, it’s especially important for people with weakened immune systems to avoid mosquito bites,” she said in a written statement.
The risk of severe illness is higher for older people and people who have some medical conditions. Severe illness can affect the brain and spinal cord, and can lead to hospitalization or death. Officials encourage people who believe they are sick with West Nile to contact their healthcare provider.
 Tips to avoid West Nile virus

To avoid West Nile infections, Health and Welfare encourages people to:

Avoid mosquitoes, especially when those that spread West Nile virus are most active between dusk and dawn.
When outdoors, wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants. 
Use insect repellents on exposed skin. Find repellents approved by the Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA, and follow product instructions carefully. Find repellents online using the EPA’s search tool or a CDC chatbot.
Use mosquito netting to cover strollers and baby carriers. 

People should also take steps to mitigate mosquitos on their property, Health and Welfare suggests, including:

If your home has damaged screens, repair or replace them.
Mosquitos like to breed in standing water. Reduce standing water on your property, including toys, trays or pots outdoors that can hold water. For bird baths, static decorative ponds and animal water tanks, change water weekly to prevent mosquito larvae from maturing into adults.
Find more tips online on Health and Welfare’s website.
