name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico’s new Legislative Council Service head says he’s eager to lead at time of ‘big change’
description: New Mexico’s Legislative Council on Friday afternoon named Ethan Watson as the next director of the Legislative Council Service, the state Legislature’s nonpartisan legal research and bill-drafting agency.
text:
Albuquerque City Clerk Ethan Watson will take over as director of the New Mexico Legislative Council Service on Sept. 14, 2026, after the nonpartisan Legislative Council selected him Aug. 14, 2026. (Photo courtesy Ethan Watson)New Mexico’s Legislative Council on Friday afternoon named Ethan Watson as the next director of the Legislative Council Service, the state Legislature’s nonpartisan legal research and bill-drafting agency.
The bipartisan Legislative Council, which includes many high-ranking state lawmakers from both parties, selected Watson over three other candidates following a roughly three-hour meeting in closed executive session. Other candidates included current LCS Assistant Director Randall Cherry, State Personnel Office Director Dylan Lange and a third interviewee from Montana.  SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Watson, who has served as Albuquerque city clerk for six years, told Source NM on Monday he is “excited” to take charge of LCS. In addition to drafting bills and conducting legal research, the LCS oversees the Roundhouse; administers legal cases and ethics complaints brought by or against the Legislature; and responds to public records requests.
“It’s an essential role to the function of the Legislature, and I’m really honored to be entrusted with that responsibility,” Watson told Source NM.
The LCS is also tasked with overseeing many of the Legislature’s recent “modernization” measures, including the hiring of district legislative aides assigned to each lawmaker, as well as the opening of year-round legislative offices in many House and Senate districts. 
Watson said he is still working to gain an understanding of what will be on his to-do list when he starts work Sept. 14. Still, he said the LCS is guiding the Legislature through a period of “big change” related to modernizing its operations, similar to reforms he implemented in New Mexico’s biggest city. 
“I’ve spent a significant period of time at the city working to modernize the processes within the city clerk’s office. I mean, we streamlined how the city handles public records requests and hearings, and we’ve also implemented a number of significant software changes within my office,” he said. 
Watson will earn a salary of $225,000. He’s taking over for Shawna Casebier, who announced her resignation in early June after nearly two years as director. Before Casebier, Raúl Burciaga had been the director for 14 years. 
Legislative Council Co-Chair and Senate President Pro Tem Sen. Mimi Stewart (D-Albuquerque), in a statement Friday said Watson is the best choice to oversee LCS because of his experience overseeing “complex administrative duties that come with a large governmental institution.”
“I’m confident in his ability to lead LCS staff with the same integrity and professionalism New Mexicans have come to expect from this institution,” she said. 
The LCS works with both chambers of the Legislature, as well both parties, to provide technical and administrative support during the legislative session. 
House Speaker Javier Martinez, also a Legislative Council co-chair, said in the Friday statement that he selected Watson because of his “measured approach to the complex issues facing our state, coupled with an excitement about building the modern legislative systems that New Mexicans deserve.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Want a text when sewage spills into CT water? State to test new alert system
description: Heavy rain can cause untreated sewage to flow into rivers and streams, making it unsafe for residents to swim or fish for days afterwards.
text:
Heavy rain can cause untreated sewage to flow into Connecticut rivers and streams, making it unsafe for residents to swim, fish or boat for up to two days afterwards. That’s no secret. But getting that information out to the public in real time can be tricky.
“The current system isn’t perfect,” the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection said in a statement.
That’s why Connecticut is piloting a new program later this year that will send out real-time alerts via text or email, letting residents know when sewage spills have been reported.
At the moment, if residents want to find out about sewage spills, they can visit the state’s performance dashboard, narrowing the spills down by location, date and impacted bodies of water. Or they can visit the state’s social media account, CT Sewage Spills on X.
But the social media account isn’t getting a lot of eyeballs. Some posts have fewer than 100 views. And state officials say the current system doesn’t work for people who want push notifications when new spills are reported to the state.
The new system will take reports about sewage spills, submitted to DEEP by municipalities and sewer utilities, and move them to a new public-facing alert system.
Once the program is up and running, subscribers will be able to sign up for all the towns they want to get alerts from.
State officials say they’ll pilot the new program in the fall and have it available to the public by the end of the year.
The new alert system will cost the state $150,000 a year, according to DEEP.
This story was first published Aug. 17, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: WyoFile
title: Documentary on Rock Springs drag troupe earns national honors
description:
“Time Warp,” which celebrates queer joy, was screened in Rock Springs and at several film festivals. Directed by Allison Berg, the film follows The Starling Company as they prepare for their first show: a shadow cast of Rocky Horror Picture Show.  
The post Documentary on Rock Springs drag troupe earns national honors appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Kenny Starling founded a drag troupe and theater company in a blue-collar southwestern Wyoming town. Allison Berg wanted to produce a documentary following residents of a conservative state as they performed a gender-bending 1970s cult musical.
The result is “Time Warp,” a film about a Rock Springs drag troupe, which won special jury mention for best documentary at the 2026 Tribeca Film Festival. Directed by Allison Berg, the film follows the members of The Starling Company as they prepare for their first show: a shadow cast of “Rocky Horror Picture Show.”  
Founding a theater company, preparing for the show and producing the documentary were long processes, but they yielded a unique glimpse into queer joy in one of the least populated states, those involved in the film say. 
Starling Company
Kenny Starling, a 29-year-old resident of Rock Springs, founded The Starling Company in 2022. Starling, who uses they/them pronouns, wanted to create more opportunities for themself while also amplifying marginalized voices and stories that might not otherwise be heard.
Starling managed the Broadway Theater in Rock Springs and served as its events coordinator. They joined the board of a local theater company, but didn’t connect with the work being done there. Around the same time, Starling met a friend who was also involved in local theater. She was from one of the two black families in town and talked about discrimination that she’d faced in the theater community, especially in college. These experiences spurred Starling to create their own drag and theater company. 
At the time, Rock Springs didn’t have any specific Pride organizations, though the town had a group called Drag for A Cause. For The Starling Company’s first show, they showed Rocky Horror while performing as a shadow cast: when a group of artists act out the movie as it plays. The troupe selected Rocky Horror due to its members’ passion for the 1975 cult musical, and its accessibility to a wide audience, said Starling, who plays Dr. Frank-N-Furter and directs the show. Rocky Horror explores gender, cross dressing and sexuality, with many characters expressing themselves outside the bounds of societal gender expectations. 
The Starling Company performs in the shadow cast of “Rocky Horror Picture Show.” (TimeWarp Films)
“I saw it as a way to bridge cultural and generational divides really early on. And that has been reinforced by every single production that I’ve done. I’ve met so many straight people dressed up as the characters from the film, acting out scenes right along with the actors, doing the callbacks,” Starling said. 
The performance of Rocky Horror received a lot of community support and was overall well received by the Rock Springs community, Starling said. The show was rated for mature audiences and only open to those over 18 unless accompanied by a parent or guardian. 
“Overwhelmingly, people take issue with queerness and with people being trans and people being gay, that stems from just not knowing,” Starling said.
“I understand the contents of my show. I know when it’s too adult for children to attend. I know how to prepare my artists for when we are doing all ages shows. And we are not inherently political. We’re not inherently sexualized. We’re just another group of artists trying to share our love of our work with the world and make the world a better place in the process. So don’t be afraid. Don’t be scared. It’s just ignorance and fear. And there’s no reason to let that control you or control us in the process.”
Making the documentary
After the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in the summer of 2022, Berg and others felt like they were “living in a timewarp” as they worried about what other rights might be revoked. (Time Warp is also the name of one of the most popular songs on the Rocky Horror soundtrack.) Berg, a New York-based filmmaker who’s produced documentaries and television shows, had the idea to make a documentary about performing Rocky Horror as a shadow cast in a conservative state. Since this was post-COVID, many live performances had been shut down. Plus, a more conservative state would present extra challenges to performing Rocky Horror, Berg said. In the first years after the pandemic, many state legislatures began passing new laws aimed at curtailing transgender rights and library books that lawmakers asserted were inappropriate for children.
Berg found a list of planned performances on a fan website, but none of them were the right fit. Then she discovered The Starling Company production. Berg messaged Starling on Instagram, but Starling initially thought it was a scam. After a video call confirmed Berg was real, Starling agreed to do the documentary. Berg sent Wyoming filmmaker Melinda Binks to Rock Springs to scout the show. Binks did the first couple of shoots and sent the footage to Berg. 
The Starling Company rehearses for a performance of “Rocky Horror Picture Show.” (TimeWarp Films)
Berg, along with cinematographers, spent the next two and a half years filming and then another two years editing in order to complete “Time Warp.” The film was screened at film festivals and in Rock Springs in 2026, with more screenings planned for the future. 
“I feel so energized to get involved and to go and see these groups performing and support the LGBTQ+ community even more. And I think that’s sort of what you want out of the film. You want people to find each other at these screenings,” Berg said. 
Queer joy in rural Wyoming
Starling defines queer joy as “unbridled joy while you’re authentically being yourself. And it stems from a place of love for yourself and for other people, for just being themselves.”
“Time Warp” is a joyful film. While it doesn’t shy away from representing the realities of being queer in Rock Springs, both good and bad, the film leaves viewers with a message of hope. From the opening scenes of the town and Starling to the final look at The Starling Company performing “Hedwig and the Angry Inch,” the film portrays an undeniable sense of belonging and acceptance. Throughout the documentary, the film reiterates that queer people live in even the more remote corners of Wyoming. 
Midway through one of the productions of Rocky Horror, the movie freezes up. Starling asks the audience to repeat the iconic line from the film, “Don’t dream it, be it,” 10 times to unfreeze the tech. It works. 
Audience members watch “Rocky Horror Picture Show” being performed in Rock Springs. (TimeWarp Films)
“That’s kind of been my life motto ever since [seeing the movie Rocky Horror], is not to just dream and fantasize and want the change you wish to see in the world, but to be the change, to be the example, and to make the world a better place,” Starling said. 
“I think that anyone could watch this film,” Berg said. “We always wanted people to feel the joy, the queer joy in the room.”
Once audiences experience that joy, Berg said, “if you watch it, you’ll want to be in that room, whether you are queer yourself or not, like you will see the joy and want to be part of it. And that’s what we were trying to accomplish.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Voting season puts focus on election administration, litigation, turnout
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: "With 600,000 ballots on the street, I think it's important for people to vote them and send them back," Secretary of State William Galvin said, calling the figure average and declaring that his "strong suggestion" is that mail-in voters return their ballots "immediately."
text:
AS THE WEEKS tick down to the primaries and there are fewer than 90 days until the November general election, two of the state’s top officials have voting on their minds.
While Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office has received a lot of outreach about election integrity and access to voter files, it’s voter turnout she’s concerned about, she told “Boston Public Radio” hosts Jim Braude and Margery Eagan this week. 
Over in Secretary of State William Galvin’s office, voters have requested 600,000 mail-in Democrat or Republican ballots ahead of the September 1 primary and “well over 100,000” have already been returned. 
“With 600,000 ballots on the street, I think it’s important for people to vote them and send them back,” Galvin said, calling the figure average and declaring that his “strong suggestion” is that mail-in voters return their ballots “immediately.” 
“I’m more concerned now about retrieving the ballots back that have been voted, because in the case of a primary, unlike a general election, they must be received by the close of polls on Election Day. There’s no grace period,” Galvin said. “The best and most sure way to do it is to not rely on the mails, to bring them to a drop box, or get it back to city or town hall in your community.” 
Vote by mail “has been a matter of controversy” that is still being litigated, Galvin continued. “We’ve got injunctive relief to protect the right to vote by mail right now, and some of the cases are still pending.” 
Massachusetts was one of 24 states that sued the Trump administration in April over a March 31 executive order titled “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections” that directed the US Postal Service to not transmit mail-in or absentee ballots from anyone not on a state-specified voter participation list.
Campbell’s office in June announced “victory,” writing that the US District Court of Massachusetts blocked the administration’s attempts “to interfere with states’ constitutional authority to administer elections.” Per Galvin’s office, the First Circuit on July 25 denied the federal defendants’ request for a stay of the ruling in the executive order. The federal government shortly after filed an application with the US Supreme Court for a stay of the First Circuit’s decision, his office said. 
Campbell and 18 other attorneys general also sued the administration over a March 25, 2025 executive order titled “Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections” that lays out proof of citizenship requirements for voting. The US District Court of Massachusetts ruled in favor of the attorneys general in June. The federal defendants appealed to the First Circuit, but oral arguments on the appeal aren’t scheduled until December, Galvin’s office said.
“I think that obviously any court decision has national implications. So I think the courts will certainly be aware of the fact that with 90 days out, you don’t try to change the rules,” Galvin said. “People use vote by mail not just here in Massachusetts, but in states including Republican-administered states throughout the country. I think we should be okay on both fronts, and that gives voters many, many options.” 
Campbell said her office is working with Galvin’s to inform people about voting and will be issuing a “Know Your Rights” guide with information about voting early and ballot access. She said her partnership with Galvin “has been a game changer” as her office files multi-state lawsuits related to voter information, election integrity and “pushing back on the Trump administration.” 
Two in three US adults are concerned about political leaders pressuring election officials to change election outcomes, according to a Kettering Foundation-Gallup Democracy for All Project poll conducted among more than 23,000 US adults from April 24 through June 10. Of those polled, 57 percent were concerned about ballots not being properly handled, counted or secured, and 52 percent were concerned about people gathering near polling places in an attempt to intimidate voters or discourage them from voting. Democrats were more likely to express concern about leaders pressuring election officials, while Republicans were more likely to express concerns about ballot handling and counting.
Campbell’s worries lie in whether voters will show up, she said when asked about Bay State Banner reporting in July that showed as many as 60,000 residents in Brockton were placed on inactive voter rolls ahead of the last municipal election. 
“I think in other states where I work with other AGs, they are more concerned — you think about battleground states — about the integrity of their elections,” Campbell said. “I’m not concerned here in Massachusetts. If we have anyone interfering with our elections, we will mobilize. We will fight back.”
“I think what I’m most concerned about is the lack of voter turnout,” Campbell continued. “If anything, I think we have to continue to do a better job of telling folks about the importance of voting, being civically engaged.” Of more than 4.9 million registered voters in Massachusetts in 2024, just over 1.2 million votes were cast, representing a turnout percentage of 25.21 percent, according to Galvin’s website. That represented a decline from a voter turnout of 37.11 percent in 2020. 
Galvin said he’s “optimistic” there won’t be interference, but understands “there’s some anxiety.”
“We certainly are not going to tolerate any interference with the election by any entity, whether that be a governmental entity or anybody else. We never have,” Galvin said, adding that a police officer is required to be present at every polling location in Massachusetts and that no political activity can occur within 150 feet of the voting.

name: National
title: Refugee admissions on track to hit record low
description: The number of refugees admitted to the United States during the first 10 months of the fiscal year is on pace to hit its lowest level on record, according to a new analysis. The new numbers reflect a steep decline in refugee admissions since President Donald Trump began his second term, according to a new […]
text:
A family waits in line to apply for asylum at the southern border between El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, in 2023. The number of refugees admitted to the United States during the first 10 months of the fiscal year is on pace to hit its lowest level on record. (Photo by Corrie Boudreaux for Source NM)The number of refugees admitted to the United States during the first 10 months of the fiscal year is on pace to hit its lowest level on record, according to a new analysis.
The new numbers reflect a steep decline in refugee admissions since President Donald Trump began his second term, according to a new analysis of State Department data by the Pew Research Center.
The U.S. has admitted 10,258 refugees — nearly all of them white South Africans — in the first 10 months of the fiscal year, which ends on Sept. 30. During fiscal 2025, part of which overlapped with President Joe Biden’s term, the U.S. admitted 38,102 refugees. In the previous year, during which Biden was president the entire time, 100,034 refugees were admitted.
The Trump administration, which has sought to limit immigration of all types, has capped refugee admissions for fiscal 2026 at 17,500, the lowest level in the past 25 years.
Refugee admissions have fluctuated over time. They declined sharply after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, when President George W. Bush temporarily halted application processing. And they fell again during Trump’s first term, when he restricted immigration from majority-Muslim countries. However, the U.S. admitted an average of 50,000 refugees per year between 2001 and 2026.
In February 2025, Trump issued an executive order prioritizing refugee admissions for Afrikaners — white South Africans descended from Dutch, German and French colonial settlers. Afrikaners were the primary architects of apartheid, a rigid system of racial segregation that lasted from 1948 to 1994.
About 80% of South Africans are Black. Trump’s order asserts that the country’s Black leaders have discriminated against the Afrikaners and demonstrated a “shocking disregard” for their rights by seizing their farmland without compensation. South African leaders deny that Afrikaners have been subjected to systemic persecution.
In recent years, the majority of refugees to the U.S. have come from the Democratic Republic of Congo, which has seen ongoing war and displacement. Many refugees also have come from countries such as Syria, Ukraine, Bhutan, Iraq, Afghanistan, Sudan, Venezuela, Eritrea, Myanmar and Guatemala.
In a 2025 Pew Research Center survey of 10,357 Americans, about 36% of respondents said that it was very or extremely important to take in refugees escaping violence in other countries. Another 39% said it was somewhat important.
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.

name: VTDigger
title: 1 dead in spate of violent incidents in Burlington
description:
One victim was stabbed to death, and the city reported one other stabbing and two instances of gunfire over the weekend. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  1 dead in spate of violent incidents in Burlington.
text:
A Burlington police cruiser is seen outside City Hall in May 2022. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
An unidentified man was stabbed to death in Burlington early Saturday morning, nearly a year to the day after a fatal beating a few blocks away set off a still-unresolved fight over public safety downtown even as city figures show violent crime declining.
Burlington police discovered a man suffering from stab wounds at around 4 a.m. Saturday morning behind 175-199 Main St., WCAX reported. The man was taken to the University of Vermont Medical Center, where he later died. 
The Burlington Police Department and the mayor’s office did not publicly identify the victim or respond to multiple requests for comment Monday on the weekend incidents. 
The police also responded to a different stabbing with non-life-threatening injuries earlier Saturday, WCAX said. And Seven Days reported a separate altercation on Friday afternoon where a juvenile slashed a man’s bike tire on the bike path near North Beach. 
The mayor’s office said there were also two different gunfire incidents over the weekend, one between two people on lower Church Street and another from a “reckless accidental discharge” of a firearm. The two incidents did not lead to any injuries. 
“These events are deeply upsetting, and when several serious incidents happen in a short period of time, it can understandably raise questions about whether we are seeing a broader change in crime and safety in Burlington,” Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak said in the press release. 
The mayor said Burlington police are investigating the stabbings and gunfire. No arrests had been announced as of late Monday afternoon. 
Saturday’s fatal stabbing comes amid years of debate over public safety in downtown Burlington, even as some measures of serious crime have declined since 2021. 
This weekend’s killing also occurred almost exactly a year after another fatal attack just blocks away. In August 2025, 42-year-old Scott Kastner was beaten during an assault that began on Church Street and spilled into City Hall Park, according to Burlington police. Kastner died days later, and two people were subsequently charged with second-degree murder. 
The case became part of a broader debate over how Burlington should respond to public drug use, homelessness and crime downtown and figured directly in the push for increased enforcement.

READ MORE

Six days after Kastner’s death, the Burlington City Council voted 9-2 for a resolution calling for enforcing the park’s closure from midnight to 6 a.m., as well as maintaining a more consistent police and public safety presence in the area.
In recent weeks, Democrats on the Burlington City Council pushed ahead with a public safety plan called “Burlington Forward,” calling for increased police activity downtown as well as stronger enforcement against illicit drug use. But the plan has its detractors. Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George slammed the plan as “performative.” 
Recent crime complaints also led Gov. Phil Scott to direct state troopers to patrol downtown this summer. Vermont State Police spokesperson Adam Silverman confirmed that state troopers were not involved in responding to any of the most recent crimes.  
In her statement, Mulvaney-Stanak highlighted statistics showing that violent crime, in particular, is declining. 
“Preliminary 2026 data show aggravated assaults are down significantly, and overall violent incidents are down compared with both 2025 and 2024,” she said in the press release. 
Data from the Burlington Police Department does show that there were 26 aggravated assault incidents reported in the first half of 2026, compared with 48 aggravated assaults in the same period for 2025. 
The police have reported 254 violent offenses so far this year, which would put it on track to be one of the least violent spans reported since 2012. Overall offenses are down from 2025 as well. 
Mulvaney-Stanak said the police department has used specific strategies to tackle violent crime incidents, such as targeting hot spots, expanding foot patrols and proactively intervening with high-risk people. 
“I know these incidents can leave us feeling worried, angry, and unsettled — particularly at a time when our community is engaged in difficult and fraught conversations about safety,” she said in the press release. “Our City team is responding as it should by conducting strong police work to hold people accountable for acts of violence, while supporting victims.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: House Ethics Chair Michael Guest violates the STOCK Act
description: House Ethics Committee Chairman Michael Guest, R-Miss., rushes past reporters without speaking after his panel met to consider the investigation of former Rep. Matt Gaetz, R-Fla., who at the time was President-elect Donald Trump's choice to be attorney general, at the Capitol in Washington, Wednesday, Nov. 20, 2024.
text:
House Ethics Committee Chairman Michael Guest, whose committee enforces compliance of the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act, violated the insider trading and transparency law, a NOTUS review of congressional financial records indicates.
Guest, a four-term Republican from Mississippi, was more than six months late disclosing three stock sales made by a family trust fund owned by his wife, Haley, involving shares of the oil giant Chevron, the lodging platform Airbnb and the cosmetics company e.l.f. Beauty.
By law, members of Congress must publicly disclose individual stock trades within 45 days of a trade’s execution. These include trades made by or on behalf of themselves, their spouses and their dependent children.
Guest’s STOCK Act violation is the seventh such violation this month by members of Congress.
It also comes less than a month after the House passed a bill, the Stop Insider Trading Act, that would in part ban federal lawmakers from buying individual stocks altogether. Guest voted for the bill, which is now pending in the Senate.
In a message Friday to the clerk of the House of Representatives, Guest wrote that he didn’t learn until Thursday of the three stock sales made on Dec. 16.
“A compliance firm missed them, discovering the oversight while preparing my annual House disclosure,” Guest wrote, adding that he’s notified House Ethics Committee staff and has “initiated additional compliance review.”
Guest indicated that each late sale was worth between $1,001 and $15,000 — lawmakers are only required to disclose values in broad ranges — and that the stock sales were made “at a loss.”
In an email to NOTUS, Guest’s chief of staff, Jordan Downs, said the congressman “does not have any decision-making role” in the trust and “was not consulted on these, or any other, transactions made by the trust.”
This is the second time Guest had violated the STOCK Act’s disclosure provisions. In 2021, he was more than eight months late disclosing sales of ExxonMobil and BP stock by a family trust benefiting his wife, Business Insider reported.
Guest’s committee is empowered to fine — and to waive fines — for STOCK Act scofflaws. The standard penalty for first-time violators is a $200 fine.
Guest “intends to pay” any late-filing fine and “doesn’t believe there will be any need to recuse” himself from the committee’s consideration of it, Downs said.
In the House, other STOCK Act violators during the past year include Reps. Michael Rulli (R-Ohio), Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan), Tracey Mann (R-Kansas), Julie Johnson (D-Texas), Linda Sánchez (D-California), Julia Letlow (R-Louisiana), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Lisa McClain (R-Michigan), Pat Ryan (D-New York), Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina), Derek Tran (D-California), Donald Norcross (D-New Jersey), Tim Walberg (R-Michigan), Rich McCormick (R-Georgia), Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Troy Nehls (R-Texas), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois), George Whitesides (D-California), Val Hoyle (D-Oregon), Austin Scott (R-Georgia), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Florida), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota), Christian Menefee (D-Texas), Daniel Webster (R-Florida), Ed Case (D-Hawaii), Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas), Laurel Lee (R-Florida) and Scott Franklin (R-Florida). Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma) was also late, although his office denies it.
Senators who’ve violated the STOCK Act during the past year include Sens. Alan Armstrong (R-Oklahoma), Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), Katie Britt (R-Alabama), Susan Collins (R-Maine), John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) and John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania).

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Jackson Hospital, Blue Cross Blue Shield reach deal to keep hospital open
description: A troubled Montgomery hospital and the state’s largest private health insurance company reached a four-year deal Monday to keep the hospital open after years of financial woes. The deal between Jackson Hospital and Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama is contingent on the hospital emerging out of bankruptcy, said John Quinlivan, Jackson Hospital’s president[...]
text:
Jackson Hospital is seen in Montgomery, Alabama on Aug. 17, 2026. Officials with the hospital, which declared bankruptcy in 2025, and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama announced an agreement Monday to keep the hospital open. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)A troubled Montgomery hospital and the state’s largest private health insurance company reached a four-year deal Monday to keep the hospital open after years of financial woes.
The deal between Jackson Hospital and Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama is contingent on the hospital emerging out of bankruptcy, said John Quinlivan, Jackson Hospital’s president and CEO, at a press conference announcing the deal on Monday afternoon. Jackson Hospital filed for bankruptcy in 2025 and has struggled financially for years. 
“The agreement does not give us everything we felt we needed, but combined with the continued support of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama, Jackson Investment Group, the city of Montgomery, Montgomery County and the state of Alabama, it enables us to execute our strategic plan,” Quinlivan said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a statement Monday afternoon, BCBSAL spokesperson Sophie Martin said the company’s focus “has remained on supporting our members and the community.”
“We appreciate the efforts of all parties involved in reaching this outcome and look forward to continuing our partnership in support of the health and well-being of our customers, the River Region and Alabamians,” the statement said.
Hospitals across Alabama are closing due to financial struggles. State charity programs and federal tax programs aim to prevent closures, but experts say it may not be enough to save hospitals.
Quinlivan demanded BCBSAL increase what it pays the hospital for patient services to that of Baptist Medical Center South, a Level I trauma center in southern Montgomery that has 492 beds. Jackson, located near downtown Montgomery, is a Level III trauma center that has 344 beds. BCBSAL did not agree to that demand due to the differing care the hospitals offer. 
The deal between the two companies will allow the hospital to improve current services and add new ones, but Quinlivan did not say what services would be added. Those services will allow the hospital to generate more revenue, but it will have to depend on aid from local and state governments and BCBSAL for grants to stay afloat for now, he said.
“We shouldn’t have to depend on governments for grants, but in the short-term we will. We have over 150 million dollars worth of infrastructure needs,” he said. “Eventually, we will be able to sustain ourselves and to reinvest in the facility, but in the short term, we’re going to need continued government support to do those things that we’re going to have to do.”
The hospital reached a “verbal agreement” with the insurance company in early July, which Quinlivan said the signed agreement was based on. He did not share details of the agreement, but said the reimbursement “rates are significantly better.”
“They’re not everything that we had asked for, and not everything we felt we needed, but they are materially better,” he said. “They certainly put us in a position where we ought to be able to do the right things here and save this hospital.”
Gov. Kay Ivey earlier this year pledged a $40 million grant to the hospital, contingent on the hospital coming out of bankruptcy. Quinlivan said the hospital has filed the necessary paperwork in U.S. Bankruptcy Court. 
In a statement Monday, Ivey noted that Jackson Hospital was near its 80th birthday and said the agreement meant it was “reborn today stronger and ever more committed to delivering the most trusted medical care to the Capital City and River Region.” 
“Jackson Hospital’s agreement to emerge from bankruptcy and keep its doors open to offer a wide range of care, including emergency services, is the direct result of a resolute partnership between state and local officials and hospital leadership,” Ivey said in a statement Monday afternoon.
The hospital has also received $10 million from Montgomery County and $15 million from Montgomery city. Jackson Healthcare, founded by Georgia Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson, has also loaned the hospital $35 million.
Messages seeking comment with Montgomery Mayor Steven Reed and the Montgomery County Commission were left Monday afternoon.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: ‘Quasi-public’ private schools have scant accountability; 100% of students get tuition vouchers
description: This story was originally published by ProPublica. At some point, my reporting colleagues and I began referring to them as the “100% schools.” We were following the money that flows from states’ public coffers into private schools through vouchers when we noticed a subset of educational facilities where tax dollars cover all or a big […]
text:
Atlas Preparatory Academy, a private school in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Every student relies on taxpayer dollars from one of the state’s four voucher programs to pay all or part of their tuition. Caleb Alvarado for ProPublicaThis story was originally published by ProPublica.
At some point, my reporting colleagues and I began referring to them as the “100% schools.”
We were following the money that flows from states’ public coffers into private schools through vouchers when we noticed a subset of educational facilities where tax dollars cover all or a big part of the tuition for every student.
In essence, these were schools that were funded like public schools but didn’t operate with the same oversight or transparency.
Our reporting found that these types of private schools exist throughout the country and that in Wisconsin — where I’m based — there were 39 that fell into that category during the most recent school year. Together, they were educating 7,923 children and taking in roughly $87 million from vouchers offered by the state.
Atlas Preparatory Academy in Milwaukee was a 100% school in my city that had low test scores and declining enrollment while also receiving more than $4.3 million in voucher money for 357 students in grades K-12. It was one of the first schools I dug into, and immediately some of the facts I unearthed in public documents made me curious.
There was, for instance, the money being made by its board chair, who also appeared to serve as a school administrator. His compensation was more than $150,000 in 2024.
This dual role would be prohibited at a traditional public school in Wisconsin, though there are no such rules for private schools.
In another transaction that would raise alarm in a public school setting, the same board chair’s accounting firm received tens of thousands of dollars from the school for accounting and consulting.
During my reporting, it became clear that the school’s operations were not only discordant with public school policies but with basic governing standards for nonprofits, experts told me.
More than a decade ago, a Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction research paper on what it called “choice schools” asked: “When is a private school really a public school?”
Though that question still resonates today, public officials supporting vouchers have yet to provide a clear answer.
Nor has there been any progress in Wisconsin or elsewhere in lining up the standards of private and public schools on a range of issues, even with the spectacular growth of private schools funded by taxpayer dollars.
Voucher schools, for instance, are not required to serve all children with disabilities. Public schools are.
Another major difference is transparency. In Wisconsin and elsewhere, information about public schools — good, bad or mundane — can be gleaned through open meetings, district YouTube channels and robust websites with detailed agendas, minutes, reports, statistics and information about enrollment, curriculum, special education services and more.
Districts have to abide by Wisconsin’s open records law, meaning that reams of records are available to anyone who formally requests them. Not so for the private schools. Voucher schools must, by law, have at least two opportunities a year for parents to meet with the governing board. But the schools do not have to make those meetings accessible to the general public.
In many states, private schools also don’t have to administer standardized tests or report those scores — in sharp contrast to the mandates for public schools. Wisconsin is different because it does require both students using vouchers and public school students to be tested, though parents can and do opt out.
In recent years, Atlas Prep has fared poorly on the state’s report card for schools, garnering the lowest rating: “fails to meet expectations,” or one star out of a possible five.
Not far from Atlas, Bay View High School, a public school, also has earned only one star on the state report card. Its website connects the public to the school’s improvement plan — its strategy to reduce dropouts and improve school culture — as well as information about local school council meetings and discipline methods, and about its science, technology, engineering, arts and math programming.
The Atlas Prep website includes a tab labeled “Build Your Own Curriculum.” When you click on it, nothing loads.
Though every student at the 100% schools we looked at relies on public funds for tuition, the money does not necessarily make up the institution’s total budget. The schools can take in additional revenue from investments, fundraising, grants or other means, but they are heavily dependent on tax dollars to maintain operations.
“If the choice schools are really some kind of quasi-public schools, then in keeping with national efforts to turnaround struggling schools, it may be necessary to subject low-performing choice schools to financial sanctions, turnaround efforts or even closure,” the state Department of Public Instruction suggested in its research paper.
That was back in 2011. Those types of accountability measures still do not exist.
Some key financial documents are available, however, for Wisconsin voucher schools — if you know where to look.
Annual IRS information filings for many nonprofit schools are easily obtainable through ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer page. And independent financial audits, required by the state, are available through the state Department of Public Instruction. I requested those for a handful of Wisconsin’s 100% schools, and I visited four.
One warm day in June, I stood in the lobby of one such school in Milwaukee, near a large fish tank. I’d sought days earlier to contact the woman running the school. An audit showed she was paying her own company rent for the building ($128,000 in one recent year). She put me off. “I’m not interested, ma’am,” she said via a phone in the foyer. “Please do not call us back again.”
On the other side of town, I rang the bell at Atlas Prep’s high school building and asked to speak to the executive director, Michelle Lukacs. I was informed she was headed to a meeting and could not speak with me.
By then, I was digging into Atlas’ finances, a process that would last several weeks and continue into July.
Over multiple emails, I shared with Lukacs what I was learning, including the compensation of the board chair, Steven E. Menden. A licensed certified public accountant, Menden had compiled the school’s IRS filing since its formation in 2001.
At times since then, Menden has been listed on the school’s website as “board advisor.” His daughter, Kaitlyn Menden, was also among the school’s most highly compensated employees in 2024. Her package was $127,674 in salary and benefits for a job in “business services.” (In an email to me, she described her role as wearing “many hats” beyond that, citing human resources duties, “oversight of the school’s technology hardware and cloud resources” and “special projects.”)
In the past couple of years, records show, Steven Menden has taken on the role of board chairman. The fiscal year 2025 IRS form showed Menden putting in a 40-hour workweek for Atlas and earning $132,505 in pay plus $19,916 in additional benefits. What’s more, his accounting firm, Menden & Associates, had an $87,250 contract.
At Atlas Prep, the school’s executive director also serves on the board that oversees the director job. At a public school, these dual roles would not be allowed, but that restriction doesn’t apply to Atlas, even though it depends on public money. Caleb Alvarado for ProPublica
Lukacs defended the school’s compensation practices, noting in an email: “Every person on our team, regardless of their role, earns their compensation and is not overpaid.”
She explained that Menden is not compensated for his board service but for “Executive Management Services.”
It would be forbidden for a public school board member in Wisconsin to also have a district management job under a legal doctrine regarding roles that are “incompatible.”
“In essence, one cannot supervise oneself, which would include hiring and firing and disciplining oneself,” said Dan Rossmiller, executive director of the Wisconsin Association of School Boards.
State law governing public officials also prohibits school board members from having a private interest in any contract over $15,000 that they bid for, vote on, negotiate or participate in. Violators can be charged with a low-level felony. There is no similar law that pertains to private school operators in Wisconsin.
In an email to me, Menden explained how the Atlas board handles potential conflicts of interest.
“Any conflicts of interest for either related or unrelated parties are resolved in favor of Atlas Preparatory Academy as outlined in our IRS mandated Conflict of Interest Policy,” he wrote. “This means that conflicted persons recuse themselves from the situation and do not vote or participate and the final decision that is made is strictly in the best financial interest of the school.”
This organizational structure does not comport with best practices for the governance of a nonprofit organization, experts told me.
“Board members are volunteers, and best practice is unambiguous that they should not simultaneously hold paid staff positions at the school they oversee — doing so collapses the separation between governance and management that gives a board its purpose in the first place,” said Chelsea Cross, a vice president at City Forward Collective in Milwaukee.
City Forward is a nonprofit group that champions high-quality school options for students and has been critical of the performance of the Milwaukee Public Schools.
Atlas Prep’s IRS filing indicated that Lukacs, the full-time executive director, earned $175,000 in salary and benefits and also had a board position. A third board member is listed as working only one hour a week for no pay.
In a public school setting, Lukacs’ situation would be akin to a district superintendent also sitting on the school board — an arrangement that would raise issues over proper checks and balances since superintendents typically are hired by and report to the school board.
Said Cross: “With 2/3 of its governing board also on the payroll — including the very executive the board exists to evaluate — Atlas Prep’s board cannot meaningfully hold its own leadership accountable.”
Lukacs disagreed with that assessment. “This is a false statement,” she wrote in an email, saying that Atlas board members “model strong personal leadership showing integrity, confidence and consistency in their actions and decision making.”
She told me she does not vote to approve her own salary “or vote in any other situation where a conflict of interest exists.” And she noted that countless hours have been invested at Atlas Prep in improving curriculum and student support. “While our standardized test scores do not yet reflect the level of achievement we aspire to, our staff has remained steadfast in its commitment to continuous improvement,” she wrote.
I had asked Atlas Prep twice for a copy of the school’s conflict of interest policy, which Menden had mentioned. As of mid-August, I had not received it.
I also requested a copy of the school’s contract with Menden’s accounting firm. I did not receive that either.
At a public school, such contracts would be subject to open record laws. I easily found a link on the Milwaukee Public Schools website to a decade’s worth of contracts for school nurses, mental health services, fitness instructors, interpreters, color printers, portable toilets, busing, professional development and so on.
But Atlas does not post those records online. It doesn’t have to.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Radio talk host Lee Elci’s challenge of Martha Marx is complicated
description: Conservative talk radio host Lee Elci was nominated to run for CT Senate against Sen. Martha Marx. But Marx wants equal time on the air.
text:
The state Senate campaign of conservative talk radio host Lee Elci seemed like it might be headed to an early end Monday after his liberal and loquacious Democratic opponent, Sen. Martha Marx of New London, demanded equal time on his station under longstanding FCC rules.
Elci accepted the Republican nomination on Aug. 9. If he wants to keep his weekday gig from 6 to 10 a.m. on WJJF, an FM radio station branded as Fox News 94.9, Marx said the choice is obvious: Take him off the air, or give her four hours to share a world view that is anathema to Fox News listeners.
“I have the gift of gab. I’ve had the gift since I was 1. I love to talk,” said Marx, a nurse and union leader who flipped an open Republican seat four years ago in the 20th Senate District that covers eight communities. “Who knows? I just might find my new calling.”
Elci said at midday Monday he expected to resolve his campaign’s uncertain status by day’s end Monday.  But nothing was resolved, other than Elci knowing he would not be back behind the microphone Tuesday.
“I got lawyers talking to lawyers. They’re just trying to work it out so I can stay on the air,” Elci said.

State Senator Martha Marx, D-New London, speaks during a press conference organized by members of the Connecticut Tenants Union at the Legislative Office Building in Hartford on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Marx’s campaign’s formal demand for equal time was first reported by The Day of New London. The station’s initial response was to take Elci off the air Monday while lawyers considered the ramifications. It was a rare day off for Elci, who’s been on 94.9 for 16 years.
“I don’t even take vacations,” Elci said. “You know, my dog died, I took a few days off. My mother died, I took a few days off. You know, my dad died, I worked that day.”
Elci clarified that was a nod to his father’s work ethic, not a disregard for his passing.
“That was, you know, me paying tribute to him. I don’t take days off,” Elci said. “I love what I do. And it’s killing me. This is not fun. And I know it’s done on purpose, so that’s adding to my angst, adding to my aggravation.”
The push to make Elci choose between running or radio most assuredly is being done on purpose. 
Marx’s campaign manager, Anna Reiter, put WJJF and its ownership on notice in a letter sent by certified mail on Aug. 13, four days after Elci filed a form creating his campaign committee and three days after a GOP vacancy committee notified the secretary of the state he was their new nominee.
Marx said her demand should have been anticipated, based on the Federal Communications Act of 1934, FCC regulations and ample precedent cited by Reiter, including television stations’ reluctance to broadcast “Bedtime for Bonzo” while Ronald Reagan, its co-star, was running for president.
“He has the same disease as Trump does,” Marx said of Elci. “He thinks he is above the law.”
By regulation, the FCC says, “no station licensee is required to permit the use of its facilities by any legally qualified candidate for public office, but if any licensee shall permit any such candidate to use its facilities, it shall afford equal opportunities to all other candidates for that office.”
When Republicans filed papers on Aug. 10 certifying a vacancy committee had chosen him as the new nominee, Elci became a “legally qualified candidate,” opening the door for the equal time claim by Marx.
If the radio station opted for equal time, the FCC regulations say, “Such licensee shall have no power of censorship over the material broadcast by any such candidate.” In other words, Marx would have no limits.
Marx said she never has been on The Lee Elci Show. She calls the content “hateful,” “misogynistic” and a bit tiresome, least to her ears. She says a running joke about Elci’s desire to end Marxism in the General Assembly has gone stale.
“I have a hard time listening to that show,” Marx said.
Marx was elected in 2022 with 52% of the vote and reelected in 2025 with 55%.
Elci, 60, who lives in East Lyme and was an unaffiliated voter until recently, is a former minor-league baseball player who played in 1988 and 1989 in the St. Louis Cardinals’ farm system as a catcher, outfielder and first baseman. He batted and threw from the right.
He said Monday he concluded after an initial talk with his station’s management that he could run and stay on the air as long as he did not talk about his candidacy or Marx. He believes the station can accommodate the equal-time requirement, but he faces another potential hurdle:
His remaining on the air could be considered an in-kind contribution by the radio station to his campaign, a potential violation of state election law for a candidate who intends to participate in the state’s public financing program. Elci said the station lawyers were seeking clarification from elections enforcement officials.
“Big picture is I wouldn’t want to put my station in jeopardy,” he said.
Elci said he needed less than a week to raise more than the $20,100 in small-dollar contributions necessary to qualify for public financing under the Citizens’ Election Program.
“So I think that’s why Marx is reacting the way she’s reacting, by being so overtly aggressive,” he said.
The nomination became open when Ronald J.  LaBonte of Salem, the Republican nominee, withdrew. Elci said he had thought about running for about six years.
“Honestly, I felt like I just wanted to do more and try to be more of a solution than what I was or am. And when this situation presented itself, I’m like, OK, and I talked to the ownership, and at the time, they were OK, and we moved forward,” Elci said. “You know, it’s going to be a tough year as it is to win.”
Then why run? He already has a significant outlet for expressing his views.
“I wanted to be an advocate for a lot of different things, and I felt like I kind of stalled out on the outside, so I wanted to jump in,” Elci said. “And that’s really it. I don’t have any other aspirations. I don’t have anything except just trying to do the right thing.”
Elci said the last few days have been an unwelcome education about the mechanics of running for office.
“I’ll be honest with you. I don’t know much about any of this,” Elci said. “Even though we talk about it all the time, I’m getting a whole different perspective on all this.”
Elci said the uncertainty — and being taken off the air for even a day — was misery. But he saw one upside, one his audience will hear about when he returns.
“No matter what happens,” he said, “I got a whole bunch of stuff to talk about.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Amid Trump administration silence, national Democrats hold ‘shadow’ hearing on fatal ICE shooting
description: Local leaders told Democratic members of Congress that the fatal U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shooting in Biddeford last month has left a lasting impact, with federal silence and inaction leaving the community to carry the burden. The members of the minority party convened the hearing to collect information with the hope of spurring accountabilit[...]
text:
U.S. Reps. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, Chellie Pingree of Maine and Katherine Clark Massachusetts question witnesses during a field hearing in Biddeford on Aug. 17, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Local leaders told Democratic members of Congress that the fatal U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shooting in Biddeford last month has left a lasting impact, with federal silence and inaction leaving the community to carry the burden.
The members of the minority party convened the hearing to collect information with the hope of spurring accountability, however the limits of Democratic oversight were underscored through demands for action that would require the cooperation of Republicans. 
ICE agents shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 in Biddeford. Thirty five days later, no video footage of the shooting has emerged. 
While the state Attorney General’s Office confirmed it is continuing to investigate, whether there is a federal investigation is unknown, according to the members of Congress who convened Monday’s hearing and the legal counsel for the victim’s family. 
“When you look at the course of history, sometimes there are events, we call them inflection points,” said Ben Gideon, legal representation for the Guerrero family. “This could serve as an inflection point going forward, and I very much hope that it does.”
Gideon and other witnesses testified on Monday about the events leading up to the fatal shooting and the fallout before the convening panel, composed of U.S. Reps. Chellie Pingree of Maine, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, and two members of the Homeland Security Committee, ranking member Bennie Thompson of Mississippi and Troy Carter of Louisiana.
“We will use what we’ve heard to investigate these operations and to demand answers and to hold this administration accountable,” Carter said, before referring to the upcoming midterm elections. “If not now, in four months.”
President Donald Trump launched a mass deportation effort when he started his second administration in 2025. Since then, with the help of congressional Republicans, he has passed a record $240 billion in immigration enforcement funding, so far. 
With a lack of subpoena power, Democrats do not have the ability to compel officials from the administration to testify. Instead, they’ve used this type of field hearing, also called a shadow hearing, to hear from willing witnesses. However, as Thompson put it on Monday, those hearings have so far been met with “crickets” from the GOP.
“I know this hearing cannot bring Johan Sebastián back,” Pingree said in her opening remarks, “but Congress has an obligation to make sure that his death is not dismissed as an unfortunate consequence of immigration enforcement, and that his life is remembered for the humanity and dignity and love that he embroidered.” 
Unanswered questions 
After the hearing, Attorney General Aaron Frey confirmed his office is continuing to actively investigate the shooting. Once it is complete and he has determined whether the evidence collected supports any action under Maine law, the entire file will be provided to the Maine Deadly Force Review Panel for review and recommendations to prevent this use of deadly force in the future, a statement from his office read. 
However, neither the office nor the panel may exercise jurisdiction over the practices of the Department of Homeland Security. “It will be the responsibility of either the federal administration or Congress to address any questions raised by such review,” the statement read. 
Every Democratic member of Congress requested information about the shooting in a letter to Homeland Security on July 15. They have not received a response, Thompson confirmed on Monday. 
Gideon told reporters that no federal agency has reached out to the family or wife, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, who heard the shots and soon after saw her husband’s body, which would be typical when such an investigation occurs. 
“As far as we can tell the federal government has chosen to turn a blind eye completely,” Gideon said. 
The state Attorney General’s Office has interviewed Rojas Alvarez. The car Guerrero was shot in has been turned over to that office as well, Gideon said. 
LaFountain said the city has not heard anything from federal agencies regarding the fatal shooting. 
“The authority was federal,” he said. “The burden has been local.” 
That burden included securing the aftermath of the shooting scene while also standing up mental health and crisis support, he said. 
“Our police, fire, public works, schools, and community organizations have been stretched ever since,” he said. “We secured the aftermath of a scene we were not permitted to investigate.”
Several of the roughly 250 people who attended the hearing, which included many state legislators and local officials, shared frustration with Maine Morning Star about the lack of communication between the federal government and state and local authorities. That included Kate Bauer Burke, a former lawyer from Kennebunkport, who said it was “appalling,” and another Kennebunkport resident Audrey Lakin, who said she attended the hearing in the hope of getting more first-hand information.
Gideon condemned the federal government for blaming the victims in shootings. 
At first, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told independent U.S. Sen. Angus King Guerrero “weaponized” his vehicle before being shot by an ICE agent, an explanation the agency has frequently used. But ICE later said he attempted to flee and “fearing for public safety” an agent shot him. But, ICE said Guerrero was not the target of the operation. 
The federal government has not said who the intended target of the operation was, but ICE has said its agents were responding to the address of a person with a final order of removal. 
During the hearing, Pingree pointed to reporting in the Washington Post that Guerrero had been driving a car owned by his roommate when he was shot. Neither Guerrero nor his roommate had final orders of removal, Pingree said. 
Sue Roche, executive director of Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project, said the organization has reviewed immigration documents provided by his family and confirmed that he had a pending asylum application and was authorized to work in this country.
The federal government has also not confirmed the name of the shooter. Throughout the hearing, the members of Congress frequently cited media reports about the background of the alleged shooter, which included accusations of domestic violence, as evidence of a lack of vetting by the federal agency. 
Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero Guerrero’s father, Omar Durán Plata (left) and mother, Dora Guerrero, traveled from Colombia for a hearing on the fatal shooting of their son in Biddeford on Aug. 17, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
Lasting impact
Traveling from Colombia for the hearing, Guerrero’s father, Omar Durán Plata, shared more about his son, while his mother, Dora Guerrero, sat beside, tears in her eyes. 
His son was responsible, honest and loving, he said, known for his big smile, kind heart, and for always being willing to help others. 
“We feel a deep pain in our souls when his little daughter, our three-year-old granddaughter, asks for her daddy and why he doesn’t come home from work,” Durán Plata said. 
Since the start of Trump’s second term, particularly in the wake of a large-scale operation in January, many immigrants and people of color in Maine have become fearful to leave their homes, go to work and drop their children off at school. 
“The arrest may take minutes, but the disruption takes months,” said Mufalo Chitam, Executive Director of the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition. 
She added, “ICE never left our state. As we speak, ICE is still picking [up] people.” 
People in Cumberland County have been detained outside court and at the airport in recent weeks, following a national trend of federal immigration authorities employing new tactics to boost arrest numbers. 
Demands
On behalf of Guerrero’s family, Gideon called on the Homeland Security Committee to immediately begin subpoenaing witnesses and documents to investigate the circumstances that led to the fatal shooting. 
However, Democrats are unable to do so on their own with Republicans in the majority. If Democrats flip the balance of power in November, Thompson told reporters he’d have “absolutely no problem with issuing subpoenas.”
Specifically, Gideon called for the committee to determine what policies allowed the agent who shot and killed him to have been deemed fit for hire, identify those responsible for hiring this agent and demand that they be held accountable. Gideon also urged the committee to determine what is behind the pattern of agents unlawfully shooting into motor vehicles and demand that the practice stop immediately. 
Further, Gideon said he intends to file a lawsuit against the U.S. government over the conduct of the officer’s shooting into a vehicle. 
Presente! Maine Executive Director Crystal Cron called on Congress to pass a pending bill from U.S. Reps. Delia Ramirez (D-IL) and Yvette Clarke (D-NY), called the “Melt ICE Act,” which would end funding for the Department of Homeland Security to detain and monitor immigrants, and redirect that funding toward wrap-around services, including housing and healthcare, for communities affected by immigration enforcement.
Public officials also reiterated their calls to fundamentally reform ICE, or if that is not possible, abolish it. 
“If Congress cannot hold ICE accountable, who can?” LaFountain asked the panel. Last month, he issued a formal proclamation calling for a transparent investigation and reform of the nation’s immigration system.
“Our state has taken action. Our city has tried to take action,” LaFountain said. “This is a federal problem that we need a federal solution for.”

name: VTDigger
title: Who gets to see themselves on a Vermont ballot?
description:
From a Tunbridge dairy farmer to a Montpelier immigrant, Vermont ballots have room for all kinds of stories.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Who gets to see themselves on a Vermont ballot?.
text:
This commentary is by Pelin Kohn, a student advising coordinator at the Community College of Vermont and second-term Montpelier city councilor. 
On July 29, I was at a community screening of “Man With a Plan,” John O’Brien’s film about Fred Tuttle. It’s a low-budget mockumentary about a retired Vermont farmer who runs for Congress. In a strange case of life imitating art, Tuttle actually won the 1998 Republican primary for U.S. Senate, though he declined to campaign seriously in the general election and endorsed the Democratic incumbent.
I loved the film, and the first time I saw it, I remember thinking that I wanted to bring it to Montpelier and watch it with my community. Four months later, I joined O’Brien and members of the film crew for a panel discussion. And now my own name was on a Vermont ballot.
Tuttle and I could hardly have come from more different Vermont stories. He was a dairy farmer from Tunbridge with deep roots in this state. I came to Vermont from Turkey in 2017 and later became an American citizen.
Still, I saw a little of myself in Tuttle.
He didn’t seem worried about whether he was the kind of person whom people expected to see on a ballot. I understood that.
On Aug. 11, 865 people voted for me in the Democratic primary for the Vermont House.
I finished third. And I am really glad I ran.
I knew from the beginning that it would be a challenging race. I was running against candidates with years of established relationships. But I thought voters should have a choice, and I believed I had something to offer.
The experience also made me think about my own path into political life in Vermont. Since coming here, I have been part of several political and leadership programs. I have met wonderful people, learned a lot, made friends and built relationships that I value. And many times, I was the only immigrant in the room.
I was grateful to be in those rooms. But I also know what it feels like to walk into a room and wonder if you quite belong there. Someone has to walk in first. Maybe that makes it a little easier for the next person.
I have spent nine years building my life in Vermont. I have worked here, raised my family here, volunteered, become an American citizen and been elected and reelected to the Montpelier City Council. I have had the privilege of serving twice as council president.
Still, this campaign made me realize something about myself that I hadn’t really put into words before. My gender is visible. My accent is audible. My name suggests I probably wasn’t born here. Who I am takes a little longer to know.
And 865 people took the time. They saw something in me, and they trusted me with their vote.

READ MORE

I think that is the part of this election I will remember most.
Vermont talks a lot about bringing new people here, keeping young people here and welcoming new families. I hope we also make room for those people to become part of our civic and political life. I hope some of the people who come here today become our school board members, selectboard members, city councilors and legislators tomorrow.
We need Vermonters whose families have been here for generations. We also need people who arrived yesterday, nine years ago or somewhere in between.
Tuttle’s Vermont story began long before mine did. But both are Vermont stories.
Since the election, I have received many texts, calls and emails that I wasn’t expecting. People thanked me for running. They thanked me for giving them another choice. Many thanked me for keeping the campaign positive. I have been touched by those messages.
Running gives people a choice. It puts another voice and another set of ideas into the conversation. You meet people you probably never would have met otherwise. You listen. You learn. And maybe somebody sees you doing it and starts wondering if they could do it, too.
I hope so.
I will continue my work on the Montpelier City Council. I will keep doing my best for the community I love. And someday there will be another person wondering if they belong in the room. Maybe another immigrant with an accent. Maybe someone without the expected political background. Maybe simply someone with an idea and a desire to serve who isn’t sure they are the kind of person who runs for office.
I hope they run. Because after this experience, the question I took from Fred Tuttle feels a little more personal:
Why are you running?
Why not?
