title: Citizens group gets temporary reprieve in Butte-Silver Bow data center lawsuit
description: A district court judge has issued a temporary pause on Butte-Silver Bow’s ability to retroactively change a deadline for a citizens group to gather signatures for an initiative that would put limits on data center construction.  A grassroots organization, 406 People First, received approval from the county election administrator for a proposed ballot initiat[...]
text:
Historic uptown Butte, Montana (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan).A district court judge has issued a temporary pause on Butte-Silver Bow’s ability to retroactively change a deadline for a citizens group to gather signatures for an initiative that would put limits on data center construction. 
A grassroots organization, 406 People First, received approval from the county election administrator for a proposed ballot initiative prohibiting “any necessary authorization to construct or expand any data center within the city-county” without approval from voters.
According to court documents, the organization was previously told by the county that it had until Aug. 14 to collect the 3,652 signatures needed to get on the ballot, but on Aug. 10, the elections administrator said the submission deadline was July 13 based on a new part of Montana law that was changed in 2025. 
406 People First argued in its court filing that in all communication with election administrator Cynthia Sherman, a July 13 date was never communicated, and in fact, Sherman had “unequivocally stated” Aug. 14 was the deadline. 
On Aug. 12, Judge Frank Joseph issued a temporary restraining order prohibiting the city-county from “destroying, returning, segregating, or refusing to count petition sheets; excluding signatures solely under the July 13 cutoff; treating Local Initiative 00-02 as finally rejected; or taking any action that would make certification or ballot placement impracticable.”
A hearing on a preliminary injunction for the suit will be held on Wednesday. 
Butte-Silver Bow is the second county to retroactively change the signature-gathering deadline for a local initiative about data center regulation that was already in progress. 
In Yellowstone County, the district court upheld a decision by the county to invalidate a similar initiative that would have required residents’ approval before data center construction. 
The decision came when the Yellowstone County Election Administrator issued a memo explaining state statute had changed. The law, enacted through Senate Bill 11, which passed unanimously through the 2025 Legislature, added requirements that signatures be submitted four weeks before ballot certification — certification is Thursday — and pushed the certification date 10 days earlier than in years past. 
“This statutory framework was reworked significantly in 2025 by the Montana Legislature and appears to have created a new timeline for certification and signature submission,” a memo from the county attorney’s office said.
Kassi Solberg, who was leading the initiative in Yellowstone County, had initially been told she had until Aug. 12 to gather more than 16,000 signatures, but under the new rule the county moved that date back to July, but after it the deadline had passed. 
According to the Bozeman Daily Chronicle, the county became aware of the updated statute after an attorney representing data center company Quantica Infrastructure reached out to the county. 
In Butte, the lawsuit argues that Sherman had already processed and “officially accepted” more signatures than was required, and the county should honor the original deadline given that the initiative was all but approved prior to the date change. 
The plaintiffs argue that if the court doesn’t intervene, the lost opportunity to “qualify and vote on an initiative is irreparable and cannot be adequately compensated.” 
In granting a temporary restraining order, the judge requires the county to “certify the ballot, send it to the Secretary of State, and take any additional steps necessary to ensure the imitative is placed on the November ballot” while further legal action is pending. 
406 Peoples First is being represented by Cottonwood Environmental Law Center.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Amid Mississippi health disparities, Jackson event offers Black men free screenings
description: On a hot summer day in downtown Jackson, over 60 people participated in the Black Men's Wellness Day 5k run and walk on Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026.
text:
Showing up to Black Men’s Wellness Day might have saved Joseph Holiday’s life, he said while attending the 5th annual event in Mississippi. 
Downtown Jackson was one stop on the national “Wellness Day Tour” hosted by the African American Male Wellness Agency, and local organizers said over 450 people joined this year’s celebration. Volunteers and vendors worked in the sweltering 90-degree heat, offering tests for blood glucose and cholesterol levels, eye exams and education about prostate and colon cancers. Holiday, a first-time attendee, took full advantage of the free health screenings, especially the one for kidney disease.
“I’ve discovered that I have high numbers for my kidneys,” he said, referring to elevated protein levels that can indicate kidney damage. Holiday said he plans to go see the doctor right away — a big shift for someone with a self-described phobia of medical providers.
“My grandmother died from medical malpractice,” he told Mississippi Today, which contributed to his distrust of the healthcare system. “I needed to come out here so I could get away from self-therapy alone and really just take a chance with letting professional people aid me in my health.”
By completing all the screenings, Holiday got a T-shirt promoting “Wellness for everybody,” and actionable information for his own. 
Joseph Holiday, a New Orleans native who now lives in Jackson, completed several health screenings at the 2026 Black Men’s Wellness Day. Credit: Anna Hu / Mississippi Today
Organizers wanted the fair to reach people who otherwise wouldn’t have gotten checked out, said Allan Cole, a marketing executive and co-coordinator of the Jackson event along with Dr. Timothy Norris, a licensed professional counselor. Cole said the wellness day was held on a Saturday so people wouldn’t need to take off work to join, and to be a “family affair.” 
“The challenge with getting men to the doctor is that men don’t like to go to the doctor,” Cole said. “It’s usually a family member, a loved one that will encourage (them).” 
Justin Turner, an assistant professor at the University of Mississippi’s School of Medicine and a member of the planning committee, encouraged attendees to get checked out early, noting that Mississippi has the highest rate of preventable deaths in the country. The Mississippi State Department of Health reported in 2022 that Black Mississippians had a 14% higher rate of death due to heart-disease than white Mississippians, and the death rate for men in general was 63% higher than for women. 
Turner pointed to several reasons why men might not seek medical care, including lack of health insurance and distrust in the healthcare system. A 2022 report from the Pew Research Center found that 55% of Black Americans had faced negative experiences at the doctor, including having their pain dismissed. Research shows that medical mistrust leads to delays in getting healthcare.
There’s also a mental aspect, Turner added. 
“A lot of men feel like they want to be in control of their life,” he said. “So if they find out they have some type of health condition, now they feel vulnerable and they lose control.”
Petrina Smith, a retired nurse practitioner, prepares to take a blood sample from a Black Men’s Wellness Day volunteer on Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026.  Credit: Anna Hu / Mississippi Today
Turner said he spoke to one man whose screening showed a blood-sugar level above 600 mg/dL, over three times the healthy level, and explained why that was concerning even though the man said he “felt fine.”
“An event like this, in a community center, provides a safe space for men to let their guard down, let their pride down,” he said, over the sounds of a DJ playing upbeat music and a game of double dutch. He said the health fair was one tool to help reverse Mississippi’s status as having among the lowest life expectancies in the nation. 
“Mississippi does not have to be last in healthcare,” he said. Referring to national statistics, he added, “And our Black men in particular die five to seven years younger than white men.”
Friendship through a 5K race
In addition to the health screenings, a central component of each wellness day is the 5k walk or run. Dozens of participants took a twisting route through downtown streets to start and finish at the park, running the last blocks with Mississippi’s Old Capitol building at their back. 
That’s where Will McDowell and Nikitna Barnes each made a new friend in each other. Looking at them chatting, an observer might not guess they had met just hours before. They showed up in nearly matching outfits, with black rimmed glasses, white athletic gear and silver jewelry. 
Will McDowell, left, and Nikitna Barnes, right, ran together during the home stretch of the 2026 Black Men’s Wellness Day 5k on Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026.  Credit: Anna Hu / Mississippi Today
McDowell, who is retired from his IT role with the City of Jackson, has run the 5k every year since Black Men’s Wellness Day came to Jackson. For Barnes, who works for the Mississippi Community College Board, it was her first time at the event and her first 5k after getting a double knee replacement surgery years ago. 
She was rounding the home stretch, near the Mississippi Museum of Art, when she saw McDowell alternating between a walk and a jog. Barnes told him, “I’m rolling with you,” and the two formed a team.
“I said, ‘Well, great.’ ‘Cause I was about to give up,” McDowell recounted. “And I said, ‘the Lord sent you to me.’”
He did several of the screenings after crossing the finish line, but much of it wasn’t a surprise. 
“I’m one of those guys that know his numbers,” McDowell said. “On top of my health, I have three sons, and I want to be around for my sons.”
Barnes said she’s seen men taking pride in not going to the doctor
“Hate is a strong word,” she said. “But I hate that they take their health for granted. It’s okay to be tough and take care of yourself at the same time.”
“You’re right, man,” McDowell said, nodding beside her. “You’re right.”
This story was produced with support from the Sarah Yelena Haselhorst Fund for Health Journalism.

title: Hagley’s New CEO Sees Museum as a Place to Discover What Is Possible

text:
Image: Hillary Olson comes to Hagley Museum and Library with nearly 30 years of experience working in natural and cultural history museums, science centers and planetariums. Photos courtesy of Hagley Museum and Library and image created using AI on 8/17/26
Museum innovator Hillary Olson plans to invite employees, visitors, educators and the wider community to help shape Hagley’s future
WILMINGTON — For Hillary Olson, Hagley Museum and Library is more than a place to study what inventors and business leaders accomplished in the past. It is a place where a child, family or researcher can begin imagining what might be possible in the future.
Olson, who became Hagley’s CEO in July, wants to build on that sense of inspiration and discovery as the museum prepares for its next era.
Hagley is now in the fifth and final year of its current five-year strategic plan, which will conclude at the end of 2026. In 2027, Hagley will begin developing its next strategic plan through a collaborative process involving employees, volunteers, board members, visitors, educators, community organizations and other stakeholders.
The new plan has not yet been written. Input gathered during the 2027 planning process will help establish Hagley’s priorities and direction for the years ahead.
“In any strategic planning process I’m a part of, when we say that we’re engaging our stakeholders, it’s not just our board, it’s not just our members,” Olson said. “It is people who don’t visit, because it’s a great time to find out why.”
The effort will consider how Hagley can reach more people, strengthen its educational programs, expand community partnerships and maintain its historic property for future generations.
“I can tell you that it will probably be a visitor-focused strategic plan,” Olson said.
Visitors will be broadly defined to include families, students, museum guests, scholars and researchers who use Hagley’s library.
A career built around museums and stories
Olson comes to Hagley with nearly 30 years of experience working in natural and cultural history museums, science centers and planetariums.
Her original academic background is in astronomy and geology. She later returned to school and earned a master’s degree in museum leadership, bringing together her interest in science with a passion for helping museums tell stories in engaging and understandable ways.
Before joining Hagley, Olson served as president and CEO of the Rochester Museum and Science Center in New York. There, she led an organization with three sites and more than 1.2 million collection objects. Her work included strategic and master planning, capital improvements, fundraising and building relationships with regional communities.
Olson said her passion is helping people engage with authentic artifacts, documents and historic places in ways that encourage them to see history, science and culture differently.
A museum visit, she said, should do more than present facts. It should give visitors an opportunity to encounter an object, understand how it was used and consider what they might create or improve themselves.
That focus on storytelling and discovery made Hagley especially appealing.
Olson had visited Hagley when she lived in Philadelphia and later returned with her young children. She remembered the powder yards, exhibitions and setting along the Brandywine.
When she learned the CEO position was available, she began studying the museum, its library, finances and programs. She was drawn to the complexity of an institution that combines industrial and business history, science, technology, horticulture, historic preservation and public education.
“I saw the wonderful complexity of it all, which is something that I’m drawn to,” Olson said.
Hagley’s board also helped persuade her to take the position. She said its members are open to change and new initiatives while remaining committed to protecting Hagley for future generations.
Inspiration built into the property
Hagley occupies 235 acres along the Brandywine and includes the site of the gunpowder works founded by E.I. du Pont in 1802. Its working machinery, millrace, historic homes, gardens, museum artifacts and collections, and business history archives allow visitors to encounter history through objects and experiences.
Olson sees those resources as tools for inspiring people to ask how things work, how they can be improved and what problems they might solve.
“The historic gunpowder yard is full of STEM,” she said. “It’s an engineering endeavor.”
Visitors can watch water turn machinery installed during the 19th century. They can study small patent models created to demonstrate inventions and improvements. They can also see how science, mathematics and engineering helped transform a gunpowder operation into the foundation of a major American company.
Olson said innovation does not always require creating something entirely new. Frequently, it begins by improving something that already exists.
“You’re not just inventing the wheel; you’re improving the wheel,” she said.
That message could be particularly valuable for children who may not yet think of themselves as scientists, engineers or inventors.
During Hagley’s gunpowder demonstrations, the sound of a small explosion immediately captures people’s attention. Olson said that excitement creates an opening to ask how people solved difficult problems hundreds of years ago — and what problems today’s students might one day solve.
“What are you going to figure out, fourth grader, in your life?” Olson said. “What is the problem that you’re going to solve?”
Bringing classroom lessons to life
Expanding school partnerships is expected to be an important part of Hagley’s planning.
Olson wants the museum to speak directly with teachers about their curriculum requirements and develop field trips that support what students are learning in school. Hagley guides create programs using the working equipment in the powder yards to demonstrate technology concepts that can be difficult to understand from a textbook.
Hagley also offers opportunities involving history, social studies, horticulture, and science. Its DuPont Discovery Loft includes current technologies like 3D printers and space for hands-on STEM activities.
Olson described the goal as providing “hands-on, minds-on” experiences that offer something beyond what children can receive in a classroom.
The programs must be educationally useful because teachers often need to demonstrate that a field trip meets curriculum standards before a school can approve the cost.
Hagley will also expand fundraising to provide free or subsidized field trips for students from underserved communities. Olson said access to transportation and admission should not prevent students from experiencing the museum’s resources.
Expanding partnerships with community organizations could help Hagley reach new audiences while also bringing in expertise and connection, meeting the needs of community members in setting rooted in the history of innovation.
Asking the community what it needs
Olson began listening immediately upon arriving at Hagley.
During her first several days, she sent a survey to the museum and library’s more than 150 full- and part-time employees. She asked what they wanted her to understand about their jobs, what they believed Hagley was doing well and what opportunities they saw for its future.
The responses reflected considerable pride in Hagley and its mission, as well as an interest in more collaboration and connection with each other.
That internal conversation is expected to grow into a broader community discussion when Hagley begins developing the new strategic plan in 2027.
Olson said outreach should include people who attend Hagley’s popular events, families who visit its museum and gardens, teachers who bring students and scholars who travel to Delaware to use the library. It should also reach residents who live in the region but have never visited.
Their absence, she said, is itself valuable information. Hagley must understand whether people are unfamiliar with its programs, do not see something that speaks to their interests or face practical barriers to visiting.
The objective is to make Hagley welcoming and relevant to more people while staying true to its strong connection to northern Delaware.
Local roots and a wider reach
Olson believes Hagley can remain a community institution while attracting more visitors from the broader region.
Its museum audience is largely local, but its library already has a national and international reputation. Scholars travel from around the world to examine its collections of business records, advertising materials and other primary-source documents. Some researchers visit for a few hours, while others remain on campus for months.
Olson sees an opportunity to expand the museum’s regional reach and impact, introducing Hagley to new visitors and people who are traveling to the Brandywine Valley.
But expanding Hagley’s audience will not mean leaving the local community behind.
“Serving the people in the immediate community is step one,” Olson said.
Preserving a complicated historic site
Hagley’s future also depends on maintaining the property that makes its educational mission possible.
Historic buildings, waterways and working machinery require specialized skills and regular investment. Hagley must address rising costs while raising money for capital improvements, operations and educational programs.
The 2027 planning process is expected to examine philanthropic support as well as earned revenue from admissions, memberships and programs.
Olson said Hagley benefits from long-serving employees, dedicated volunteers, support from members of the du Pont family and many other donors, and a board willing to consider change while protecting the institution’s legacy.
That balance — preserving the past while encouraging discovery — helped attract her to Hagley.
Few institutions bring together industrial history, science, a dynamic library and archive, gardens, historic homes and hands-on education in one place. Olson believes those resources can be used to inspire more people to understand how earlier generations solved problems and to imagine what they might make possible themselves.
The answers will come not only from Hagley’s leadership. They will also come from the employees who care for its collections, the teachers seeking new ways to reach students, the families and guests who use its grounds, and the community that surrounds it.
At a glance

What: Hagley Museum and Library’s next strategic planning process
When: Hagley is in the final year of its current five-year strategic plan, which concludes at the end of 2026. Development of the next plan will begin in 2027.
Who will participate: Hagley employees, volunteers, board members, donors and sponsors, visitors, educators, community partners, academics, researchers and people who do not currently visit
Likely areas of discussion: Visitor engagement, educational access, community partnerships, digital engagement, regional growth, fundraising, capital improvements and long-term sustainability
Central question: How can Hagley use its history, library, land and collections to help more people discover what they can create, improve or make possible?

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: 4th District GOP candidate Chris McGowan says US must be ‘prudent’ entering wars
description: Chris McGowan, the Republican running for Iowa’s 4th Congressional District, said Monday he believes the federal government needs to be “extremely prudent” in deciding when to enter wars — though he declined to comment specifically on if the decision for the U.S. to enter into conflict with Iran met this definition. McGowan, the Siouxland Chamber […]
text:
Chris McGowan, the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce president and 4th District Republican candidate, delivered remarks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Chris McGowan, the Republican running for Iowa’s 4th Congressional District, said Monday he believes the federal government needs to be “extremely prudent” in deciding when to enter wars — though he declined to comment specifically on if the decision for the U.S. to enter into conflict with Iran met this definition.
McGowan, the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce president and a veteran, told the crowd gathered to listen to his speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox that five of his six children are currently serving in the U.S. military. He said his own experience as a former member of the Iowa Air National Guard and his children’s service makes the use of military force is a “critically important concern for me,” and something he would want to weigh in on if elected to Congress.

It is also a subject McGowan said he talked about with President Donald Trump after the president endorsed his campaign in February. McGowan said at the end of their conversation, he told Trump, “Sir, I believe the most seminal statement that you made in your 2024 inaugural address was the following: ‘We’re going to build the most powerful military the world has ever seen, and we’re going to judge our success not only by the wars we win, but perhaps more importantly by the wars we never get into.'”

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Monday was the third day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood
Democratic secretary of state candidate: Ryan Peterman

He also reflected on his experience meeting former President Ronald Reagan when he was 17 years old.
“President Reagan had a mantra — that mantra was peace through strength,” McGowan said. “I have every intention of following President Reagan’s mantra as it relates to the very conservative use of military force, and only when diplomacy and all other avenues have failed.”
Speaking with reporters, he said he believes Congress needs to “understand the gravity of the situation” for the U.S. military to enter a conflict — while acknowledging some information must be kept classified.
“I spent some time as an intelligence officer, and I get how important it is to protect that information,” he said. “But I do believe that there has to be a substantial threat, it has to be an imminent threat, and it has to justify the use of force after all diplomacy has failed.”
Though full-scale fighting has paused, the U.S. is currently in a war with Iran. A memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries to negotiate a larger peace deal expires Monday, and there does not appear to be a clear plan to end the war that began Feb. 28.
When asked if Iran meets his definition for presenting a substantial, imminent threat, McGowan said he does not have all the information Trump and military leaders had access to when they decided to enter the war and that they’ve shared with members of Congress since.
“I’m not a member of Congress,” McGowan said. “I don’t have access to all of the information that the administration and the Department of War have that they made the decision first with Midnight Hammer and subsequently with Epic Fury. I will say this: it’s critically important that members be briefed, especially on the Senate Armed Services and the House Armed Services Committees. And I would like nothing more than to see those bodies in concert with the Department of War and the administration, when these very important decisions are executed.”
The 4th Congressional District, covering much of northwest Iowa, is currently represented by U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra. Feenstra decided to not seek reelection in 2026, instead running as a Republican candidate for Iowa governor. Feenstra lost to candidate Zach Lahn in the GOP gubernatorial primary in June.
McGowan did not face a contested primary election to become the 4th District Republican nominee. In the general election, he faces Democrat Dave Dawson, a former state lawmaker. While several of Iowa’s congressional races are expected to be highly competitive in the midterms, the 4th District is considered a “solid Republican” seat by political forecasters.
The Republican candidate said he was committed to running a campaign “rooted in civil discourse.” He also said he plans to have a debate with Dawson ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
“I know that my opponent and I are going to disagree on the issues, and that’s okay,” McGowan said. “But we need to do that without being disagreeable. We need to elevate the conversation and be an example and role models to others.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Board of State Canvassers approves ballot language for money out of politics proposal
description: An effort to bar certain utilities and government contractors from making political contributions cleared its final major hurdle Monday, finalizing its language for the November ballot. After members of the Michigan Board of State Canvassers determined that Michiganders for Money Out of Politics had submitted enough valid signatures needed to make the ballot[...]
text:
Michiganders for Money Out of Politics submitted its signatures in Lansing to make the November 2026 ballot. May 27, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. An effort to bar certain utilities and government contractors from making political contributions cleared its final major hurdle Monday, finalizing its language for the November ballot.
After members of the Michigan Board of State Canvassers determined that Michiganders for Money Out of Politics had submitted enough valid signatures needed to make the ballot, the board convened once more to finalize the language voters will consider when casting their ballot.
While the board is made up of four members – two Republicans and two Democrats – canvasser Paul Cordes, a Republican, was not present at Monday’s meeting. Board Chair Richard Houskamp, a Republican, Vice Chair Mary Ellen Gurewitz and canvasser Heather Cummings, both Democrats, voted to approve the following ballot language:
“A PROPOSED INITIATED LAW TO PROHIBIT CAMPAIGN CONTRIBUTIONS FROM CERTAIN REGULATED UTILITIES AND GOVERNMENT CONTRACTORS AND APPLY CAMPAIGN FINANCE LAWS AND REGULATIONS TO ADDITIONAL TYPES OF POLITICAL COMMUNICATIONS 
“The proposal would:  

 Prohibit regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to these utilities/contractors from making direct or indirect campaign contributions to those who run for or hold offices that impact them.  
 Expand laws regulating spending on political communications, including those requiring disclosing donor information, to apply to communications clearly identifying candidates or ballot questions, even if they do not expressly advocate voting for/against them.  
 Expressly apply the law requiring disclosure of who paid for political communications to internet political communications.”

“We applaud the Board of State Canvassers’ vote today to maintain our initiative’s ballot language that more than half a million Michiganders signed to put before voters,” Christy McGillivray, co-chair of the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics Steering Committee, said in a statement. “Michiganders are ready to finally rein in pay-to-play politics and out-of-control political spending in Lansing this November. Our campaign is continuing to build momentum in every corner of our state and making sure voters turn out to vote yes on this game-changing initiative.”
The Board of State Canvassers determined the effort had gathered enough signatures to make the ballot at its July 24 meeting. After the board approves an initiative’s signatures, the Legislature has 40 days to accept or reject the proposal. If the Legislature does not take up the proposal, it is placed before voters in the general election.
The ballot initiative had been challenged from an opposition group, Protect MI Free Speech. A message seeking comment was left with the group’s spokesperson, John Selleck, but was not returned by the time of publication. This story will be updated when a response is received.

title: Federal judge tosses out DOJ lawsuit seeking Minnesota voter data
description: A federal judge on Monday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit seeking Minnesota voter rolls. The Department of Justice is now 0-23 in its effort to obtain voter information maintained by the states. The U.S. Department of Justice sued Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon in September over his refusal to hand over Minnesota’s voter registration […]
text:
Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon speaks Friday, Aug. 9, 2024 before a public accuracy test of voting equipment ahead of the primary election at the elections office at Dakota County Administration Center in Hastings, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)A federal judge on Monday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit seeking Minnesota voter rolls. The Department of Justice is now 0-23 in its effort to obtain voter information maintained by the states.
The U.S. Department of Justice sued Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon in September over his refusal to hand over Minnesota’s voter registration list, which includes voters’ names, birthdates, addresses and partial Social Security numbers. 
“Normally, when the Department of Justice under either or both political parties asks states for elections-related information, it’s very specific,” Simon told the Reformer in September. “Now we’re seeing huge and sweeping data requests for millions of Minnesotans and tens of millions of Americans in the eight affected states that we have never seen before, for purposes that are murky at best and that have caused a lot of suspicion and alarm across the country.”
President Donald Trump and his allies have falsely alleged widespread voter fraud dating back to Trump’s loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020.
“The government suggests it is permitted to use a civil action as a ‘fishing expedition,’” U.S. District Judge Katherine Menendez wrote in her order dismissing the case. “But an ordinary litigant isn’t allowed to seek discovery first and allege a claim later, and the federal government has no special privilege to do so either.”
Voter fraud is extremely rare. ProPublica reported on Friday that the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota subpoenaed 130 people as part of the Justice Department’s high-priority criminal investigation into illegal voting; only one has been referred for prosecution. 
The DOJ has shared voter information with the Department of Homeland Security, which sent agents to states, including Minnesota, to pursue voter fraud cases. Those agents demonstrated “a complete lack of understanding” of illegal voting investigations, assistant U.S. Attorney Joe Teirab — a former Republican candidate for Congress — wrote in an email obtained by ProPublica.
Federal judges in the following states have already tossed out similar cases: Michigan, Oregon, California, Maryland, Colorado, Wisconsin, Maine, Arizona, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, New Mexico, Illinois, New Jersey, Kentucky, Virginia, New York, New Hampshire, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, the District of Columbia, and Nevada.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas officials confident people on Medicaid expansion will retain health coverage
description: Arkansas Secretary of Human Services Janet Mann said Monday that she expects the more than 215,000 people on the state’s Medicaid expansion to retain some form of health coverage, despite the Trump administration’s moves to end the hybrid program. Mann told lawmakers she’s confident the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services will grant the […]
text:
Secretary Janet Mann (left) and Division of County Operations Director Mary Franklin (right) of the Arkansas Department of Human Services answer questions from the Arkansas Legislative Council’s Hospital, Medicaid, and Developmental Disabilities Study Subcommittee on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Secretary of Human Services Janet Mann said Monday that she expects the more than 215,000 people on the state’s Medicaid expansion to retain some form of health coverage, despite the Trump administration’s moves to end the hybrid program.
Mann told lawmakers she’s confident the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services will grant the state’s request for a two-year extension of the expansion, also known as Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me, or ARHOME. Arkansas sought the temporary reprieve after the Trump administration denied the request to extend the expansion through the end of 2031.
The state can transfer ARHOME enrollees to fee-for-service Medicaid coverage or managed care. Each option has several potential models to consider, and DHS officials are “making a pros and cons list for all of those scenarios,” Mann said.
“We are considering everything but ending the program,” she told the Arkansas Legislative Council’s Hospital, Medicaid, and Developmental Disabilities Study Subcommittee.
The majority-Republican Legislature is expected to take up the matter in the session starting in January.
If CMS does not give the state its requested two-year grace period, all ARHOME recipients can be moved to fee-for-service coverage Jan. 1, Mann said.
“That would be bumpy for the beneficiaries and fairly quick,” she said. “I think it would be disruptive, potentially, to providers and beneficiaries. I’m hoping to avoid a disruption.”
In 2013, Arkansas became the first Southern state to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. Nine states still have not taken this action.
Arkansas is also the first to use a hybrid expansion model that purchases private health insurance for low-income people with federal funds.
Switching to managed care would lower the 2.5% insurance premium tax DHS collects annually on the expansion population and uses to pay for the state’s share of Medicaid, Mann said, and switching to fee-for-service coverage would eliminate the tax revenue altogether.

Arkansas healthcare providers alarmed by potential end of state’s Medicaid expansion


Republican Rep. Les Eaves of Searcy asked if removing the Medicaid expansion population from private insurance coverage would change the prices of commercial insurance premiums. 
Mann said there would likely be “a disruption in the marketplace,” but she did not have specific examples and has requested input from the Arkansas Insurance Department.
Medical providers and experts have expressed concern about the added costs an already strained Arkansas healthcare system could face without the expansion.
Any changes to the Medicaid expansion program are likely to impact hospitals’ upper payment limit, which is the maximum amount of Medicaid reimbursement hospitals pay healthcare providers, Mann said.
Arkansas hospitals receive among the nation’s lowest reimbursement rates from both private and government-run insurers, but labor, equipment and administrative costs have increased in the past several years. Some hospitals have cut services to keep their doors open.
Health insurer Centene announced in July that it will stop participating in the state’s Medicaid expansion next year. The company’s decision was unrelated to CMS’ denial of the ARHOME extension.
The denial spawned from new guidance under last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act regarding budget neutrality, which requires ARHOME to not cost the federal government more than would be projected without the program, according to Mann’s letter to CMS earlier this month asking for a two-year extension.
Mann’s letter emphasized that DHS has been preparing to roll out new work requirements for the expansion population, another mandate put in place by the federal budget changes. Thousands are expected to lose coverage because of the mandate.
Arkansas has begun a ‘soft launch’ of Medicaid work requirements. What does that mean?

On July 1, DHS began checking to ensure that Medicaid recipients are in compliance with the upcoming requirements. The agency gives noncompliant Arkansans 30 days to comply or provide proof of eligibility for an exemption.
After the ALC subcommittee’s meeting Monday, American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network issued a statement in support of DHS’ request for a two-year extension.
“Access to health coverage results in earlier cancer diagnoses, when the disease is more treatable and less costly and cancer outcomes are improved,” the organization wrote. “Continuity of coverage is vital for cancer patients. We cannot let patients get caught in the middle of this renewal process and have their care taken from them.”

name: VTDigger
title: Accessible housing means dignity, not just ramps and doorways
description:
Housing that truly serves people with disabilities means safety, independence and a connection to community.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Accessible housing means dignity, not just ramps and doorways.
text:
Dear Editor,
I am writing to share what accessible housing truly means for someone living with a disability. I hope my perspective helps readers and legislators understand the importance of creating housing options that allow people like me to live safely, independently and with dignity and respect from everyone around me.
The home I live in now does not meet many of my accessibility needs. It is a multilevel building, which makes navigating the space difficult and sometimes unsafe. I also do not have an outdoor area where I can comfortably spend time enjoying fresh air or nature. These limitations affect my independence and my quality of life.
I live very close to many other people who do not always understand my disability. At times, this can lead to situations where I feel disrespected or not treated with the dignity every person deserves. When that happens, it can become frustrating and emotionally overwhelming. I do not want to have to become defensive or react strongly just to be heard or respected. I simply want to live in an environment where people treat one another with consideration and kindness.
What I hope for is not extravagant. It is simply a home that allows me to live a full and meaningful life.
A single-level home would make it much easier and safer for me to move around independently. Accessibility features such as an emergency pull cord would provide reassurance that help is available if I fall or experience a medical issue. In the bathroom, a shower with a built-in seat would provide stability and safety, removing the risk of a seat shifting while I am bathing.
Having access to outdoor space is also very important to me. I would love to have a yard with trees where I can enjoy nature, garden and allow a dog to run safely. Being able to step outside my home and sit peacefully without being surrounded by smoking or drinking would allow me to relax, listen to birds and experience the calm that nature provides.

READ MORE

Location also matters. Living in a place where I can easily access community events such as the farmers market or attend my church would allow me to participate more fully in my community. Right now, I often have to rely on support staff to get from place to place. If they are unavailable, I am sometimes unable to reach important destinations during the day.
Accessible housing is not just about ramps and doorways. It is about independence, safety, health and the ability to live a meaningful life within the community.
I hope our legislators will continue working toward housing solutions that truly meet the needs of people with disabilities. With thoughtful planning and investment, it is possible to create homes that allow individuals like me to thrive rather than simply get by.
Natalie SinkewSt. Albans, Vt.

name: Delaware
title: Ortega, Darby ask attorney general to investigate Wilmington towing practices
description: Officials cite 19,083 vehicle tows, incomplete financial records and questions about how cars are selected, held and disposed of WILMINGTON — A state representative and Wilmington City Council member are asking the Delaware Attorney General’s Office to investigate the city’s vehicle-towing and parking-debt collection practices, citing records they say raise[...]
text:
Image: State Rep. Josué Ortega and Councilwoman Shané Darby want the Delaware Department of Justice to use its authority to obtain records from the city and its towing contractor and independently examine the program.
Officials cite 19,083 vehicle tows, incomplete financial records and questions about how cars are selected, held and disposed of
WILMINGTON — A state representative and Wilmington City Council member are asking the Delaware Attorney General’s Office to investigate the city’s vehicle-towing and parking-debt collection practices, citing records they say raise questions about financial accountability, enforcement and the loss of residents’ vehicles.
State Rep. Josué Ortega and Councilwoman Shané Darby submitted the referral after reviewing city records covering 19,083 vehicles towed from fiscal years 2020 through 2025.
The officials are not alleging that any individual committed a crime or asking the attorney general to accept their conclusions. They want the Delaware Department of Justice to use its authority to obtain records from the city and its towing contractor and independently examine the program.
“The reason we are asking the attorney general to look at this is straightforward,” Ortega said. “Some of the questions raised by those records can be answered only by an office empowered to compel the city and its towing contractor to produce records that a member of the public cannot reach on their own.”
The Attorney General’s Office had not publicly announced whether it would open an investigation as of Monday.
Wilmington’s tow volume questioned
According to the referral, Wilmington towed more vehicles during the six-year period than all other Delaware municipalities that responded to related public-records requests combined.
The officials said Wilmington’s per-capita towing rate was roughly twice that of comparable Delaware cities.
They contrasted Wilmington’s system with Newark, which generally immobilizes vehicles for parking debt instead of towing them. Immobilization allows an owner to recover the vehicle after resolving the debt without the vehicle being immediately removed and impounded.
The figures and comparisons were presented by Ortega and Darby based on records obtained through Delaware’s Freedom of Information Act. They have not been independently audited by the Attorney General’s Office.
Questions about money collected
A central issue is whether the city can document how much parking debt it collects when a vehicle is towed.
According to the referral, an assistant city solicitor responded to a public-records request by saying the city “does not maintain records responsive to this request” when asked for the amount of ticket revenue collected through towing.
Ortega and Darby said the city’s reported revenue appears to account for a flat vehicle-release fee but does not separately identify payments toward the parking tickets that triggered the tow.
“Delawareans expect that when a government takes a person’s car, the records will show the debt that justified the tow,” Ortega said. “When those records cannot be produced, an independent look is warranted.”
Thousands of vehicles reportedly scrapped
About 29% of all vehicles towed during the period were scrapped rather than returned to their owners, according to the referral. Among vehicles towed specifically for parking debt, the figure was approximately 58%.
Under the city’s arrangement, the towing contractor retains proceeds from vehicles that are scrapped or resold, the officials said. The city then waives the underlying ticket debt when ownership is transferred to the contractor.
Ortega said towing itself is not evidence of misconduct but argued that government must be able to document what happened to a vehicle and the debt associated with it.
“Cities tow cars,” he said. “But how a city tows cars matters.”
Few appeals and no recorded owner victories
The referral also raises questions about the appeals process.
Of approximately 4,564 tows reviewed over an 18-month period, only 30 vehicle owners appealed, according to the officials. None of the records showed an appeal decided in favor of the owner.
Appeals are heard within the same city department responsible for ordering tows and collecting the debt, the referral said.
Darby said investigators should examine whether the process provides vehicle owners with a meaningful opportunity to challenge a tow.
“Why not one appeal is recorded as decided in an owner’s favor — those are questions that require access to records the council cannot reach on its own,” she said.
Uneven enforcement alleged
The officials also questioned how the city selects vehicles for enforcement.
More than 2,000 vehicles reportedly carried balances above the city’s threshold for booting, but only a small percentage were towed during any particular month. Some vehicles with the largest unpaid balances were apparently not targeted.
The referral does not conclude that the differences resulted from favoritism or intentional discrimination. It asks investigators to determine whether the city follows consistent criteria when choosing which eligible vehicles to boot or tow.
Vehicles held for years
Ortega and Darby identified 182 vehicles that were held for more than 180 days after the city ordered them towed under collection-related accounts.
Fifty-eight of those vehicles had no recorded release or final disposition, according to the referral. Some had reportedly remained in the records for more than five years.
The city identified five vehicles as having been disposed of through Justice of the Peace Court lien proceedings initiated by its towing contractor. However, the officials said the contractor’s operational records did not contain corresponding entries documenting a release, sale or other disposition.
One was a 1990 Lotus Esprit whose record reportedly contains only its towing date. The five vehicles had a combined estimated private-party value of at least $55,000 based on current published valuation guides, while the contractor’s records listed each with a zero balance, according to the referral.
Those valuations are estimates and do not establish the vehicles’ condition or value when they were towed.
Earlier review raised similar concerns
The referral contends that questions about Wilmington’s towing records predate the current contractor.
In 2018, an assistant city solicitor told AAA Mid-Atlantic that the city had never received vehicle-sale records from its towing contractor and said monthly reporting would begin.
AAA’s 2019 report examined 3,671 vehicles towed during a 15-month period. It found records of only 468 notices to owners and said 1,320 vehicles appeared never to have been released.
Although Wilmington has since changed towing contractors, Ortega and Darby contend that gaps in recordkeeping remain.
City did not respond before referral
The officials said they presented their questions to the city in July and gave the administration until Aug. 14 to respond or announce an audit. According to their release, the city did neither.
Darby sponsored a 2024 City Council resolution calling for a comprehensive audit of Wilmington’s towing and parking-enforcement practices. The administration declined to conduct it, she said.
Ortega previously worked in the city’s Office of Constituent Affairs from 2016 to 2021, where he said he handled complaints from residents about towing.
“This request is not adversarial to the city of Wilmington,” Darby said. “I represent the city. I want its systems to work fairly, uniformly and lawfully.”
The referral asks the attorney general to determine what the city collects when it tows a vehicle for parking debt, whether payments are reconciled with the underlying tickets, how enforcement targets are selected, whether appeals are handled fairly and what happens to vehicles that are not reclaimed.
At a Glance

What happened: State Rep. Josué Ortega and Wilmington Councilwoman Shané Darby asked the Delaware Attorney General’s Office to investigate Wilmington’s towing, impoundment and parking-debt practices.
Period examined: Fiscal years 2020 through 2025.
Vehicles involved: 19,083.
Vehicles reportedly scrapped: About 29% of all towed vehicles and approximately 58% of those towed for parking debt.
Appeals reviewed: Thirty appeals among roughly 4,564 tows during an 18-month period. None was recorded as decided for the vehicle owner.
Long-term impounds: The referral identifies 182 vehicles held longer than 180 days, including 58 with no recorded release or disposition.
What the officials want: An independent investigation with authority to obtain records from the city and its towing contractor.
What happens next: The Attorney General’s Office must decide whether to open an investigation. The referral itself does not establish wrongdoing.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming sage grouse slumped in 2026, as long-term trendline also points down
description:
Spring lek counts suggest numbers cyclically peaked in 2025 at a level that was 26% below the bird’s 2006 high, though other population metrics indicate more stability.
The post Wyoming sage grouse slumped in 2026, as long-term trendline also points down appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Biologists, wardens and volunteers who monitor sage grouse documented fewer males strutting this spring at their Wyoming leks. That cyclical downturn indicates that population highs keep falling for a sagebrush-dependent species that continues to fare poorly in its largest stronghold.
The 2026 decrease at leks — where birds gather to display and attract mates in the spring — was expected: Wyoming’s population cycles every nine years or so, and those swings are natural and part of basic sage grouse biology. More significantly, the slump downward signals that the statewide population topped out in 2025 at a level that was 26% below its 2006 peak and 15% below its 2016 peak. The trend line for these cycles points noticeably downward, and since the turn of the century the average number of male sage grouse gathered at active Wyoming leks has fallen from 29 to 23 birds, a roughly 20% drop. 
“The reality is, there’s fewer average number of males per active lek at each of the [cycle] peaks,” said Nyssa Whitford, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s sage grouse and sagebrush biologist. 
What exactly to make of the numbers is up for debate among experts. Some metrics — like lek counts during troughs in the cycle — look better for Wyoming sage grouse.
The average number of male sage grouse gathered at active Wyoming leks has fallen from 29 to 23 birds, a roughly 20% drop, since the turn of the century. (Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Yet other metrics signal sage grouse population declines over the last quarter century. Game and Fish tracks the “peak males” known to exist — it’s a measure of the highest number of males observed at all leks biologists surveyed, even if grouse counters made only a single visit. (Not all leks are visited, but the agency’s goal is to get to 90% of them annually.)
“This [declining] trend also holds true for peak males,” Whitford said. “There are fewer peak males on the landscape.” 
When the population cycle topped out in 2006, there were over 44,000 “peak males” observed statewide, according to Game and Fish data. The measure only slightly fell to 43,329 peak males by the high point of the next cycle in 2016. But surveys clocked a sharp drop in peak males observed during the 2025 high point with 31,123 birds observed, marking a 29% decline since 2006. 

A greater sage grouse hen with her brood. (Tom Koerner/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)

And the proportion of “active leks” — where at least one strutting male was seen — also continued to slide. The percentage of active leks hit 90.8% during the 2006 peak but fell to 82% in 2016 and 80.1% during the most recent peak in 2025. 
It’s no secret that sage grouse, which depend on the steadily degrading sagebrush ecosystem, are in a long-term decline across their range spanning 10 western states — they were recently extirpated from North Dakota. A 2021 U.S. Geological Survey report estimated an 81% decline in the species over the preceding 53 years. Wyoming remains a stronghold — home to nearly 40% of the estimated 200,000 to 500,000 birds still on the range. 
Short-term snapshot
During their spring surveys, lek count crews detected an average of 13% fewer sage grouse statewide compared to 2025. Wyoming used to divide its population into areas monitored by eight regional conservation groups, but Game and Fish dissolved those groups early this year. Now the state agency calls the regions “management areas,” Whitford said. Lek counts fell in all eight of them. 
Compared to 2025, the average number of male grouse decreased by 25% in southwest Wyoming, 13% in the Snake River Basin and 12% each in the Bighorn Basin, southcentral Wyoming and the Wind River Basin. Birds fared slightly better in northeast Wyoming (8% decline), Bates Hole/Shirley Basin (7% decline) and the Upper Green River Basin (5% decline).
(Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Northeast Wyoming, including the Powder River Basin, is the only area where sage grouse lek counts fell in 2025, too. Besides Jackson Hole’s tiny, isolated grouse population, that northeastern region is home to the smallest and most vulnerable groups of birds in Wyoming. Population cycles run slightly differently there, Whitford said, averaging closer to seven years peak to peak. 
Habitat loss from the nearly 180,000-acre House Draw Fire east of the Bighorns in Johnson County hasn’t helped their cause. The first year after the 2024 wildfire converted vast tracts of sagebrush to grassland, and counts of strutting males at 20 known leks within the fire scar fell by 40%. 
“In 2024, there were 136 peak males within the fire perimeter,” Whitford said of surveys before the area burned. “There were 29 peak males observed this year in the fire scar.” 
The 2025 House Draw Fire, pictured, reduced the number of active sage grouse leks from eight to three within the wildfire’s 180,000-acre footprint southeast of Buffalo. (Chris Kirol)
That’s a 79% decrease, explained by what appears to be the abandonment of lek sites where the sagebrush was scorched. The number of active leks fell from eight to three between 2025 and 2026, Whitford said. 
“The leks that are still active are closer to the edge,” she said. “We do see this lag effect with fires. The first year, the birds are really trying. Then the second year, I think they’re like, ‘No thank you.’” 
Sage grouse fared very differently in the Red Canyon Fire scar their first year dealing with habitat loss. That 2025 blaze in the Bighorn Basin burned in a mosaic-like pattern, and birds seem to be holding on better. There were eight active sage grouse leks in the Red Canyon Fire scar this spring, Whitford said, which is the same number as before the wildfire. Average lek counts have also held steady at 13 birds. 
“We’re really just not seeing much of an effect,” Whitford said.  
Deeper into the data
Retired Game and Fish sage grouse coordinator Tom Christiansen told WyoFile it’s important to note that long-term changes in Wyoming sage grouse metrics depend on the period being examined. 
“The key thing in all of these trendlines is when they start and when they end,” Christiansen said. “If you went back to 1995, the line would be flatter.”
For Christiansen, sage grouse population low points are more important than when the cycles are peaking. 
“You have to look at the valleys,” he said. “There’s no doubt that numbers of grouse over the long-term have gone down. The question is, have they gone down in the last 30 years?”
Wyoming Sage Grouse coordinator Tom Christiansen, who’s since retired, surveys leks in 2015. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr. / WyoFile)
The lowest sage grouse counts since the start of modern recordkeeping came in 1996, when there were an average of 12.5 males per active lek. The most recent 2013 and 2021 population troughs did not get this low, although they still slumped to 16.8, low enough for a former Game and Fish biologist to call the data “alarming.” 
Other sage grouse biologists don’t put a ton of weight into the average-males-per-active-lek measure that Wyoming uses to track its population. That metric “obscures the reality” and is “biased in both directions,” said Tom Remington, a former director of the Colorado Division of Wildlife.
“As populations increase, new leks form and by definition are small and so it tends to bring the average down of males per lek,” Remington said. “And as populations bottom, you’re left with the biggest leks. A lot of those peripheral leks that are transient go away, so those small numbers get taken out of the equation.” 
Remington’s take is that the total number of strutting grouse observed — the “peak males” metric — is the more important gauge of populations. By that measure, Wyoming sage grouse numbers have been more stable since the turn of the century.
There were 15,499 peak males observed during the 2002 trough, 18,274 observed during the 2013 trough and 16,316 counted during the most recent 2021 trough. 
There are likely a few years to go before Wyoming sage grouse numbers bottom out again. Based on the average nine-year cycle, the next nadir won’t come until 2029 or 2030. 
With vegetation sparse and parched from the warmest winter and sparsest spring snowpack on record, conditions aren’t looking especially good for sage grouse. 
“We have entered the downward portion of the cycle, and [the drought] is not going to help arrest that trend,” Whitford said. “The habitat is key.” 
Christiansen, who still helps with sage grouse lek counts in the Golden Triangle, home to the largest lek on the planet, echoed the observation. 
“They didn’t look good to me,” he said of conditions on the range. 
Wyoming wildlife managers will get a sense of how sage grouse chicks fared this year come the fall hunting season, which runs from Sept. 19-30. Hunters can help biologists determine the ratio of chicks to hens — a key measure of population productivity — by dropping wings in barrels distributed around sagebrush country.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: Methadone access expands in CT
description: WSHU's Ebong Udoma and CT Mirror's Calista Oetama discussed her article about a new initiative to help people get opioid use disorder treatment.
text:
Using methadone to detox from other opioids can come with stigma. One program is hoping to ease that.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Calista Oetama to discuss her article, “CT’s first state-funded methadone vans expand access to treatment,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read the story here.
WSHU: Hello, Calista. You say you decided to look into this as a follow-up to a story published two years ago by your colleague at the Connecticut Mirror, Andrew Brown. What was Andrew’s story about, and what was your follow-up here?
CO: So, my colleague Andrew Brown spent years covering the opioid crisis in Connecticut. In 2024, he published a story about the travel burdens faced by clients seeking methadone, which is considered the most effective medication for treating opioid use disorder. It’s a really tightly regulated substance, so people who seek it for opioid use disorder can only get it by going to a certified clinic in person. A couple of researchers from Yale and Virginia Tech found that a Connecticut resident traveling by car might have to drive 45 minutes one way to reach a clinic, while taking public transport might take three hours for some people. So if you work a nine-to-five or you’ve got to drop your kids off at school in the morning, it’s just not feasible. Even though this care is considered life-saving by many people. So Andy’s story was about that, and he mentioned at the end that Connecticut was planning to use $4 million taken from opioid settlement funds to develop these two big mobile units that can go to places with high overdose rates and less public transport to dispense methadone to people who might need it. Two years later, I was kind of wondering what happened to those vans, and I decided to reach out to a bunch of providers. They pointed me to the two organizations that were running the units, and it turns out the timing was great because one van launched last month, and the other, which I visited, will officially hit the road tomorrow.
WSHU: And that’s one that’s dedicated to the southeastern corner of Connecticut, correct?
CO: The one that just launched in July was dedicated to the southeast. The one I visited is dedicated to the northeast.
WSHU: Okay. Now let’s talk about the northeast. It’s a pretty rural area of the state, so transportation is a big issue. How have they been able to help out by having these vans out there?
CO: Well, my colleague and I visited the van over there. It took us an hour to get there from Hartford, and it was mostly like one straight road with a lot of forests and fields. It’s definitely hard to get around on a bus, and I could immediately see how hard it would be for people to travel there. So these vans, they’ll go to places like in northeastern Connecticut that have had like historically high rates of overdoses. They’ll park at a known location, and then people can come to receive their dose one by one. They just line up with the van in the front.
WSHU: So they put out a notice that they’re coming to the area, and how does that work?
CO: They advertise it through word of mouth, which is how they get most of their clients, and then they’ll put out a notice saying we’re going to be parked here. Please come if you need to.
WSHU: Okay, could you just tell us about the process itself? They try to explain that to you, right?
CO: So they basically kind of gave us a tour of the vans as we got there. So a client will enter from the back of the van. They’ll climb up a couple of steps to the receptionist’s office. They sign in with the nurse over there and then get their dose. They’ll take their dose and then they’ll move through the next part of the van. And if they need case management or counseling sessions, they can talk to people there and receive them if needed. It’s all pretty private. There are partitions everywhere, and there’s going to be noise machines so that people can’t eavesdrop on these conversations. And once everything’s done, they exit through a door on the side of the van. No worries about making contact with any other person other than the people staffing the van.
WSHU: And how often will the vans be out in these areas?
CO: They’ll be out Mondays through Fridays from 7 a.m. to 11 a.m. This is usually when people, you know, wake up, start working, or right before then.
WSHU: Okay. The other thing that I’m really curious about is the funding structure for this. How is it being funded, and can that be sustained?
CO: That’s a really good question. So Connecticut has received more than $185 million in opioid settlement funds, and the Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services has pledged about $4 million of those to outfit these two vans. So that’s like $2 million per van, which is quite expensive. The reason why they’re so expensive is that methadone is so tightly regulated. These units need to comply with a bunch of guidelines set by different state and federal agencies. There’s maintenance, gas, salaries, so it’s quite hefty in terms of both the size of these vans and the cost it takes to run them. I’ve talked to some of the providers, and they said that they definitely want this van to continue long-term, even when these opiate settlement funds stop funding the vans in 2027. They say they’ve accounted for this expense in their budgets, and they’re hoping that there will be enough people seeking these services to continue getting funding from other sources as well.
WSHU: Now, there’s also been some legislation that is pushing back against methadone treatment centers like these. Could you just tell us a little bit about the legislation that’s been in the works and some that have been passed that might affect the future of methadone clinics?
CO: One calls for the reversal of updated guidelines that initially expanded access during COVID, which was a time when I think lawmakers on both sides of the political spectrum realized just how deadly the opioid crisis was. This bill wants to reverse this expansion of treatment, and providers and advocates I spoke to said it’s unlikely to pass since bipartisan support for maintaining this current level of access- that you can get methadone prescribed to you if you go to a clinic or a methadone van- seems to remain quite strong.
But there’s another bill, also a bipartisan one, that wants to pull access in the opposite direction, making it even easier to get methadone. Right now, because methadone is a Schedule II controlled substance, you can prescribe methadone for pickup at a pharmacy, unlike other opioid use disorder medications like Buprenorphine or Naltrexone. But this bill wants to make direct pickup possible. Advocates I spoke to are quite in favor of this. They’re saying it’s going to normalize it even more and reduce stigma. But I think it is quite a big step to deregulate Methadone further, and providers seem a bit skeptical about how much support it will receive. So I’m really interested to see where that goes. It just seems like these two bills, despite being in their early stages, it’s clear that the issue of access is still getting a lot of attention.
WSHU: In the meantime, the methadone vans are trying to destigmatize the use of methadone.
CO: Absolutely.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Medical marijuana home cultivation licenses surge in South Dakota
description: A South Dakota Health Department official told lawmakers Monday that the number of medical marijuana patients in the state who are licensed to grow medical cannabis at home has grown by more than 1,000% over the past four years. Whitney Brunner, administrator of the state’s medical cannabis program, told the legislative Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee[...]
text:
A marijuana plant at the Dakota Herb grow operation near Tea, South Dakota. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota Health Department official told lawmakers Monday that the number of medical marijuana patients in the state who are licensed to grow medical cannabis at home has grown by more than 1,000% over the past four years.
Whitney Brunner, administrator of the state’s medical cannabis program, told the legislative Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee during a meeting at the Capitol in Pierre that the number of home cultivators grew from 61 in fiscal year 2022 to 715 in fiscal year 2026 — an increase of 1,072%. Medical marijuana has been legal in South Dakota since 2021, but recreational marijuana use remains prohibited.


Home cultivators may not grow more than two flowering cannabis plants and two non-flowering cannabis plants, according to state law.
Patients can add a home cultivation license to their medical marijuana card for $20. Applicants must submit a photo of the grow room, a photo of the lock on the door and a diagram of the grow location. Brunner said those diagrams are often hand-drawn and lack detail.
“The lack of regulation in this area is a bit concerning for us,” Brunner told lawmakers.
Brunner said she doesn’t want to assume home cultivators are abusing the licenses, but said the department is considering tighter regulation.
The feds have embraced medical marijuana. Now what?

“We have looked into if there is anything more that can be done, but I think that’s a greater conversation to be had,” Brunner said. “It does present some legal and safety considerations if we were to attempt to regulate this further.”
Brunner did not say if new regulation would require legislation. Committee member Sen. John Carley, R-Rapid City, told South Dakota Searchlight after the meeting that lawmakers hope to learn more.
“We were glad the department had more information,” Carley said. “Many of us will be looking at that exact item and will come back to that concern next meeting.”
The rise in home cultivation comes amid growth in the overall program. At the end of June, there were 19,375 medical marijuana cardholders in South Dakota — a 30.5% increase from 14,843 last fiscal year.
“We did experience a true spike in early fiscal year 2026 but, by fall, that number had started to level off,” Brunner said, adding that the number of cardholders in the state “remained fairly stable” most of the year.
Most cardholders are in their 30s and 40s, according to department data, and more than 70% report severe debilitating pain as a reason for their cannabis use.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Rental aid available in Louisiana for Tropical Storm Arthur damage
description: Affected renters, homeowners and students from Avoyelles, Lafourche, Pointe Coupee, St. Landry, St. Tammany and Terrebonne parishes are eligible to receive a temporary grant to pay for housing while their homes are repaired or rebuilt.
text:
A truck stands in water after Tropical Storm Arthur caused flooding in Avoyelles Parish in June 2026. (Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries)Federal rental assistance will be available to Louisiana residents who can’t live in their homes because of damage from Tropical Storm Arthur. The storm hit in late June, flooding areas in the central and southeastern parts of the state.
Gov. Jeff Landry’s Office of Homeland Security and Emergency Preparedness announced Monday the financial aid will be administered through the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Affected renters, homeowners and students from Avoyelles, Lafourche, Pointe Coupee, St. Landry, St. Tammany and Terrebonne parishes are eligible to receive a temporary grant to pay for housing while their homes are repaired or rebuilt.
The money can be used for rent, security deposits, water, gas and electric service. The grants don’t cover internet service, cable or transportation costs, nor does it cover the cost of home repairs or food assistance.
The initial grant covers one to two months of rent, a duration that FEMA will decide on a case-by-case basis according to the governor’s office. People who receive the initial grant will be able to apply for more funds, with up to three months of rent approved at a time.
Recipients must document how they used their initial grant to qualify for continued assistance.
Applicants can use the online portal at DisasterAssistance.gov, FEMA’s app and help line, 800-621-3362, or visit any FEMA disaster recovery center.
The two locations in Louisiana are at the Terrebonne Parish Main Library in Houma and the Innis Branch of the Pointe Coupee Parish Library.
Applications for FEMA rental assistance grants are open until Oct. 1.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Combined plea must be tossed after illegal search, NJ Supreme Court rules
description: A man must be allowed to withdraw his guilty plea to felony murder after an illegal search undercut his combined plea agreement, the state Supreme Court ruled Monday.
text:
A man must be allowed to withdraw his guilty plea to felony murder after an illegal search undercut his combined plea agreement, New Jersey Supreme Court Justice Rachel Wainer Apter wrote in a decision out Monday. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey’s Supreme Court tossed a man’s murder conviction after ruling a search that underpinned an armed robbery charge subject to the same plea agreement was illegal, but the court stopped short of extending the ruling to all defendants in the same position.
The justices ruled Jamar Myers, who was convicted for his role in a string of robberies targeting pharmacies and convenience stores — including one that turned fatal — must be allowed to withdraw his guilty plea because the state’s loss of incriminating evidence would have changed the parties’ bargaining positions in advance of his guilty plea.
The unanimous decision rejects prosecutors’ argument that tossing Myers’ murder conviction would prejudice them because they may not be able to marshal all the evidence they had against him in 2016 for a new trial in 2026.
“We are sympathetic to the State’s argument on prejudice. But in the specific circumstances of this case, we hold that defendant must be permitted to withdraw his felony murder guilty plea.’” Justice Rachel Wainer Apter wrote.
Myers was arrested in 2011 when, following a robbery at a Hamilton 7-Eleven, local police stopped a car occupied by him and two co-defendants.
A search of the vehicle turned up cash, a handgun, and clothing that matched that worn by assailants, including at a Trenton pharmacy robbery where a pharmacist was fatally shot while trying to disarm a robber a week earlier.
An officer had pulled the three over because he thought it was suspicious they they didn’t react to a spotlight used to illuminate the inside of their vehicle. Though the car had been reported stolen, the officer was unaware of that fact until after the traffic stop began.
The Supreme Court previously ruled that search was illegal, finding the officer who initiated it had no information about the suspects at the time of the stop aside from their sex and race.
The faulty search allowed Myers to withdraw his guilty plea for that 7-Eleven robbery, but because he had entered into single plea to resolve charges from multiple robberies, his other convictions spawned by that plea must be tossed as well, the court found.
Judges should encourage parties, when presiding over plea agreements that cover multiple indictments, to clarify their intentions on the record to avoid similar pitfalls, the high court said.

The Office of the Public Defender, which represented Myers, praised the decision and lauded the court for asking its criminal practice committee and Judge Michael Blee, the judiciary’s acting administrative director, to consider whether to make changes to plea forms.
The office encouraged the officials to consider adding a section clearly explaining the effect a successful appeal could have on a combined plea agreements.
“Providing that clarity at the outset would help ensure that all parties understand the potential impact of an appeal,” said Assistant Public Defender Alison Gifford.
